World.title: Here's what the NFL should put in the end zone instead of "End Racism"
World.content:
In case you missed it, the NFL will once again put "End Racism" & "Stop Hate" in the end zones, as well as allow social justice messages on helmets for the 2026 season. It's clearly virtue signaling that does nothing of substance. It was objectively a knee-jerk reaction to the woke wave of 2020. Instead of virtue signaling with statements about racism in a league that is predominately Black, I have a few "social justice" messages that would actually make a positive impact.



Before I share my suggestions, let me take you back to 2020.

The NFL first introduced "End Racism" in its end zones in 2020, following the nationwide race riots and destructive protests after the death of George Floyd and growing pressure from NFL players. On July 27, 2020, the league told teams that "End Racism" and "It Takes All of Us" would be stenciled in opposite end zones during Week 1 and home openers. They obviously framed the death of Floyd as racism and went along with a narrative that America and its police force, many of which helped keep teams and fans safe at every stadium around the country throughout the season, are racist. The NFL said the initiative was designed to show "how football and the NFL brings people together to work as one and use our example and our actions to help conquer racism." There you have it. They explained without a doubt that they believe racism is a major issue and it must be "conquered" through messaging in the end zones. I'm chuckling writing this.

NFL RESTARTS SOCIAL JUSTICE MESSAGING WHILE BATTLING DOMESTIC ABUSE, DRUNK DRIVING AND PROSTITUTION ARRESTS

Commissioner Roger Goodell subsequently confirmed that the social justice messaging was part of the league’s "Inspire Change" program, which was developed in consultation with players and the NFL Players Association. The move came shortly after Goodell acknowledged that the NFL had been "wrong" for not listening to players earlier regarding racism.



One of the best responses to all of this was from Barstool's PFT Commentator, who said, "I used to be racist as f--- until the NFL painted "End Racism" in the end zone." That was the perfect way to expose the nonsensical nature of the initiative. It was divisive and eye-roll inducing. The fact the league is still pushing this messaging is laughable, but if they really wanted to tackle issues facing our nation and the black community, here are a few messaging suggestions to replace "End Racism":

End Fatherlessness

Fatherlessness is an epidemic. There is a large number of children growing up without their biological father living in the home, and research consistently links the absence of a father in the home with disadvantages in education, behavior, economic stability and later-life outcomes. The NFL should lean into this because the issue is particularly pronounced among Black Americans.

A Congressional Research Service report found that 64% of African-American children lived apart from their biological fathers in 2012, compared with about one-third of children overall. Research on the Fragile Families data found that 51% of African-American fathers in the study had been incarcerated by the time their child was five, and children whose fathers had been incarcerated showed significantly more behavioral problems. These disadvantages can carry into school and eventually the workforce: studies have found paternal incarceration is associated with lower school readiness and educational outcomes, while research by American economist Raj Chetty and colleagues found that Black boys who grow up in communities with greater Black father presence have higher employment rates and are less likely to be incarcerated as adults. There are other factors that effect children in these communities, but the evidence suggests that having an involved father can be an important protective factor that improves a child's chances of succeeding academically, economically and socially. It would be an initiative the NFL could lean into that could have a positive impact in a tangible way.

WHAT MY SON'S ULTRASOUND TAUGHT ME ABOUT ABORTION — AND MASSACHUSETTS IGNORES

End Abortion

There is no denying that abortion is a very emotional, highly debated topic in America. It's undoubtedly been an issue that has effected the black community more than any other in America. Since 2020, stats show an estimated 4+ million abortions have occurred from 2020 through 2023, according to the Guttmacher Institute. Again, the issue is particularly significant in the Black community: in 2022, Black women accounted for 39.5% of reported abortions despite representing a much smaller percentage of women of reproductive age, and their abortion rate of 24.4 per 1,000 women was 4.3 times the rate for White women (5.7 per 1,000).

The NFL was so upset and bent out of shape by the death of George Floyd that they made a definitive stance against unjustified deaths, so how about standing up against the injustice of child death, NFL? You could help save millions of innocent lives if you made an effort to provide resources, curriculum, and dove head first into community outreach in this area.

COLIN KAEPERNICK IS RIGHT ABOUT THE NFL'S 'PERFORMATIVE' RACISM CAMPAIGN — BUT HE'S ALSO A HYPOCRITE

End Hunger

Hunger is a major issue in Black communities in the United States, with 9.2 million Black Americans experiencing food insecurity in 2023—about 22.4% of the Black population, compared with 10.4% of non-Hispanic White Americans. Black children are especially vulnerable: 27% lived in food-insecure households, meaning roughly 1 in 4 Black children did not have consistent access to enough food. Hunger can obviously affect a child’s health, concentration, academic performance and long-term development.

The NFL is uniquely positioned to help because of its enormous reach and resources in many of the communities most affected. The league could expand its existing community programs by partnering with food banks, funding mobile food pantries, providing meals to children during the offseason and directing team charitable dollars toward local food-security programs.

The NFL already has a framework for this through Inspire Change, which has directed more than $375 million toward social-justice and community organizations, including programs focused on economic advancement and opportunity. If the NFL wants to make a tangible difference in Black communities, fighting hunger is one area where its money, visibility and local team infrastructure could produce an immediate and measurable impact.

The NFL has the ability to actually do something of value, not just virtue signal after the death a Black man that was politicized to make people believe police officers were hunting black folks, America was foundationally racist, and racism was more than just a fringe issue causing institutional harm to the black community.

World.title: Maria Bartiromo’s lawyer says she was not fired from Fox News
World.content:
Maria Bartiromo’s lawyer on Friday said that the Fox News and Fox Business anchor was not fired from the company where she worked for more than 12 years.

“For many years, Maria Bartiromo hosted three No. 1-rated television shows on Fox channels,” said Bryan Freedman, Bartiromo’s attorney.

On Thursday, Fox abruptly announced in a statement that it had parted ways with Bartiromo, without offering any further details or context. The last episode of Bartiromo’s daily Fox Business show aired on Thursday. On Friday, those hours of programming came on the air with the same titles and graphics, but without Bartiromo’s name in them.

“The irresponsible reports that have been published stating that Maria Bartiromo was fired or is no longer an employee of Fox are absolutely and unequivocally false,” Freedman said Friday. “Make no mistake, we have the receipts and witnesses and they will come out whether through the courthouse or otherwise.”

He added: “Those reporting her firing or the incredulous facts supporting that fiction have exhibited a complete and utter reckless disregard for the truth.”

A Fox News Media representative, when asked about Freedman’s statement, said the company’s press release about parting ways with Bartiromo “speaks for itself.”

Before Freedman’s statement, on Thursday night the Status media industry newsletter reported that Bartiromo was fired after she had shared with the White House guidance from Fox management about claims made by President Donald Trump about recent elections. The New York Times and Wall Street Journal also reported later Thursday that she was dismissed after sharing internal Fox communications with the White House. NBC News has not verified those reports.

Immediately following Fox’s announcement on Thursday, Bartiromo’s bio and show pages were wiped from Fox’s websites.

Bartiromo had been Fox Business’ global markets editor since joining the channel in 2014. On Fox Business, she hosted “Mornings with Maria” on weekdays and “Maria Bartiromo’s Wall Street” on Fridays, while also anchoring “Sunday Morning Futures,” a business-focused show on the larger Fox News Channel.

For years, Fox News Media touted Bartiromo’s shows at ratings winners. She joined Fox after a trailblazing 21-year career at CNBC, where she hosted “Closing Bell,” a cornerstone of the business network’s programming.

Bartiromo drew attention for taking a more openly conservative turn in her reporting at Fox after leaving CNBC, where her work had been largely apolitical.

She also became very close to Trump, who appointed her to the board of the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts. The center’s website still lists her as a board member as of Friday afternoon.

In 2021, Bartiromo’s comments and shows were cited as exhibits in a defamation lawsuit filed by the voting machine maker Dominion Voting Systems against Fox News. Dominion alleged that the cable network operator had knowingly broadcast false claims that Dominion had rigged the 2020 presidential election.

Fox News eventually agreed to pay $787 million in a settlement with Dominion.

Another voting machine firm, Smartmatic, also filed suit against Fox in 2021, naming Bartiromo as a co-defendant. The Smartmatic case is ongoing.

World.title: Missouri Supreme Court rules new GOP-drawn map can’t be used in November
World.content:
The Missouri Supreme Court ruled Thursday that the state’s redrawn congressional map cannot be used in this year’s midterm elections, dealing a blow to Republicans.

The court ruled that a referendum on whether the state can use the map going forward must be included on the November ballot, meaning Missouri’s fall elections will take place under its previous district lines.

The new map was designed to draw one of the two Missouri Democrats in Congress, longtime Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, out of his seat.

“More than 305,000 Missourians demanded a say in who will represent them in the halls of Congress. Despite the cynical and deeply shameful attempt to silence many of our neighbors, the people fought back and won,” Cleaver said in a post on X following the ruling, adding that “democracy prevails.”

The ruling comes after a protracted battle between advocacy group People Not Politicians Missouri, which sought to block the Republican redistricting effort, and the state GOP leaders who defended it.

Missouri redrew its congressional map in 2025 at the behest of President Donald Trump. In response, People Not Politicians Missouri gathered more than 300,000 signatures to force a veto referendum. And while the group exceeded the signature requirements for getting on the ballot, Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins refused to certify it, saying that it was unconstitutional. The group appealed to the state Supreme Court, which heard arguments on the matter on Wednesday.

The ruling comes just days before the state’s Sept. 8 deadline to finalize its ballot for the general election. The state ran its August primary election using the Republican-drawn map.

Judge Ginger K. Gooch wrote in her ruling that Hoskins and those acting with him “are restrained and enjoined from implementing, using, or mandating the use of the congressional redistricting in HB 1 for the November 2026 general election or at any other time thereafter unless and until HB 1 is approved by the voters at the November 2026 general election and takes effect 30 days thereafter.”

The court’s decision means Cleaver will now be seeking re-election for his old seat, which skews heavily Democratic. He won by almost 24 percentage points in 2024.

The redesigned 5th District, which was struck down by Thursday’s ruling, was drawn so that Trump would have won by more than 17 points in 2024.

Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway vowed in a statement following the ruling to appeal the decision to the U.S. Supreme Court.

“Never before in American history has a court overturned a congressional map after a primary and before a general election. This unprecedented decision clearly violates federal law and has thrust our state into a full‑fledged constitutional crisis,” Hanaway wrote. “We are confident that the federal courts will not allow every Missouri voter to be disenfranchised—which is what today’s decision does.”

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., also weighed in, celebrating the decision and referencing the U.S. Supreme Court’s May decision to uphold a Virginia Supreme Court decision that did away with a voter-approved congressional map that would have expanded Democratic-leaning districts.

“We are watching closely to determine if they apply the same standard here, or choose to do the bidding of the Republican Party again,” Jeffries wrote.

People Not Politicians executive director Richard von Glahn celebrated the ruling.

“This victory reaches beyond Missouri. In a year when map-drawing has become a national weapon, courts across the country are watching what happens here. A Missouri win for the referendum is a signal that the people still hold the power,” von Glahn said in a statement.

Missouri is one of a handful of Republican-led states that took up mid-decade redistricting efforts at Trump’s urging to shore up the party’s narrow House majority.

Trump criticized the ruling in a Truth Social post, calling the ruling “horrible, ridiculous, and unConstitutional.”

“The Election Process, as usual, is being disturbed in America! Missouri must be able to use the map that was in effect just a couple of months ago, in the Primary,” Trump wrote.

The Republican National Committee also blasted the ruling in a statement.

“The RNC is evaluating every option to challenge this decision, and we will not stop fighting for Missouri voters,” said Ally Triolo, the RNC’s Election Integrity Communications Director.

The last time one of the state’s maps was considered by a voter referendum was in 1922, after the Republican-led state Legislature redrew the districts. Voters at the time rejected the new map.

World.title: Two trapped workers pulled alive from Nepal tunnel more than a week after deadly floods
World.content:
POKHARA, Nepal — Two workers in Nepal were pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel Friday, nine days after devastating floods swept the Himalayan region and left thousands of people dead or missing.

In a rare glimmer of hope, emergency teams rescued two men — a mechanical foreman named Sanjay Sah, 30, and a mechanical supervisor named Kabir Maharjan, 45, according to Nepal’s army and the country’s National Disaster Risk Reduction & Management Authority. A body was also recovered, Nepal’s army said.

00:33 Two Nepal flood survivors rescued from hydropower tunnel 00:00 00:00

Rescue officials said the voices of other workers could be heard inside the tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant along the Trishuli River in Nepal’s border district of Rasuwa. At least 557 workers are still believed to be missing there, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the main tunnel, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal.

In a video shared by Nepalese authorities, Sah said he spent his days trapped underground “chanting mantras to give myself hope” while hearing others trapped and calling out for help.

Sah said the “primary duty” of his job is “to safeguard everyone’s life,” adding that there were some 40 to 50 people in the tunnel at the time of the incident.

“I made sure to evacuate everyone else, but I didn’t get the chance to escape myself,” he said, speaking from the hospital in the video.

He said there could still be other survivors on his side of the tunnel, while there could be workers on the powerhouse side of the tunnel “who didn’t make it out in time.”

Nepal’s army released images of the dramatic rescue on its official Facebook page, including one showing the first rescued worker covered in mud and being carried from the site on a rescuer’s shoulder.

“When hope is alive, even the impossible becomes possible,” the image caption read.

The rescue operation at the Trishuli 3A hydropower project Friday. Nepali Army

Officials said both men were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu, the capital, for treatment.

“I can’t explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to God,” Amir Maharjan, the brother of one of the rescued workers, told The Associated Press. He said the family was on its way to the hospital to see him.

The large-scale operation has involved 75 army personnel, 18 police officers and multiple experts, the army said.

Army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet said one of the survivors told rescuers that more people were still alive inside the tunnel.

“We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people,” Communication Minister Bikram Timilsina wrote on his Facebook page.

More than 900 workers are missing from about a dozen hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, according to local officials.

Rescuers have been struggling to access the hydropower projects, many of which are in remote, mountainous areas, with bad weather adding to the difficulties. The flooding damaged roads and collapsed sections of tunnels, filling them with mud and other debris and blocking some entrances.

Aided by foreign experts, rescue teams have been working around the clock using controlled blasts, excavators and earth-moving equipment to try to reach the trapped workers amid concerns about air quality in the tunnels and the workers’ access to drinking water.

Nepal’s army said Friday that a separate rescue effort had recovered two bodies from a tunnel at the Langtang Hydropower Project.

Rescuers first heard voices from inside the tunnel Friday morning. Nepali Army

Authorities in Nepal say at least 1,294 people were killed and more than 5,000 remain missing after the Aug. 26 disaster, which is believed to have been set off by a high-altitude glacier collapse on the border between Nepal and China’s Tibet region.

Nepal’s disaster agency estimated Friday that flooding caused at least 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees ($2.5 billion) in damage to infrastructure and property.

Nepalese authorities said a national day of mourning will be observed on Sept. 7 in honor of those who lost their lives during the flood. The national flag will be flown at half-staff at government offices and Nepali embassies and missions abroad.

Rescue efforts are also still underway in China, where a mudslide hit a major land crossing between the two countries, with the only road to the site in Tibet’s Gyirong county fully reopening only Wednesday. Chinese officials say at least 31 people were killed and 531 are missing on the Tibet side of the border.

More than 800 foreign nationals are among those missing in the area, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims. According to the State Department, 75 Americans remained unaccounted for as of Wednesday, while 16 had made their way to safety.

Sunil Pandey reported from Pokhara, Nepal, and Adela Suliman from London.
