He said that 1,240 firearms and 7.3 tonnes of drugs were seized in the same period, while six meth labs were dismantled. 💰 Atizapán killings tied to money demand: García Harfuch said one of two men arrested over the multiple homicide in México state had a “commercial relationship” with victim Jonathan Meléndez and had been demanding money from him before the killings.

García Harfuch said one of two men arrested over the multiple homicide in México state had a “commercial relationship” with victim Jonathan Meléndez and had been demanding money from him before the killings. 🇲🇽🇺🇸 Defense minister addresses cartel drone reports: Responding to a Fox News report on U.S. operations against cartel drones at the border, Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla Trejo said the drones are mostly used by migrant smugglers to scout routes free of authorities. He didn’t confirm or deny Mexican military involvement in the U.S. takedown operations.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Friday morning press conference in Guadalupe, a municipality that is part of the metropolitan area of Zacatecas city.

She was accompanied by Zacatecas Governor David Monreal and various members of her cabinet, including Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez and Security Minister Omar García Harfuch.

Among Mexico’s 32 federal entities, Zacatecas has recorded one of the largest reductions in homicides this year.

At today’s mañanera, officials presented the latest security data for the state — statistics that allowed them to portray Zacatecas as an example of the success of the federal government’s national security strategy.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was García Harfuch’s remarks about the motive for a multiple homicide in México state.

Government reports 85% decline in homicides in Zacatecas

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported that there was an average of 0.17 homicides per day in Zacatecas in August, a reduction of 85% compared to September 2024, the final month of Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s presidency.

She said that the daily homicide rate so far this year is 0.2, a reduction of 50% compared to 2025.

Figueroa highlighted that the daily homicide rate in 2026 is down 96% compared to 2021, when an average of 4.5 murders per day were committed in Zacatecas.

In the first seven months of 2026, there were 51 homicides in Zacatecas, the eighth lowest total among Mexico’s 32 federal entities.

More than 3,800 arrests in Zacatecas since October 2024

According to data presented by García Harfuch, 3,824 people were arrested in Zacatecas between Oct. 1, 2024 — the date Sheinbaum was sworn in as president — and Aug. 31, 2026, for allegedly committing high-impact crimes such as homicide, kidnapping, extortion and violent robbery.

He also reported that 1,240 firearms and 7.3 tonnes of drugs were seized in the state in the same period. In addition, authorities dismantled six clandestine methamphetamine labs in Zacatecas, García Harfuch said.

photo-harfuch

He acknowledged that “there is still a lot to be done” to improve security in Zacatecas, noting that rival criminal groups continue to fight turf wars in the state. García Harfuch said that federal authorities are “maintaining and strengthening” intelligence and investigation “actions” in the state as well as “territorial presence” and “coordination” with state and municipal authorities. The aim, he said, is to detain “generators of violence” in Zacatecas.

García Harfuch subsequently noted that three people were arrested in connection with a car bomb explosion outside a municipal police station in Ojocaliente, Zacatecas, last Sunday night.

García Harfuch: Multiple homicide in México state related to a demand for money

García Harfuch said that one of two men arrested in connection with a multiple homicide in México state this week had a “commercial relationship” with one of the victims, namely Jonathan Meléndez, keyboard player with the well-known band Camilo Séptimo. The security minister was referring to Diego Sebastián Rosen Ferlini, an Argentine national who was detained in connection with the murders of Mélendez, his pregnant wife, their three-year-old daughter and a domestic worker. The victims were found dead in an apartment in the municipality of Atizapán de Zaragoza late Tuesday.

Asked how much money the alleged murderer was demanding from Mélendez, García Harfuch responded:

“I don’t know but I’ll ask the [México state] Attorney General’s Office. What is a fact is that he was demanding money. There was a demand, there were certain threats and this terrible multiple homicide was committed.”

Defense minister: People smugglers use drones to locate routes that are ‘free’ of US authorities

A reporter asked the president whether she could confirm the “participation” of Mexican authorities in U.S. operations to take down suspected cartel drones at the Mexico-U.S. border.

His question was related to a Fox News report that was published on Thursday.

Citing a senior U.S. War Department official, Fox reported that the U.S. military “took down ‘approximately 100′ suspected cartel drones in August alone” at the United States’ southern border.

Citing the same official, Fox wrote that “each operation was planned and closely coordinated with the Mexican military and border authorities to prevent interference or unintended conflicts between forces operating on either side of the border.”

Operation Ardent Vanguard Update 11 cartel drones defeated by the Army’s Multipurpose High Energy Laser as of Sep. 4. More than 300 defeats using kinetic and non-kinetic systems this year, with more than 100 occurring in August. “JTF Southern Border’s combined arms approach… pic.twitter.com/KexEOvgM9D — U.S. Northern Command (@USNorthernCmd) September 4, 2026

Sheinbaum referred the reporter’s question to her defense minister.

“Firstly I want to highlight that the relationship with the armed forces of the United States has been very good, very positive,” Ricardo Trevilla Trejo said.

He said that U.S. authorities have informed the Mexican government that drones are mainly used in the border region by people who smuggle migrants into the United States.

“They are commercial drones. They only capture images … and what they’re seeking to find are routes that are free, where there is no presence of [U.S.] authorities,” Trevilla said.

The defense minister didn’t confirm or deny Fox’s reporting that the Mexican military was involved in the planning of U.S. operations to take down drones.

World.title: ‘Sexy and hot, like Mexico’: How Mexican beauty brand AORA is taking on the global market
World.content:
Pyramid-inspired palettes, bilingual packaging and vivid shades drawn from Mexico’s streets are just some of the hallmarks of AORA, a Mexican beauty brand that’s challenging the beauty industry with its plastic-free packaging and strong Mexican identity.

“We wanted to bottle the feeling of Mexico,” co-founder Rodrigo Peñafiel told Mexico News Daily. “We wanted to bottle that feeling you get when you visit a beach in Oaxaca; that feeling you experience when you visit Mexico City for the first time.”

Since the opening of its flagship store in Mexico City in 2022, the brand has expanded into major retail chains, landed collaborations with international celebrities including Sofía Vergara, and most recently, served as one of the makeup brands used during Bad Bunny’s 2026 Super Bowl halftime show.

International expansion, however, didn’t come as a surprise. For Peñafiel and his co-founder Nour Tayara, going global was always part of the plan.

“Why would we build a small local brand when we have the opportunity to bring something big into the world?” Peñafiel said.

Combining Tayara’s experience in marketing and innovation roles within L’Oréal with Peñafiel’s background in public relations, the pair set out to create a brand that offered more than just clean, high-quality products. They wanted to create a luxury product with a strong focus on identity.

“We do luxury makeup by working with the best factories in the world. Because if we want to compete, let’s compete with spectacular quality. But what we’re bringing — we’re bringing culture,” Tayara said.

The brand’s DNA: Mexico

Rather than downplaying AORA’s Mexican identity to appeal to international consumers, the founders have made it central to the brand, drawing inspiration from the country’s creativity, colors, architecture and connection to nature.

From the brand’s signature Mírame Eyeshadow Palette to their lipsticks, pencils and accessories, AORA’s products evoke Mexico’s cultural icons, historic landmarks and scenes from everyday life.

“In our palette, you can see a hint of Frida Kahlo, of Matías Goeritz, of Chichén Itzá,” Peñafiel said. “The shades inside our palette could evoke any street in Mexico with a yellow house and a green Volkswagen parked outside,” he added with a chuckle.

Launching the brand from Mexico also meant producing its marketing campaigns in the country. From their photoshoots to their male and female models, everything is done in Mexico with Mexican talent.

“Every detail about the brand reflects Mexico. We could not have created this brand if we hadn’t launched it here,” Tayara remarked.

A retail presence at Sephora

AORA’s authentic vision has propelled the company into a new growth stage after entering Sephora in the United States, making history as the first 100% plastic-free beauty brand sold at the retailer, and the first brand to use both Spanish and English on its packaging.

“Sephora is betting on a brand that’s very colorful from Mexico and is betting on its first plastic-free brand in its portfolio,” Tayara pointed out.

In a competitive market dominated by European and U.S. brands, AORA is disrupting the beauty industry and aims to demonstrate that luxury also stems from cultural heritage.

“We started something that didn’t exist before, which is creating luxury beauty in Mexico,” Tayara said. “We come to challenge the industry in the language, in the visuals, in the products and in sustainability,” he said.

For the co-founders, AORA’s debut in Sephora goes beyond having its products on the shelves of one of the world’s leading beauty retailers. It also signals support for a Mexican brand and recognition for the Latino consumer market in the U.S.

“I think there’s a recognition of the amount of people in the U.S. that are of Latino descent and speak Spanish. It is an amazing message and signal Sephora is sending to the industry,” Tayara acknowledged.

A growing curiosity in Mexican identity and design

AORA isn’t the first brand to place Mexican identity as the center of its appeal. In recent years, global brands have increasingly sought partnerships that draw on Mexico’s visual identity, cultural heritage and creative talent.

In 2025, cosmetic brand Rare Beauty, founded by U.S. actress and singer of Mexican descent Selena Gomez, launched an exclusive, limited-edition makeup kit in collaboration with the Mexican seasoning Tajín.

Back then, Gomez described the collaboration as a “celebration of what makes us unique — our culture, our energy and the moments that bring us together.”

Last year also saw H&M launch a collection in collaboration with fashion designer Lorena Saravia, marking the first time the Swedish brand collaborated with a Mexican designer.

Joining the trend is Mestiz, a design studio founded by Daniel Valero in San Miguel de Allende, which recently collaborated with French design house Hermès to design their shop windows in Mexico.

Mexico’s appeal to consumers

“Mexico is trendy,” Peñafiel said with a smile. “I think there’s a celebration of Mexican culture that hasn’t been seen before. The challenge was to pass the front page of the news that we see every day about the dangers of Mexico, because the reality is that when people come here, they are amazed and fall in love with the food, with the culture, with the colors, the beaches, the brands,” he said.

As AORA seeks to reshape perceptions of Mexican luxury abroad and share a positive image of the country, its founders say the brand’s ultimate purpose is more personal — to make consumers feel attractive.

“We buy beauty because we want to feel good about ourselves. Because we want to feel sexy,” Tayara said.

“Yes, we want our clients to feel sexy and hot, like Mexico,” Peñafiel said.

Gabriela Solis is a Mexican lawyer turned full-time writer. She was born and raised in Guadalajara and covers business, culture, lifestyle and travel for Mexico News Daily. You can follow her lifestyle blog Dunas y Palmeras.

World.title: No, September is not earthquake month in Mexico City
World.content:
One of the most visceral and profound fears we Mexico City residents have is the seismic alert going off. And that’s no exaggeration.

Particularly for those of us who lived through the September earthquakes — which, in an almost absurd coincidence, all occurred on the 19th of different years — that sound is a near-physical reminder of the catastrophe.

Born and raised in Mexico City, I grew up listening to my parents’ stories about the terrible 1985 earthquake, when Mexicans united to help the military and first responders rescue people from the rubble.

“The response from their community was immediate,” Gaceta UNAM magazine noted at the time, “and extended to the most diverse tasks, such as the distribution of medicines, food, drinking water and clothing, as well as transportation to shelters.”

Therefore, it is no surprise that my generation grew up attending drills at school. We learned about the seismic nature of Mexico City, largely due to the confluence of tectonic plates in our country and the presence of two magnificent volcanoes.

It wasn’t until September 2017, in my first year of university, that I truly understood what it was all for. The tedium of the drills turned into outright terror when the seismic alert sounded.

And yes, September is back. As it happens year after year, there’s this morbid expectation that another seismic catastrophe will shake the nation’s capital. And why not? On Sept. 19, it has become all but customary.

To avoid this irrational fear, MND put together this explainer about why it’s practically impossible to predict earthquakes (yes, even in turbulent Mexico City), and why it’s an infinitesimal coincidence that they’ve occurred on the same day in different years.

No, there is no way to predict an earthquake — but we can prepare for them

Ranging from 7.1 to 8.1 on the Richter scale, 1985, 2017 and 2019 are the years that have marked the strongest earthquakes in Mexico City’s recent history, as documented by the National Seismological Service (SSN). Leaving hundreds of thousands of people homeless and an uncertain death toll of hundreds on each occasion, it is understandable why these natural disasters instilled panic among the residents of the capital.

And, understandably, there’s a superstition that September is the month of earthquakes. Although fitting, it’s nothing more than a popular belief that science has taken pains to disprove.

In fact, SSN records show that there have historically been more earthquakes in December than in any other month. But what does this mean?

In Mexico, more than 15,000 earthquakes have been recorded so far in 2026, according to SSN monitoring. The number changes daily because the country has consistently high seismic activity.

Furthermore, this does not mean that all of the underground movement has been harmful to the population. Sometimes, it’s barely perceptible on the surface.

Although the records are accurate, they can only be taken after the telluric event. In other words, the technology we currently have is not predictive, but only serves to maintain a record of the country’s seismic activity.

This is because, according to the SSN, “not even the most advanced research has been able to develop a predictive technique for earthquakes, […] in the face of any seismic event, the only thing that can help us is prevention.”

This does not refer to the prevention of earthquakes per se, which are inevitable natural events, but to measures to mitigate the impact of these phenomena on the population. The drills we hated so much in elementary school are the best way to prepare for an event like this.

Tepeyóllotl, have mercy on us!

Through the National Center for Disaster Prevention, the Mexican government acknowledges that it is an extremely rare coincidence that the three strongest earthquakes in the country’s recent history occurred on the same day.

Almost ludicrous, and certainly grim, for those of us who live in the capital.

It’s almost as if the fearsome Tepeyóllotl, the great lord of seismic movements in the Mexica pantheon, were laughing at us and saying, “Let’s give the capital’s residents a little scare.”

So no, it’s not possible to predict earthquakes. We know why they happen, and that the movement of tectonic plates is inevitable. At best, it has given us our majestic Sierra Madre mountain ranges and the pair of magnificent volcanoes that crown the center of the country. At worst, it has left terrible death tolls across the territory, as part of the cost of living in a seismic country.

Let us entrust ourselves, then, to the lord of the mountains. Perhaps only he, with his guttural roar in the bowels of the earth, can calm the subterranean movements that plague the ever-unstable Mexico City.

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: ‘A pact with organized crime’: Opposition’s response to Sheinbaum’s second year report
World.content:
Listen to this article

In a 67-minute speech at the National Palace on Tuesday, President Claudia Sheinbaum delivered her second annual government report. A month shy of completing her second year in office, she touted achievements across a wide range of areas and declared that her administration is “transforming public life in this country.”

Later on Tuesday, prominent opposition politicians presented a fundamentally different view of the state of the nation, asserting that Mexico, as a country, has not in fact improved under the leadership of Sheinbaum and her predecessor Andrés Manuel López Obrador (2018-24).

While opinion poll results show that Sheinbaum is a highly popular president, millions of Mexicans oppose her government.

In speeches in a general session of Congress on Tuesday, two of Mexico’s best-known opposition politicians, Sen. Ricardo Anaya of the National Action Party and Sen. Alejandro Moreno of the Institutional Revolutionary Party, outlined some of the main grievances that they — and many other Mexicans — have with the federal government and the broader Morena party-backed “fourth transformation” political movement that was founded by López Obrador and is now led by Sheinbaum.

They included grievances about insecurity, even though the president on Tuesday touted a 51% reduction in homicides (in July compared to the final month of López Obrador’s term).

They included claims that the government is shielding a ruling Morena party governor accused by U.S. prosecutors of drug trafficking in league with the Sinaloa Cartel, even though Sheinbaum has said on repeated occasions that her administration won’t protect anyone who has committed a crime.

And they included accusations that the government is attempting to silence or censor government critics, even though the president says her administration will always respect freedom of speech.

Jorge Álvarez Máynez, national leader of the Citizens Movement party, also offered an appraisal of Mexico almost eight years after Morena first came to power. His remarks, and those of Anaya and Moreno, are covered below.

Ricardo Anaya, National Action Party (PAN) senator and former presidential candidate:

“It was said that Mexico is at peace, that homicides had already gone down. I wish that were true; it isn’t.”

In the Legislative Palace of San Lázaro on Tuesday afternoon, Sen. Ricardo Anaya told his colleagues that he was at the rostrum to “seriously respond” to Sheinbaum’s second government report, which he asserted was “unfortunately riddled with lies.”

In his speech, Anaya sought to demonstrate that the Morena party government is failing to uphold its own ethos: “Don’t lie, don’t steal and don’t betray the people.”

“First they promised not to lie. This morning it was said that Mexico is at peace, that homicides had already gone down. I wish that were true; it isn’t,” the senator said.

“And I don’t say it with my numbers, I say it with yours, with those of the Executive Secretariat of the National Public Security System [SESNSP],” he said.

Mi respuesta al informe de Claudia Sheinbaum:

Maquillan las cifras, esconden el robo y protegen a los narcopolíticos. Prometieron no mentir, no robar y no traicionar al pueblo. Fallaron en las tres. pic.twitter.com/mNr6cx12NQ — RicardoAnayaC (@RicardoAnayaC) September 2, 2026

Anaya, who contested the 2018 presidential election as the candidate for the PAN, said that the average daily homicide rate before Morena took office in late 2018 was 70.

“In this six-year term of government, according to you, it’s 63. Seven fewer [homicides per day] is the apparent miracle,” he said.

“But this document — yours, not mine — has another column,” Anaya said as he held up a crime statistics report.

“It’s called ‘other crimes that threaten life and physical integrity.’ There are deaths listed there as well, but those — in a devious and deceitful manner — weren’t counted in this morning’s report. Those deaths, with you [in office], went from 15 to 40 per day,” he said.

Anaya also said that the number of daily reports of disappearances has increased from 16 to 31 under Morena’s rule.

“Disappearances doubled,” he said.

“So, do the math with me because it’s a primary school calculation. Homicides went down by seven per day in one column [but] went up by 40 in the other two,” Anaya said.

“Even though they fudge the numbers, in Mexico no one was brought back to life,” he said.

Anaya apportioned blame for the allegedly fudged numbers to authorities in Mexico’s 32 federal entities, the majority of which are governed by Morena. His claim that homicide statistics are being manipulated has also been expressed by security analysts and others.

Anaya proposed a “public and technical review of the methodology” used by the SESNSP — which compiles crime data it receives from state Attorney General’s Offices — “so that no dead person can change columns.”

“Counting correctly is not a technicality; it’s the first requirement for governing truthfully,” Anaya said.

The PAN senator also accused the government of seeking to silence critical voices with its General Guidelines for the Protection of the Rights of Audiences.

“Huachicol fiscal is the largest robbery in the history of our country.”

Anaya asserted that the government has also broken its “do not steal” maxim.

“Huachicol fiscal is the largest robbery in the history of our country,” he said, referring to a fuel smuggling/tax evasion offense in which high-ranking members of the Mexican Navy and customs officials were allegedly involved.

“And it’s not [just] the opposition saying it. The federal tax prosecutor said it in this chamber: 600 billion pesos (US $35.45 billion),” Anaya said.

“… Six-hundred billion pesos is the hospital that wasn’t built, it’s the medicine that wasn’t supplied,” he said.

“It’s a second promise broken,” Anaya said before proposing the creation of a “special commission to investigate huachicol fiscal,” a crime that Sheinbaum says her government has “practically” eliminated.

The commission, he said, should be “plural,” but chaired by “the opposition.”

Anaya said that the commission could begin by looking into allegations that a company called Portacelis is involved in huachicol fiscal.

“The company is called Portacelis and the name that appears again is that of the friend of Andy, Amilcár Olán,” he said, referring in the first instance to Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, a son of ex-president Andrés Manuel López Obrador and Morena’s former secretary of organization.

“The problem isn’t that Andrés Manuel López Obrador has been stripped of his [U.S.] visa. The problem is that you don’t want to ask a single question. … That is the country you’ve built — one in which your surname determines whether you’re investigated or exonerated,” Anaya said.

“Sovereignty isn’t impunity.”

Finally, Anaya asserted that the government hasn’t fulfilled its pledge to “not betray the people.”

“In a country ravaged by homicides, oppressed by extortion, the worst possible betrayal has a verb, the verb pactar,” he said, alleging that the federal government has a pact with organized crime.

To support his claim, Anaya referred to U.S. prosecutors’ drug trafficking accusations against Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya, a Morena politician who is currently on leave.

“A grand jury decided to bring criminal charges against Rubén Rocha Moya for drug trafficking. A federal judge issued an arrest warrant. The State Department formally requested his provisional detention for the purpose of extradition. Today marks 126 days, and they keep telling us there is no evidence,” he said.

Anaya asserted that there is indeed evidence linking Rocha to drug trafficking, citing an allegation that he met with Sinaloa Cartel kingpin Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, among other supposed examples of proof.

“Proof is not lacking here. What we have in abundance is protection,” he said.

“… Sovereignty is not impunity,” Anaya said, referring to Sheinbaum’s assertion that Mexican authorities can’t detain and extradite Rocha unless they are satisfied that the United States allegations are supported by sufficient proof.

“… The same apparatus that protects Rocha Moya, imprisons Ernesto Ruffo,” he said, referring in the second instance to a former PAN governor of Baja California who faces organized crime, fuel theft and tax evasion charges.

Alejandro Moreno, national leader of the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) and a federal senator:

“Eight years after the Morena governments began, the outcome is a country that is divided, fractured, indebted, bogged down and engulfed in violence.”

Speaking before Congress on Tuesday, Senator Alejandro Moreno was also highly critical of the current federal government and its predecessor — i.e. the administration led by former President López Obrador.

“Eight years after the Morena governments began, the outcome is a country that is divided, fractured, indebted, bogged down and engulfed in violence,” he said.

Moreno, a former governor of Campeche, asserted that the Sheinbaum administration doesn’t have a “national project” or “answers” to the problems Mexico faces.

Although Sheinbaum has an approval rating of 68% according to the most recent El Financiero poll, the senator claimed that her government is rejected by Mexicans.

Claro, en MORENA sí “Juntos han hecho historia”, pero por haber hecho un pacto inconfesable entre el gobierno y la delincuencia organizada. Un pacto que se ha convertido en un régimen criminal transnacional y que hemos denunciado ante todos los organismos internacionales por… pic.twitter.com/oOeS2Qd8M1 — Alejandro Moreno (@alitomorenoc) September 2, 2026

He asserted that the government is seeking to “put an end to free media outlets” and “destroy the voices of the opposition, canceling the most fundamental freedoms in our country.”

Moreno went on to say that “the Morena government is impunity disguised as false defense of national sovereignty.”

He accused the Sheinbaum administration of protecting Morena governors and other officials wanted by “foreign governments and mainly the government of the United States.”

Moreno also accused the government of making a “shameful pact” with organized crime, a claim that the Trump administration has also made.

He said that if the government had a “modicum of decency,” it would “break its pact with the organized crime cartels and take away the protection of” López Obrador, Andy López Beltrán, Senator Enrique Inzunza, Baja California Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila and Tamaulipas Governor Américo Villarreal.

“They’ve ruined peace; they’ve destroyed Mexicans’ quality of life.”

Moreno also claimed that the current government “has ruined peace” and “destroyed Mexicans’ quality of life.”

“They systematically eliminated everything that had a stamp of autonomy,” he said, referring to the government’s abolition of various watchdog agencies, including the now-defunct National Transparency Institute.

Moreno asserted that at elections in 2027, “with a large party and citizens coalition,” the opposition will win a congressional majority.

“And have no doubt, in 2030, with the people of Mexico behind us, we’re going to win the presidency of the republic,” he said.

Jorge Álvarez Máynez, national leader of Citizens’ Movement and a former presidential candidate:

“Hospitals and healthcare centers still don’t have medicine.”

In a video posted to social media, Jorge Álvarez Máynez, MC’s candidate at the 2024 presidential election, said that eight years after Morena took power, “Mexico is not making progress.”

Ya son 8 años de Morena en el poder. Y aún con todo el poder, México no está avanzando. El gobierno prometió mucho y ha cumplido poco. Pero México es más que su gobierno. México tiene alternativa. pic.twitter.com/ywiO7JYpsx — Jorge Álvarez Máynez (@AlvarezMaynez) September 2, 2026

“Insecurity continues affecting the lives of millions of families,” he said.

“Hospitals and healthcare centers still don’t have medicine,” Álvarez Máynez asserted.

“And people continue battling to reach the end of the month,” he said, referring to the challenge of making ends meet.

Álvarez Máynez also said that after eight years of Morena governments, “corruption and abuse of power have not gone away.”

“… They promised to be different from the PRI but they failed to deliver on that too,” he said.

“We have a government that promised a lot but which has achieved very little,” Álvarez Máynez said.

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: How Taiwanese imports are fueling Mexico’s record tech exports
World.content:
Data came out last week showing that Mexico’s exports were worth a record high US $81.4 billion in July, an increase of almost 44% compared to the same month of 2025.

In the first seven months of 2026, Mexico’s export revenue totaled $471.4 billion, a year-over-year gain of 27.7%, according to the national statistics agency INEGI.

In July, almost three-quarters of Mexico’s export income came from the shipment abroad of non-automotive manufactured goods. Within that category, revenue from the export of electrical and electronic equipment and appliances soared 134% annually. Among those products are inputs for AI servers and other computer equipment. Mexico is currently shipping large quantities of such goods to the United States.

On the surface, the AI-related export boom appears to be great news for Mexico, but the reality is more nuanced.

As Pedro Casas, CEO of the American Chamber of Commerce of Mexico, wrote in an article that MND published this week, “a significant share of the inputs” in the AI-related products Mexico is exporting is not Mexican, or even North American, but rather Taiwanese. That means that a significant share of the revenue Mexico receives from the export of such products has already been spent on imported inputs.

In a recent LinkedIn post, economist Gilberto García-Vaquez wrote that “a single trailer of servers” entering the U.S. from Mexico “can be worth as much as a thousand cars.”

“But most of that value entered Mexico as imports before the servers ever left,” he added.

In his article, Casas wrote that Mexico, “in many instances,” is “assembling and integrating components that arrive from Asia, then shipping the finished product north.”

“That’s not nothing — assembly creates jobs and keeps supply chains on this side of the Pacific,” he wrote. “But it’s not the same as manufacturing a vertical regional integrated supply chain.”

In that context, this “Mexico in Numbers” article looks at some of the key numbers related to Mexico’s exportation of AI servers and other electronic products — and the Mexican content (or lack thereof) in those goods.

* The data in this article comes from various sources, each of which is mentioned below. In some cases, the numbers cited are estimates rather than proven figures.

More than 1/3 of US server imports come from Mexico

As we reported on Aug. 14, a report by the Economic Studies Department of Grupo Financiero Banamex found that Mexico’s share of U.S. server imports through the first half of 2026 was 34.5%, just behind Taiwan’s 36%. In the second quarter of 2026, Mexico’s share of the U.S. market for imported servers was nearly 40%.

During the first half of the year, Mexico exported more than US $60.4 billion worth of computer servers to artificial intelligence data centers in the United States, according to Banamex. In May, it surpassed Taiwan in sales.

Banamex said that “Mexico has established itself as an assembly platform close to the U.S. market, while design, technological integration and chain coordination activities (for artificial intelligence computing production) remain concentrated in Asia.”

Taiwan’s exports of artificial intelligence servers to the United States were worth $72.2 billion in the first half of 2026, according to Banamex.

As MND wrote last month, “Mexico and Taiwan have captured the U.S. market for artificial intelligence data center servers, which had previously been dominated by China.”

“In 2017, China accounted for 60.4% of U.S. purchases of computer equipment, while in the first half of 2026 its share fell to 2%.”

The vast majority of inputs in computing and other electronic products made in Mexico are foreign

According to a recent report by Swiss multinational investment bank UBS, more than 95% of inputs used in the manufacture or assembly in Mexico of computing and other electronic products are imported, primarily from Asian countries such as Taiwan. In other words, less than 5% of the content in such “Made in Mexico” products is actually Mexican.

“Mexico is capturing an important role in the North American AI supply chain, but much of the value of the products it exports is still generated abroad. Computers and electronics rely heavily on imported inputs, limiting their domestic value-added and employment multipliers,” UBS says in its report.

The bank also says that “a server assembled in Mexico can have a very high export value without generating a proportionally large amount of Mexican income, employment, or local demand.”

Similarly, the Financial Times (FT) reported in August that the “surge in high-value exports is yet to translate into proportional local benefits” in Mexico.

“Each dollar of investment in the highly automated [AI server] plants creates far fewer jobs than more manual sectors such as car parts,” FT wrote, also noting that “Mexico manufactures very few of the parts” used in the country’s AI server sector.

Fernando Alba, deputy economy minister in the state of Chihuahua, told FT that in current conditions Mexico could realistically aspire to reach 3-7% Mexican content in each server, compared to 39% for autos.

“It could do electronics, cooling and product design but making chips was very unlikely, he said, as the country lacks the engineering and design knowhow, as well as enough energy and water,” FT reported.

Alba also said: “A car is a value chain disseminated up and down the country. … It’s much harder to do that with AI servers. We are much less prepared.”

In its report, UBS says that “Mexico does not need to produce advanced chips to capture more value from the AI boom.”

“The more immediate opportunity is to build a broader ecosystem around the manufacturing capacity already being established. Potential areas include electronic components, cooling and power systems, testing and packaging, design, and other specialized industrial inputs,” the bank said.

Mexico’s imports from Taiwan have surged

FT reported in August that “Taiwanese manufacturers are rapidly expanding factories in Mexico to assemble servers, which are now the country’s top U.S. export, overtaking autos that dominated its trade for decades.”

As noted above, the vast majority of the inputs going into servers assembled in Mexico — whether by Taiwanese manufacturers, Mexican manufacturers or anyone else — comes from abroad. Taiwan is a top supplier of those inputs.

“Much of the increase in technology imports is coming from Taiwan,” UBS notes in its report.

Therefore, it is not surprising that official data shows that Mexico’s imports from the East Asian island have significantly increase.

According to Bank of Mexico data, Mexico’s imports from Taiwan totaled US $43.91 billion in the first six months of 2026, an increase of 200.5% compared to the same period of last year. In all of 2026, Mexico imports from Taiwan were worth $46.58 billion, less than $3 billion above the total in the first half of this year.

As Mexico News Daily reported in April, much of the recent significant rise in trade between Taiwan and Mexico is in the semiconductor industry. In other words, Taiwan is sending large quantities of chips and other electronic components and inputs to Mexico, where they are used in the assembly of AI servers and other computer hardware, much of which is sent across the border to data centers in the United States.

World.title: Chiapas town reclaims Guinness World Record for world’s biggest cheese ball
World.content:
Blessed are the cheesemakers, for they shall … make a cheese ball weighing 1,611 kilos.

Cheese producers in the small town of Pijijiapan, Chiapas, have re-entered the Guinness Book of World Records after stringing together the largest ball of quesillo in history, earning the acknowledgement on Aug. 29 at the city’s Campo Nuevo Milenio field.

Alfredo Arista, official adjudicator of Guinness World Records, verified compliance with the requirements necessary to recognize the new world record and presented an award to Mayor Carlos Alberto Albores.

Mayor Albores said that the eight cheese-producing companies participating conducted three test runs before undertaking the record-setting effort. He said an estimated 15,500 liters of fresh milk were required to produce the giant ball of cheese.

Once the master cheesemaker and cheese producers finished preparing the string cheese, the difficult task of forming the ball got under way. To do it, a special rotating structure with metal platforms was built, allowing the ball to be rotated and manipulated while its dimensions and weight increased.

The strings were progressively wound over almost four hours, until a single piece weighing more than 1.7 tonnes was realized.

The Tourism Ministry lauded the achievement, saying in a social media post that the record was established thanks to “the tradition, talent and hands of Chiapas’ cheese-producing families who are keeping alive one of the special characteristics that distinguishes the region.”

“Behind this large ball of string cheese lies a lot of work, tradition and pride,” said Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez. “This is a great opportunity for more people to get to know Pijijiapan, its flavors, its communities and everything this destination has to offer.”

The Pacific Coast town of Pijijiapan — with a population of just over 18,000 souls and the county seat of the municipality of the same name — is well known for its exceptional dairy products, especially its fresh cheeses, particularly a renowned doble crema.

One goal of last week’s event was to reclaim the Guinness Record it had lost to cheesemakers in Reyes Etla, just 20 kilometers north of Oaxaca city, when cheesemakers there constructed a ball weighing 636.2 kilos in 2024.

Pijijiapan had established the initial record in 2023 (making a cheese ball weighing 558 kilos), and organizers said they planned to climb back atop the cheesemaking mountain by assembling a cheese ball weighing more than 1,500 kilos.

At the same time, municipal officials sought to protect the identity, origin and tradition linked to the production of Pijijiapan cheese by obtaining an official Declaration of Protection of the Geographical Indication “Quesillo de Pijijiapan, Chiapas.”

In support of this goal, the state Economy Ministry filed an application with the Mexican Institute of Industrial Property (IMPI) requesting the formal designation.

With reports from La Jornada, El Financiero and UnoTV

World.title: Mexico City’s Cutzamala water supply system hits 81%, highest level in a decade
World.content:
Steady August rains have helped replenish the Cutzamala reservoir system, Mexico City’s primary source of water, boosting supply to 81% capacity, its highest volume in a decade.

According to data from the National Water Commission (Conagua), the Cutzamala System has experienced 13 consecutive weeks of recovery, dating to the beginning of the rainy season on June 4.

During the final week of August, 15.02 million cubic meters of water from rainfall and runoff were captured in the Balsas River basin, where the system’s physical infrastructure and reservoirs are located.

The Cutzamala System supplies 5 million inhabitants of the greater Mexico City Metropolitan Area and provides 18% of the water the area consumes, around 422 million liters daily.

Conagua’s monthly report for August indicated that the Valle de Bravo dam was at 86.58% capacity with 341.47 million cubic meters of water; Villa Victoria dam held 78.10% of its capacity with 145.06 million cubic meters; and the El Bosque dam was at 72.98% with 147.71 million cubic meters.

These totals dwarf the numbers the system reported the past three years and come two years after policymakers were faced with concerns that a Day Zero might be approaching.

The current volume of water is roughly equivalent to that recorded in August 2017, but storage steadily declined during the following years. By 2021 and 2022, the system was operating at 50.31% and 50.15%, respectively.

Then, a drought in 2023 reduced the water supply even more dramatically so that in 2023, the system was operating at 36.71% of its capacity. In 2024, it rose slightly to 42%. Ahead of the 2025 rainy season, Conagua reported that storage had reached 56%, but cautioned that the crisis had yet to be averted.

However, plentiful rains boosted the Cutzamala water supply so thoroughly that it remained at nearly 70% by spring 2026.

This year’s August data shows that the three dams had increased their level by more than 30 million cubic meters compared to the same period in 2025, helped considerably by five days in which more than 20 mm of rainfall was recorded in the Balsas and Lerma river basins. Aug. 16 was particularly beneficial to the system, as downpours added 18 mm to Villa Victoria, 34 mm to Valle de Bravo and 26 mm to El Bosque.

On Aug. 1, total storage was 577.56 billion cubic meters, equivalent to 73.81%. By the 30th, the volume had reached 634.25 billion cubic meters, or 81.05%.

Conagua says the system is on track to reach its maximum capacity for the year by Oct. 31 (the date rainfall is expected to drop to near zero in its area of ​​influence), projecting 98% capacity.

With reports from La Jornada, Excelsior, N+, UnoTV and Milenio

World.title: MND Local: From Puerto Vallarta to Punta de Mita, 4 stories of a region in transition
World.content:
Puerto Vallarta and the surrounding region are undergoing rapid change. However, with new investment and infrastructure comes mounting pressure on public services, transportation, housing and the coastline.

In this week’s roundup, we examine questions surrounding the municipality’s growing payroll, the deeper forces behind Vallarta’s worsening traffic, the long-awaited Amado Nervo Bridge, and the continuing debate over development at Punta de Mita.

Questions raised over Vallarta’s growing municipal payroll

Puerto Vallarta’s municipal government is facing questions over the size and cost of its workforce after independent councilor Melissa Madero presented an analysis of the city’s 2026 payroll.

According to reporting by Urritia Comunica, Madero stated the municipal council originally approved 2,707 positions for 2026. Her review of current records alleged there were 3,375 active positions, 668 more than authorized, representing an additional cost of more than 151 million pesos (US $8.8 million).

She also pointed to what she described as 778 unauthorized positions, including assistants, coordinators and other administrative roles, with an estimated annual cost of nearly 180 million pesos.

Perhaps more striking is the contrast she drew between administrative staffing and the city’s operational services. Madero alleged that positions have increased in areas connected to the mayor’s office while other departments responsible for services such as public safety, parks, gardens and municipal infrastructure face staffing and resource pressures.

Madero says she intends to take the matter first to the municipal comptroller and, if necessary, to Jalisco’s Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office.

Although only allegations, the questions are significant.

As Puerto Vallarta spends heavily to keep pace with a rapidly growing city, residents have every right to ask where their municipal money is going, and whether the bureaucracy is growing as quickly as the services people actually depend on.

Vallarta’s traffic problem is about more than cars

If it feels like there are more cars on Puerto Vallarta’s roads every time you leave the house, you’re not imagining it.

Traffic congestion has become one of the city’s defining daily frustrations, with a road network that was never designed for the population and development Vallarta is now supporting. New housing construction and the sheer number of people moving around the metropolitan area are putting additional pressure on already limited routes.

But there’s another part of the story that doesn’t always get enough attention: Who’s living here, and where?

The cost of living in Puerto Vallarta, particularly housing costs, has risen sharply in recent years. For many local workers, remaining in the city is becoming increasingly difficult. As rents push people farther from the center, some workers who once lived close to their jobs are now commuting from places such as Ixtapa, Las Juntas, El Colorado, Bahía de Banderas and farther afield.

That means more vehicles on the road. Not necessarily because more people suddenly decided they wanted a car, but because the geography of everyday life changed, thereby creating a need for one. At the same time, Puerto Vallarta continues to attract new residents, businesses and visitors, adding to demand for roads that were already struggling.

So, the traffic problem isn’t simply about too many cars. It’s another symptom of a city trying to figure out how to accommodate growth without pricing the people who keep it running out of the places where they work.

The still not-quite-ready-yet bridge

For anyone who regularly crosses between Puerto Vallarta and Bahía de Banderas, the Amado Nervo Bridge has become something of a local obsession. And this week, there was another reminder that while the long-awaited connection is getting closer, it isn’t ready for prime time just yet.

The bridge crosses the Ameca River, connecting the Ixtapa area of Puerto Vallarta on the Jalisco side with San Vicente in Bahía de Banderas, Nayarit. When completed, the roughly 2-kilometer project is expected to cut travel times between the two municipalities by about 25 minutes and accommodate thousands of vehicles each day.

Construction is now reported to be about 90% complete, with an opening currently expected later this year.

But that hasn’t stopped some drivers from attempting to get onto the new connection. It is easy to understand the impatience. The Ameca River has long been a bottleneck for a metropolitan area that has grown dramatically on both sides of the bay.

The new bridge won’t solve every transportation problem facing Vallarta and Bahía de Banderas. But once it finally opens, it’ll give commuters another option and, perhaps more importantly, provide a much-needed piece of infrastructure for a region that’s been growing faster than its roads can handle.

Punta de Mita’s coastline is the latest development battleground

The fight over development in Punta de Mita and its coastline isn’t going away.

Last week, the Committee of Punta de Mita and environmental groups called on authorities to move beyond announcements and actually remove the rock barrier at Playa Las Cocinas and begin restoring the affected beach.

The demand follows recent statements from Environment Secretary Alicia Bárcena regarding the site. Local environmental groups say the issue now is what happens next.

Will authorities follow through with restoration rather than simply declaring that action is being taken?

The dispute is part of a larger conversation playing out across Riviera Nayarit. Development has transformed Punta Mita and its surrounding communities into some of the region’s most valuable real estate, but the coastline itself remains a public and environmental resource.

The latest demands from Punta de Mita residents and environmental groups show that the argument isn’t simply about one project or one stretch of beach. It’s about what happens when a coastline becomes extremely valuable, and who gets to decide how much of it can be changed in the name of development.

World.title: Los Ilinizas Fire Burns About 200 Hectares in Ecuador
World.content:

ECUADOR · ENVIRONMENT

Key Facts —What happened: A fire started in Los Ilinizas Ecological Reserve on 1 September 2026. —How big it is: About 200 hectares of páramo burned, a preliminary figure. —What it means: Páramo is the sponge that stores the region’s water, and fire damage means it holds less. —The catch: Reports differ on whether the fire is fully out, and no final burned area has been published. —Who it hits: Visitors who hike the reserve and communities that rely on the highland water. —What comes next: Officials may update the burned area as technical evaluation continues.

A blaze in Ecuador’s Los Ilinizas Ecological Reserve has burned about 200 hectares of páramo, the high grassland that stores the region’s water.

Where the fire is burning

The Los Ilinizas fire is in the El Chaupi sector of Mejía, in Pichincha province. That is part of Ecuador’s Andean highlands, south of the capital Quito.

El Chaupi is a small rural district inside the canton of Mejía, a local administrative area. The fire was reported at 22:23 on 1 September 2026.

The reserve spans parts of Cotopaxi, Pichincha, and Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas provinces. It is named after the Iliniza twin volcanic peaks.

The burned area sits on the Pichincha–Cotopaxi divide, which explains why some reports place it in Cotopaxi. The exact location is within the reserve’s high-altitude zone, mostly páramo grassland and shrubs.

Why the páramo matters

Páramo is the spongy high-altitude grassland of the Andes. It absorbs rain and releases water slowly into streams and rivers.

That water feeds the streams and rivers of the surrounding highlands. Losing páramo means the ground holds less of it.

Páramo sits above the tree line, on the highest ground of the northern Andes. Ecuador’s environment ministry treats these páramos as a priority for water regulation.

Crews said they were working to keep the fire away from water sources. The fire also destroys plants that hold soil in place, so erosion can worsen after rains.

Who is fighting the fire

Fire brigades from Mejía, Latacunga and Cayambe led the response. The armed forces, the Red Cross, the environment ministry and local volunteer brigades were also on the ground.

Latacunga sent 20 forest firefighters, and a drone was used for thermal monitoring. An air rescue squadron flew over El Chaupi to map how far the fire had spread.

The national risk secretariat, known as the Secretaría Nacional de Gestión de Riesgos, coordinated the effort. Workers from the private forestry firm Aglomerados Cotopaxi also joined the fight.

Firefighting in high mountains is tough. Steep slopes and thin air make it hard for crews to work.

How the fire started and its status

The fire was reported at 22:23 on 1 September 2026. The cause is not yet known.

Crews were still damping down on the afternoon of 3 September, El Comercio reported. Later that day La Gaceta reported the fire brought under control, and no final figure for the burned area has been published.

ECU 911, the national emergency system, reported the fire controlled on 3 September, after two days of firefighting. Crews remained on site for liquidation and mop-up.

Estimates of the burned area range from more than 170 hectares to about 200. Authorities say the figure is still under technical evaluation.

In Ecuador, many fires are linked to human activity, but that is not confirmed here. Officials have not stated a cause.

Ecuador’s 2026 fire season

Ecuador is in its peak fire season, which runs from July to September. Dry conditions have increased the risk.

As of 3 September 2026, the national risk secretariat had recorded 2,831 fire events this year. That includes 2,814 forest fires and 17 interface fires, destroying 18,027.73 hectares of vegetation across 20 provinces.

The worst-hit provinces are Imbabura, Loja and Carchi, according to the risk secretariat. The Los Ilinizas fire is one of many in a challenging season.

Guayaquil saw almost four times more surface burned than in 2025, yet the number of fires there dropped. That is according to a report from El Universo.

The report also found that 98 percent of the city’s fires were linked to human activity.

What this means for visitors

Los Ilinizas is a popular hiking destination, known for its volcanic peaks and scenic trails. But authorities have not announced a full closure of the reserve.

Visitors should stay away from active fire zones and follow any local restrictions. No official travel advisory has been issued, so check with local authorities before you go.

Even if the reserve is open, smoke and firefighting activity can be dangerous. No specific trail closures have been reported, but that could change as the fire evolves.

The environment ministry, which manages the reserve, has not issued a statement on access. The situation can change quickly, so watch for official updates.

The bigger picture

This fire is one of many in Ecuador this year. The dry season has made conditions worse.

Protecting páramo is crucial for water security. The fire highlights the fragility of these ecosystems.

Páramo is not just important for water. It also stores carbon and supports unique plants and animals, according to the environment ministry.

The loss of páramo can have long-term effects. Recovery can take decades, experts say.

What to watch next

Officials may update the burned area and containment status. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

For now, the priority is stopping the flames. The full impact on the reserve will be known only after the fire is out.

Crews will keep working until the fire is out. That could take days or weeks.

After the fire, experts will assess the damage. They will look at how much páramo was lost and what can be done.

Visitors should watch for official updates. The situation can change quickly.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Los Ilinizas fire? It is a forest fire in Ecuador’s Los Ilinizas Ecological Reserve. It started on 1 September 2026 and has burned about 200 hectares of páramo. Why is the páramo important? Páramo grassland stores water and releases it slowly. It feeds the streams and rivers of the surrounding highlands, so damage can affect the region’s water supply. Who is fighting the fire? Fire brigades from Mejía, Latacunga and Cayambe led the response. They were supported by the armed forces, the Red Cross, the environment ministry and local volunteer brigades. Is the fire under control? ECU 911 reported the fire controlled on 3 September, after two days of firefighting. Crews remained on site for mop-up, and the burned area is still under evaluation. Is the reserve closed to visitors? Authorities have not announced a full closure. Visitors should avoid active fire zones and follow local restrictions.

World.title: Bolivia VP Accuses First Lady Over Unverified Audio
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BOLIVIA · POLITICS

Key Facts —What happened: Vice President Edmand Lara released an unverified audio on 31 August 2026. —How big it is: The roughly eight-minute clip is central to a criminal complaint filed September 1 against Urquidi and Cerimedo. —What it means: The accusation exposes a public split between the vice president and the president’s inner circle. —The catch: Prosecutors rejected the complaint against the first lady within 48 hours for lack of evidence. —Who it hits: The complaint targets First Lady Urquidi and Fernando Cerimedo, who is in custody on a separate attempted femicide charge. —What comes next: Cerimedo faces a broader investigation with new charges, and no timetable for the audio’s forensic examination has been announced.

An unverified recording has opened a new front in Bolivia’s political crisis. It sets the vice president against the president’s own household.

The accusation and the recording

On Monday, August 31, 2026, Vice President Edmand Lara called a press conference in La Paz. He played an unverified audio recording that he said features First Lady María Elena “Bibi” Urquidi and Argentine political consultant Fernando Cerimedo.

Lara says the recording captures the two of them. He says the voices discuss removing Mirko Sokol, then the police commander.

The aim was to halt an investigation into a businessman he links to drug trafficking. Lara also says the recording points to Urquidi trying to influence the president through Cerimedo.

Neither the recording nor that reading has been tested by any authority. The recording is roughly eight minutes long, according to Latin Times.

Lara says he will hand it to prosecutors for a forensic examination. Bolivians call that a pericia.

Who is Fernando Cerimedo?

Fernando Cerimedo is an Argentine political consultant known for advising far-right leaders across Latin America. He worked for Argentine President Javier Milei, and regional reporting also links him to La Derecha Diario, a right-wing news site.

In Bolivia, Cerimedo worked with Rodrigo Paz’s campaign and the early months of his administration. Paz says he never held an official post and had no authorisation to represent the presidency.

Cerimedo is currently in preventive detention in Santa Cruz, Bolivia, on an attempted femicide charge. That is the charge Bolivia uses for the attempted killing of a woman because she is a woman.

Prosecutors allege he was behind the shooting of his former partner, the lawyer Nadia Beller, by two men. Cerimedo denies any involvement in the attack.

The first lady’s alleged role

First Lady María Elena “Bibi” Urquidi is the wife of President Rodrigo Paz. Lara’s complaint asks prosecutors to investigate her for influence trafficking and five other offences.

She has not been charged. Lara says a woman’s voice on the tape talks about pushing Sokol out.

One line reported in the Bolivian press, translated from Spanish, runs: “If he doesn’t remove Sokol, we can’t move forward.” There is no confirmation of who is speaking.

President Paz has defended his wife publicly. On August 27 he said he had “a career of public service, with a wife who has been irreproachable.”

He added that the scandal was not proof of anything.

Urquidi has not issued a public statement on the recording’s authenticity. Her personal position on the allegations remains unconfirmed.

The dispute over the voices

Minutes after Lara’s press conference, Cerimedo’s ex-partner denied that the voice is his. The lawyer Nadia Beller wrote in Spanish that it is not Fernando Cerimedo’s voice.

She said she knows his voice perfectly, including its timbre, his accent and the way he speaks.

Beller also said she does not recognise the woman’s voice on the recording. She pointed to irregularities in the recording that she said indicated it had been fabricated.

Beller is pursuing an attempted femicide case against Cerimedo. Her statement challenges a key element of Lara’s accusation.

No forensic analysis has confirmed the identity of any speaker. The recording remains officially unverified.

The legal complaint and its fast rejection

On Tuesday, September 1, 2026, Lara’s legal team filed a criminal complaint with prosecutors. It asks prosecutors to investigate the two for six alleged offences, including aggravated influence trafficking and criminal association.

The complaint also includes improper use of influence, criminal organisation, contracts harmful to the state, and illicit enrichment. The audio clip is central to the filing.

Within 48 hours, prosecutors rejected the complaint against Urquidi. They said her alleged participation “has not been detailed or determined” and cited a “lack of elements of conviction.”

In the same resolution, they expanded the case against Cerimedo by four further charges. Those are money laundering, usurpation of functions, material falsity, and use of falsified documents.

The political context

The row lands in the middle of a wider crisis for President Rodrigo Paz’s government. Paz remains in office, but his administration is fighting corruption allegations and has lost ground in Congress.

Prosecutors are looking at fuel smuggling, gold trafficking and suspected cover for cocaine flights. None of those cases names the president as a defendant.

Bolivia jailed a former president, Luis Arce, on corruption charges in December 2025. The current president has not been charged.

The vice president’s public attack on the first lady is unusual. It signals a deep split between Lara and the president’s inner circle.

What happens next

Lara says he will submit the audio for a forensic examination. No timetable for that examination has been announced.

Cerimedo remains in preventive detention on the attempted femicide charge and the illicit enrichment case. His defence maintains the shooting of Beller was staged.

President Paz has said he will not be swayed by recordings. He spoke on August 31, the day Lara released the audio.

Paz said: “I don’t pay attention to audios, I pay attention to what justice says.”

The political fallout could affect Paz’s ability to govern. The vice president’s accusations add to the pressure on an already weakened administration.

Background on Bolivia’s political crisis

Rodrigo Paz took office in November 2025. Nine months in, his administration is fighting corruption allegations and has lost ground in Congress.

The country’s institutions are under strain as the political elite battles in public. This feud adds another layer of uncertainty for Bolivia’s future.

For foreign investors, the political crisis raises concerns about policy continuity. Bolivia’s economy is fragile, and the infighting could delay reforms.

The situation is fluid, and no one can predict the next development. What is clear is that Bolivia’s political crisis is far from over.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the unverified audio about? The audio allegedly captures First Lady María Elena Urquidi and consultant Fernando Cerimedo discussing the removal of Bolivia’s police commander. The recording is not authenticated, and its contents are disputed. Who is Fernando Cerimedo? He is an Argentine political consultant who advised President Javier Milei and worked for Bolivia’s President Rodrigo Paz. He is currently detained in Bolivia on attempted femicide charges. Has the audio been verified? No competent authority has authenticated the recording. Cerimedo’s ex-partner says the voice is not his, and no forensic analysis has been completed. What charges does the vice president’s complaint include? The complaint asks prosecutors to investigate Urquidi and Cerimedo for influence trafficking, criminal association, organized crime, and other offenses. These are allegations, not proven facts. What does this mean for Bolivia’s government? The public feud between the vice president and the first lady signals instability inside the ruling camp. It could further weaken President Paz’s embattled administration.

World.title: Bolivia Fuel Regulator Takeover and Closure Plan
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BOLIVIA · ENERGY

Key Facts —What happened: Bolivia’s government took over its fuel regulator, the ANH, and plans to close it. —How big it is: The ANH oversees fuel supply and distribution across the entire country. —What it means: A new regulator will take over, but its name and structure are still unknown. —The catch: The closure isn’t done yet; the agency is only under temporary intervention. —Who it hits: Bolivians facing fuel shortages and anyone relying on stable fuel supplies. —What comes next: A new regulator is expected, but no timeline has been given for its creation.

Bolivia is short of fuel, and the government wants its fuel watchdog gone. So far it has only taken the agency over.

What the ANH does

The ANH is Bolivia’s hydrocarbons regulator. It oversees and controls the supply of fuels like gasoline and diesel.

It replaced the old Hydrocarbons Superintendency in May 2009. The agency monitors fuel distribution and logistics, and coordinates with the state oil company YPFB.

The ANH also conducts control operations against fuel diversion and smuggling. But the government says it doesn’t do enough of these operations.

In plain terms, the ANH is the watchdog for fuel in Bolivia. It tries to ensure that fuel gets to where it’s needed and isn’t stolen or smuggled.

Why the government wants it gone

On August 17, 2026, Hydrocarbons and Energy Minister Marcelo Blanco announced the decision to close the ANH. He said the agency ‘does not conduct operations’ and needs to be replaced with something more focused on field controls.

The government also points to broader problems in the fuel sector. There are allegations of corruption and fuel smuggling that the ANH has failed to stop.

Former hydrocarbons minister Álvaro Ríos supports the closure. He says institutions in the sector have had years of corruption problems and alleged diversion of fuels.

But there are no specific corruption cases named against the ANH itself. The criticism is more general, about the sector as a whole.

The replacement: a new regulator in the works

The government says it will create a new regulatory body to replace the ANH. But the exact name and legal form are not yet fixed.

Blanco said it could be “another agency, directorate, or another type of entity.” It would keep the same powers but do far more inspections.

The new regulator will also include formal participation by the Bolivian Police. This is part of the anti-corruption and anti-smuggling effort.

As of early September 2026, the closure has not been legally completed. The government has instead opted to intervene in the ANH and change its director while the new entity is designed.

The new interim director: Jorge Luis Gumucio

On September 3, 2026, Jorge Luis Gumucio was appointed as interim executive director of the ANH. He replaced Freddy Zenteno Lara.

Gumucio previously served as vice minister of energy planning and development. That is part of the hydrocarbons and energy policy area.

His appointment is part of the government’s intervention in the ANH, ordered by President Rodrigo Paz. The intervention is set to last up to 180 days.

Gumucio’s background beyond that vice ministry is not detailed in current reports. His focus is on managing the agency during the transition.

The fuel crisis context

Bolivia is facing a severe shortage of gasoline and diesel. Long queues and irregular supply have hit several cities.

The government blames logistical problems, especially at the port of Arica in Chile. More than 40 million liters of diesel were reportedly stuck there for days.

President Paz has called YPFB’s problems an ‘endemic illness.’ He has ordered a deep restructuring of the state oil company.

Fuel smuggling is also a major issue. Subsidized diesel is being diverted across borders, which the government says worsens shortages.

Policy measures and pricing changes

In August 2026, the government introduced a new reference price for diesel. It applies only to large-scale buyers, not ordinary motorists.

Supreme Decree 5676, issued on August 16, 2026, set the price at 18 bolivianos per liter for these buyers. That is about US$1.47, using the official rate of 12.26 bolivianos per dollar on September 2, 2026.

The decree covers three categories. Direct users buy 120 to 5,000 liters a month at service stations.

It also covers direct clients buying 5,000 to 19,999 liters at storage plants. And it covers large consumers known as GRACOS, who buy 20,000 liters or more at storage plants.

For these buyers, the price rose from 9.80 bolivianos (about US$0.80) to 18 bolivianos. That is an increase of about 84%.

Ordinary drivers filling their tanks still pay 9.80 bolivianos per liter. The government says the decree does not change the pump price for vehicles.

This measure is meant to reduce smuggling by narrowing the gap between subsidized and international prices. Officials say it will not affect the basic food basket.

The end of the fixed exchange rate

Bolivia abandoned its long-standing fixed exchange rate of 6.96 bolivianos per dollar in June 2026. The central bank now sets a flexible official rate.

On September 2, 2026, that rate stood at 12.26 bolivianos per dollar. This shift explains why prices are moving at all.

The weaker boliviano makes imported fuel more expensive in local currency. It also raises the cost of subsidies for the government.

For investors, the flexible rate adds another layer of uncertainty. Currency swings can affect any business that deals in dollars.

Intervention in YPFB and the ANH

Supreme Decree 5699, issued in early September 2026, placed both YPFB and the ANH under government intervention for 180 days. The move aims to fix the fuel supply crisis.

Hydrocarbons Minister Marcelo Blanco has said YPFB will step back from selling fuel over time. The company will focus on its core roles of import, refining, and storage.

The intervention allows the government to replace top officials and restructure operations. It is a temporary measure while deeper reforms are designed.

The ANH’s interim director, Jorge Luis Gumucio, will lead the agency during this period. His main task is to keep fuel moving while the new regulator is built.

What this means for foreigners and investors

For foreigners and investors, the uncertainty around the ANH’s future is a red flag. Regulatory instability can affect fuel prices and supply reliability.

The new regulator, once created, will have significant power over fuel distribution. How it operates will matter for anyone doing business in Bolivia’s energy sector.

The involvement of the police in the new regulator is unusual. It signals a tougher stance on smuggling but also raises questions about efficiency.

Until the new entity is legally established, the ANH continues to function under interim leadership. That means the rules of the game are in flux.

What comes next

The government has not yet issued a decree formally creating the new regulator. That decree is still pending, according to reports.

The intervention in the ANH is temporary, lasting up to 180 days. During that time, the government will design the new entity.

Observers will watch whether the new regulator actually improves fuel supply. The government has promised a ‘different vision’ focused on control.

For now, Bolivians continue to face fuel shortages. And the future of fuel regulation in the country remains uncertain.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the ANH in Bolivia? The ANH is the Agencia Nacional de Hidrocarburos, Bolivia’s fuel and hydrocarbons regulator. It oversees fuel supply, distribution, and control operations. Why is Bolivia closing the ANH? The government says the ANH is not doing enough control operations against fuel smuggling and corruption. It plans to replace it with a new regulator that includes police participation. Who is the new interim director of the ANH? Jorge Luis Gumucio was appointed interim executive director on September 3, 2026. He previously served as vice minister of energy planning and development. Has the ANH been officially closed? No, as of early September 2026, the closure has not been legally completed. The government has only ordered a temporary intervention of up to 180 days. What does this mean for fuel supply in Bolivia? The uncertainty adds to existing fuel shortages. The government says it will create a new regulator, but no timeline has been given for when fuel supply will normalize.

World.title: Venezuela Prison Transfers: 94 Moved From El Rodeo I
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

VENEZUELA · JUSTICE

Key Facts —What happened: On 3 September Foro Penal reported at least 94 political prisoners transferred out of El Rodeo I. —How big it is: Foro Penal has verified the destination jail in only 24 of those cases. —What it means: Foro Penal cannot yet say where most of the men were taken. —The catch: Most destinations remain unverified, and families were not informed in advance. —Who it hits: The transferred prisoners and their families face uncertainty about locations. —What comes next: Foro Penal is still checking where the other detainees were taken.

A rights group says dozens of political prisoners were moved from a Venezuelan jail, but only some destinations are known.
