What Foro Penal reported

Foro Penal, a Venezuelan rights group that tracks political prisoners, reported the transfers on 3 September. Its vice president, Gonzalo Himiob, gave the figure in a statement at 3:45 p.m.

Himiob said the group had received information of “at least 94 transfers of political prisoners from El Rodeo I.” He spoke in Spanish.

He added that Foro Penal had “verified 24 cases in which the destination jail is already known.”

The group is still checking the other cases. Himiob said, “We continue verifying the information.”

Foro Penal did not name the destination prisons in its initial statement. The group has not offered an explanation for the movements.

What El Rodeo I is

El Rodeo I is one of three jails in the El Rodeo complex, near Guatire in Miranda state. It was built in 1980 to hold about 750 inmates.

Foro Penal says political prisoners were among those held there. The prison has also held common criminals over the years.

Riots there in mid-2011 killed more than 30 inmates. About 2,500 prisoners were moved out afterwards.

Its exact population is not public. Venezuelan authorities have given no reason for the transfers.

The numbers: 94 transfers, 24 confirmed

The key figure is at least 94 reported transfers. But only 24 have a known destination, according to Foro Penal.

That leaves at least 70 cases where Foro Penal has not yet confirmed the destination jail. The group has not said whether the families of those detainees know where they are.

A second group, Clippve, has located at least 32 of the transferred prisoners. They were taken to Yare and Fuerte Guaicaipuro in Miranda state, and to La Planta in Caracas.

Clippve is the Comité por la Libertad de los Presos Políticos. It campaigns for the release of political prisoners.

Foro Penal’s count of 328 was made before the transfers. The group has not said how the movements affect the count.

How the count is put together

Foro Penal compiles its counts from reports by families, lawyers, and other sources. The group updates its numbers regularly as prisoners are released or new arrests occur.

The Venezuelan government does not publish its own count and denies that political prisoners exist. This makes independent verification hard.

Foro Penal’s numbers are based on its own tracking. The government may dispute them or say the detainees are common criminals.

The transfers add another layer of difficulty. Prisoners moved without notice may vanish from the count.

What the families know

Clippve raised the alarm on 2 September, as buses entered the prison. It said some men were moved without their families being told.

The opposition delegation at the dialogue table with the government raised the issue the next day. Dinorah Figuera, who heads the delegation and presides over the National Assembly elected in 2015, asked for the transfers to be reviewed.

Families are demanding direct contact with the prisoners, visits within the week, and full disclosure of destinations. Foro Penal is working to confirm destinations.

Until then, families are left waiting. They do not know if their relative is safe or where they are held.

The lack of notice is the core of the complaint. Families say they learned about the moves only through the news.

Some families have not heard from their relatives since the transfer. They do not know which prison to call or visit.

What a transfer means in Venezuela

In Venezuela, moving a prisoner between jails is a routine administrative act. But it becomes serious when the family is not told.

Venezuelan law requires prison authorities to inform the family of a prisoner’s location. The rules also require that lawyers be able to reach their clients.

Rights groups say these rules are often ignored in practice. A transfer without notice can leave a prisoner unreachable for weeks.

Lawyers lose contact when a client is moved without warning. They cannot file papers or prepare a defense if they do not know where the person is.

Foro Penal has not said whether the law was broken in these cases. It has only said that destinations are still being verified.

How the count has fallen in 2026

The count of political prisoners has fallen sharply in 2026. Releases began that January, after the capture of Nicolás Maduro on 3 January.

The incoming government announced a first wave of freings soon afterwards. An amnesty law then took effect on 19 February 2026.

An amnesty law then entered into force on 19 February 2026, producing 109 full releases. Foro Penal counted 436 people released from detention between 8 January and 24 February.

Foro Penal reported more than 573 political prisoners still detained as of 24 February 2026. By April, that number had dropped to 490.

It fell again to 404 in June. As of 31 August 2026, the count stood at 328.

What this means for the government-opposition talks

The transfers come as the government and opposition hold dialogue talks. The governing party, known as chavismo, has been in talks with the opposition since Maduro’s capture.

Opposition negotiators at the talks raised the transfers. They worry that moving prisoners without notice could undermine trust.

The talks have already produced some prisoner releases. More than 1,000 people have been let out of detention since January, according to Diario Libre’s account of the process.

No official response from the government has been reported. The impact on negotiations remains unclear.

What happens next

Foro Penal says it will keep verifying the transfers. It expects to release more information as destinations are confirmed.

The group has not said when it will publish an updated list. Families and lawyers are pressing for answers.

The Venezuelan government has not commented on the transfers. No official statement has been made.

Observers will watch whether the prisoners appear in future counts. If they disappear, that could signal a problem.

Foro Penal may also take legal action if it finds rights violations. The group has not announced any such step yet.

The dialogue talks could be affected if the transfers continue. Opposition leaders have already called for a review.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Foro Penal? Foro Penal is a Venezuelan non-governmental organization that tracks political prisoners. It provides legal aid and reports on detentions. How many political prisoners are in Venezuela? As of 31 August 2026, Foro Penal counted 328 political prisoners. This number changes as people are released or arrested. Why were prisoners transferred from El Rodeo I? The reason is not confirmed. Foro Penal only reports that at least 94 were moved to other prisons. Are the transferred prisoners safe? There is no information on their condition. Foro Penal is verifying their locations. What can families do? Families can contact Foro Penal for help. The group is working to confirm where the prisoners are.

World.title: Venezuela Supreme Court Renewal Advances
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

VENEZUELA · JUSTICE

Key Facts —What happened: On September 1, 2026, the National Assembly approved a reform to the law governing the Supreme Court. —How big it is: Every magistrate goes, principals and alternates alike, from the 20-seat court. —What it means: A new court could change rulings on business disputes, property rights, and political cases. —The catch: The process is tied to a political deal, so independence is not guaranteed. —Who it hits: Foreign investors, property owners, and anyone with legal disputes in Venezuela. —What comes next: The Assembly must name a new nominations committee and then appoint new magistrates.

A full renewal of Venezuela’s Supreme Court is now legally possible after a key reform passed. The process could reshape the judiciary and affect business and property rights.

The meeting that signals change

Diosdado Cabello met Caryslia Beatriz Rodríguez on Thursday 3 September 2026. She is president of Venezuela’s Supreme Tribunal of Justice, or TSJ.

Cabello runs the government’s politics and internal security portfolio. He is also one of the ruling party’s most powerful figures.

La Patilla reported the meeting on the basis of photographs circulated on 3 September. It did not give a location, and neither participant has described what was discussed.

The outlet noted the meeting came ‘just as the renewal of all TSJ magistrates is being prepared.’ That renewal is part of a broader political accord between chavismo and opposition sectors.

What is the Supreme Tribunal of Justice?

The TSJ is Venezuela’s highest court, similar to the U.S. Supreme Court. It has the final say on legal disputes, including those involving the government.

Its magistrates, or judges, are appointed by the National Assembly, the country’s legislature. A special committee, the Judicial Nominations Committee, screens candidates before the Assembly votes.

The court’s composition matters because its rulings affect everything from criminal cases to business contracts. A court that is seen as independent can boost investor confidence.

In Venezuela, the court has often been accused of being loyal to the government. Analysts at Transparencia Venezuela call this renewal the first real institutional test of the transition.

How the renewal process works

The process starts with a reform of the Organic Law of the TSJ. That statute sets out how the court is run.

On 1 September 2026 the National Assembly passed the reform in second discussion. The vote was unanimous.

The reform amends a single article, article 65, which governs the Judicial Nominations Committee. It does not alter the size of the court, which has had 20 magistrates since the 2022 restructuring cut it from 32.

The committee grows from 21 seats to 23. Twelve now go to civil society groups and eleven to lawmakers, so civil society holds the majority.

The Assembly then votes. Under the Constitution, appointing magistrates needs a two-thirds majority.

The political agreement behind the renewal

On 12 August 2026 negotiators for the government and the opposition agreed to replace every TSJ magistrate. This was part of a dialogue process aimed at a political transition.

Opposition negotiator Dinorah Figuera, head of the opposition delegation and president of the National Assembly elected in 2015, read a joint statement. It said the implementation calendar would start in August 2026 with ‘official announcements and concrete actions.’

The agreement also includes creating a body to review applicants’ credentials. This is seen as a first major institutional test of the transition.

The United States is sponsoring the negotiations, according to Infobae. The renewal is meant to replace all current magistrates, many of whom were appointed in 2022.

Who is Caryslia Rodríguez?

Caryslia Rodríguez is a lawyer who graduated from the Central University of Venezuela. She also has a master’s degree in military criminal law.

She was appointed a magistrate of the TSJ’s Electoral Chamber on 26 April 2022. That came in the restructuring that cut the court from 32 seats to 20.

On 17 January 2024 her fellow magistrates elected her president of the full court.

Her career has been marked by political ties. Infobae has called her a judicial operator loyal to the government.

Spanish daily El Mundo reports she came up through the youth wing of Acción Democrática, an opposition party, before joining chavismo. She led the Electoral Chamber that certified the disputed 2024 presidential result for Nicolás Maduro.

That ruling is why her role in the handover is watched so closely.

Why the court’s composition matters for business

For foreign investors, the TSJ is the final arbiter in disputes over contracts, property, and investments. If the court is seen as biased, it raises the risk of doing business in Venezuela.

Cases over expropriated property and unpaid state debts end up at this court. Who sits on it therefore matters to anyone owed money in Venezuela.

What a renewed court would mean for expropriation and contract disputes is untested. No party to the talks has said the reform touches pending cases.

The new balance on the nominations committee gives civil society a majority for the first time. That could bring more independent judges, but loyalty, not independence, may still be the test that decides who is appointed.

What happens next

The reform now goes to the Official Gazette for publication. Once published, the National Assembly will name a new Judicial Nominations Committee, according to El Nacional.

The committee will screen applicants and recommend candidates to the Assembly. The Assembly then votes, needing a two-thirds majority to appoint magistrates.

The negotiating table is due to resume around mid-September, Infobae reports. Pending items include creating the credentials review council and lifting political disqualifications, including those affecting María Corina Machado.

The next signal is the opening of the nomination process. How openly it is run will say a lot.

Background: the court’s recent history

The TSJ has undergone major changes in recent years. In 2022, the government restructured the court, reducing its size from 32 to 20 magistrates.

That restructuring was widely criticized by opposition groups. They said it cemented government control over the judiciary.

The current renewal effort aims to reverse some of those changes. The proposed reform would bring the court back to 32 magistrates.

This history explains why the renewal is so closely watched. It is not just about new faces; it is about the balance of power.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Supreme Tribunal of Justice in Venezuela? It is the highest court in Venezuela, with final authority over legal disputes. Its magistrates are appointed by the National Assembly. Why is the court being fully renewed? The renewal is part of a political agreement between the government and opposition to replace all magistrates. It aims to rebuild trust in the judiciary. How many magistrates will the court have after the renewal? The court will keep its current 20 magistrates, as the reform does not change the number. An earlier reform in May 2026 had already increased it to 32, but that was later reversed. Who is Diosdado Cabello? He is a senior ruling-party leader and government official. He met with the TSJ president to discuss the court’s renewal. What does this mean for foreign investors? A new court could change rulings on business disputes and property rights. But the process is politically driven, so independence is not guaranteed.

World.title: Brazil Scientist Warns of Strongest El Niño in 100 Years
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · CLIMATE

Key Facts —What happened: Brazilian scientist Carlos Nobre warned the coming El Niño could be the strongest in over a century. —How big it is: Forecasters expect sea-surface temperatures to exceed 2.9°C above normal in key regions. —What it means: Expect disrupted farming, hydropower, and fisheries across Latin America in coming months. —The catch: NOAA puts a 69% chance on the strongest El Nino since 1950, its records’ full reach. —Who it hits: Farmers, energy companies, and travelers in Brazil, Peru, and Central America face the biggest risks. —What comes next: Peru declared a state of emergency covering 893 districts across 22 regions on 1 September.

A top Brazilian scientist says the coming El Niño could be the strongest in over a century. Here’s what official forecasters predict and what it means for the region.

Nobre’s warning

Brazilian scientist Carlos Nobre spoke at the Fourth Latin American Green Economy Forum in São Paulo on September 3. He said the El Niño now forming ‘promises to be the strongest in more than 100 years.’

Nobre holds the Chair in Climate and Sustainability at the University of São Paulo’s Institute of Advanced Studies. He is also a retired researcher at Brazil’s National Space Research Institute, INPE.

He urged state governments to fight illegal fires between now and January. He said organized crime has kept burning the Amazon even as deforestation rates fell.

What forecasters say

The World Meteorological Organization said in late July that a strong El Niño is developing. It expects the event to strengthen between August and October 2026.

Its models forecast sea-surface temperatures to exceed about 2.9°C above normal in key Pacific regions. That is a seasonal average, not a single-day reading.

Columbia University’s climate forecasting institute, IRI, calls it a ‘remarkably strong 2026 El Niño.’ Most models expect a very strong event from August 2026 to February 2027, peaking late this year.

At the peak, 25 of 26 models put this in the very strong band. Fifteen of them go past +3°C, beyond IRI’s top category.

The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is known as NOAA. It puts the chance of a very strong event above 90% for late 2026 and early 2027.

No agency uses the phrase ‘strongest in 100 years.’ Their comparison records only go back to 1950.

NOAA goes furthest of the three. It gives a 69% chance that this event is the strongest since 1950.

How El Niño works

El Niño is a natural climate pattern marked by warmer-than-usual surface waters in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean. It shifts rainfall and temperature patterns around the globe.

In Latin America, a strong El Niño usually means heavy rain and landslides in Peru and Ecuador. It also brings drought to the Amazon, to northeastern Brazil and to Central America.

These changes can disrupt agriculture, energy production, and daily life for millions. The current event is still building, with the worst impacts likely in late 2026 and early 2027.

Farming impacts

Brazil is the world’s largest exporter of soy, coffee, and sugar. A strong El Niño can bring drought to the north and excess rain to the south, both of which hurt yields.

In Argentina, El Niño often brings wetter conditions that can help or hurt wheat and corn, depending on timing. The exact impact for the 2026-27 season is not yet clear.

Peru’s anchovy fishery is the world’s biggest by volume. Catches fall sharply in El Niño years, because warmer water drives the fish away.

No specific 2026 crop or fishery projections are confirmed yet. But the 1997-98 and 2015-16 events both caused heavy farm losses across the region.

Energy and water

Hydropower is the main electricity source in Colombia, Ecuador, and Brazil. El Niño can bring drought, which lowers reservoir levels.

Governments then ration power or burn costlier fuel instead. Past El Niño years have drained reservoirs in both Colombia and Ecuador.

The Rio Times found no current rationing warnings from Colombia or Ecuador as of September 4. But the risk is real, and officials are watching closely.

The Panama Canal runs on rainwater, so drought can force it to cut ship traffic. No restrictions have been announced for this event.

Government responses

Peru declared a state of emergency in 893 districts on September 1. It covers 22 of the country’s regions plus Callao, the port district next to Lima.

The decree lasts 60 days and cites ‘imminent danger’ from the 2026-27 El Niño. It came after regional and local governments said they could not cope alone.

In February, Peru declared a 60-day emergency in 179 districts across 21 regions after heavy rains. Peru’s then interim president, José Jerí, signed that decree.

Other countries have not yet declared similar emergencies, but they may follow as the event strengthens. The WMO warns that extreme weather is likely to increase in the coming months.

What this means for you

If you live in or visit Latin America, expect odd weather. Look for heavy rain on the Pacific coast, drought in parts of Brazil, and heat in Central America.

These shifts can disrupt travel, from canceled flights to closed roads. They can also push up food and energy prices as crops fail and hydropower falters.

Coffee, soy, and fishmeal are particularly vulnerable, so world prices could swing. Businesses should review their supply chains and contingency plans.

The last two very strong El Niños both did serious damage, and this one could match them. Early action can reduce the worst impacts, but the next year will be challenging.

The bottom line

Carlos Nobre’s warning is a wake-up call, but it matches what official agencies are saying about severity. His century-scale framing goes beyond what they assert.

The full impacts will unfold over the next year, affecting millions of people and the global economy. Stay informed and prepared if you have ties to Latin America.

No one can predict exactly how bad it will get. But the evidence points to a serious event that demands attention from governments, businesses, and individuals alike.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Carlos Nobre say exactly? Carlos Nobre said the El Niño now forming ‘promises to be the strongest in more than 100 years.’ That is the wording EFE reported from his speech in São Paulo. How strong do forecasters expect this El Niño to be? The WMO expects sea-surface temperatures to exceed 2.9°C above normal, which is very strong. NOAA gives a 69% chance of a historic event, and IRI calls it ‘remarkably strong.’ What are the main risks for Latin America? Heavy rains and floods in Peru and Ecuador, drought in the Amazon and northeastern Brazil, and potential crop failures across the region. Hydropower and fisheries are also at risk. Has any country declared an emergency? Yes, Peru declared a state of emergency in 893 districts on September 1. Other countries may follow as the event develops. How long will this El Niño last? Forecasters expect it to peak in late 2026 and continue into early 2027. IRI sees little sign of El Niño fading before about March 2027.

World.title: Ecuador Court Orders Arrest of Ex-President Bucaram
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

ECUADOR · JUSTICE

Key Facts —What happened: A court ordered the arrest of former president Abdalá Bucaram after a sixth hearing collapsed. —How big it is: This was the sixth failed attempt to open the sentencing hearing since July. —What it means: Bucaram faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted of organized crime. —The catch: The arrest order only takes effect when Bucaram is discharged from the clinic. —Who it hits: Bucaram, his son Jacobo, Oren Sheinman and Leandro Berrones are the four defendants. —What comes next: Police will arrest Bucaram upon his discharge and bring him to court for sentencing.

A court in Guayaquil has run out of patience with the delays in the COVID-19 tests case. Bucaram ruled Ecuador for six months in 1996-97.

The arrest order and the failed hearing

On September 3, 2026, a criminal court in Guayaquil declared the sentencing hearing in the COVID-19 tests case failed. The reason: former president Abdalá Bucaram did not show up, again.

The court then ordered his arrest. It told the police Search Block, a special manhunt unit, to watch the clinic where Bucaram is staying.

This was the sixth failed attempt to open the sentencing hearing since July. The case as a whole has run much longer, and dates back to 2020.

Prosecutor Lidia Sarabia called the situation ‘inadmissible, unheard of and unprecedented,’ according to Primicias. She also requested the arrest order.

Who is Abdalá Bucaram?

Abdalá Bucaram Ortiz was president of Ecuador from August 1996 to February 1997. That is about six months in office.

Congress removed him on February 5, 1997 with 44 votes, declaring him unfit to govern. It went on to remove two more presidents in the years that followed.

He then fled to Panama and lived there for about 20 years. Two cases from that time, over school backpacks and secret government funds, ran out of time in 2017 with no verdict.

That allowed him to return to Ecuador on June 15, 2017. Since then, he has faced new legal troubles, including the current COVID-19 tests case.

The COVID-19 tests case explained

The case is called Pruebas Covid-19, which means COVID-19 tests in Spanish. Prosecutors say Bucaram and others ran an organized crime ring that sold rapid COVID-19 tests and medical supplies during the pandemic.

The alleged scheme ran from March to August 2020, when Ecuador was in a health emergency. Prosecutors put it at 21,000 rapid tests, plus masks and other supplies.

The ‘Agentes AMT’ in the case name are officers of Quito’s Agencia Metropolitana de Tránsito. Prosecutors say they used their positions to escort the sellers from Quito to Guayaquil.

One of them, Leandro Berrones, is a co-defendant. Prosecutors have not put a money figure on the case in public.

The charge carries up to 10 years in prison in Ecuador.

Why the hearing failed six times

The sentencing hearing has been postponed many times. The latest delays are because Bucaram says he is hospitalized and recovering from surgery.

His lawyers say he had heart surgery on August 26. They say a new heart problem on August 31 put him in intensive care.

The clinic has not been named in public. A police officer sent to check on him could not confirm he was there, Expreso reported.

Hearings in a separate weapons case against him were also delayed, once by a blackout. That blackout hit the firearms trial on August 25.

Bucaram’s long legal history

Bucaram has faced legal troubles for about 40 years. He has been accused of embezzlement, defamation, and corruption, but many cases ended without a final verdict.

Bucaram was convicted of embezzlement in the Mochila Escolar case and of criminal defamation twice. But the 20-year limit on enforcing the embezzlement penalty ran out in 2017, letting him return without serving a day.

In 2020, he was arrested at his home in Guayaquil over alleged illegal commercialization of COVID-19 tests. That arrest was part of the investigations that led to the current case.

He has also faced a case over alleged illicit trafficking of firearms and ammunition. Hearings in that case have also been delayed, including due to blackouts.

What happens next

The court ordered the police Search Block to keep permanent watch on the clinic. When Bucaram is discharged, police will arrest him and bring him before the court.

Then the judge can finally read the sentence in the COVID-19 tests case. It is not clear when that will happen, as Bucaram’s health condition is not fully known.

The arrest order is not immediate. It only takes effect upon his discharge from the clinic.

Once arrested, Bucaram will be brought before the court. The sentencing hearing will then proceed with his presence.

Why this matters for Ecuador

Bucaram’s trial is part of a wider push in Ecuador to hold former officials to account. Several ex-presidents have faced legal scrutiny in recent years.

The case has drawn public attention because it involves a former head of state. Many Ecuadorians remember Bucaram’s chaotic six-month rule.

His removal in 1997 was a rare moment when Congress ousted a president. That decision was based on mental incompetence, a controversial move.

Now, nearly 30 years later, Bucaram is back in the legal spotlight. This trial is a test of whether the justice system can handle powerful figures.

The defendants and their roles

Four people are on trial: Bucaram, his son Jacobo Bucaram Pulley, Israeli citizen Sheinman Oren, and Leandro Berrones. Berrones is a former officer of Quito’s municipal transit agency, the AMT.

Prosecutors accuse Oren and Berrones of running the scheme. They accuse the two Bucarams of helping it.

The four were first detained in August 2020, weeks after the raids. The trial itself opened in April 2025 after seven earlier postponements.

Despite decades of proceedings and two defamation convictions, Bucaram has never served a day in prison.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why was the arrest of ex-president Bucaram ordered? The court ordered his arrest after a sixth attempt to hold the sentencing hearing in the COVID-19 tests case failed. The judge declared the hearing failed and issued the arrest order. What is the COVID-19 tests case about? Prosecutors accuse Bucaram and others of organized crime for selling COVID-19 tests and medical supplies during the pandemic. The alleged scheme ran from March to August 2020. Is Bucaram in custody now? No, he is still in a clinic under police surveillance. The arrest order will be executed when he is discharged from the clinic. Who else is on trial in this case? Bucaram’s son Jacobo, Israeli citizen Oren Sheinman, and Leandro Berrones are also defendants. Berrones is a former AMT officer. What happens if Bucaram is convicted? He could face up to 10 years in prison for organized crime. The sentence will be read once he appears in court.

World.title: Mexico Extradition Halted Again for a Senior CJNG Figure
World.content:
MEXICO · DEFENSE & SECURITY

Key Facts — What happened A federal judge suspended the handover of Audias Flores Silva, known as El Jardinero, to the United States.

— Who decided it Judge Alberto Ávila Muñoz of the Sixteenth District Court in criminal matters in Mexico City issued the order.

— The real story This is the second suspension this year in the same file, after an appeals court revived a dismissed challenge.

— The catch A suspension pauses the transfer while the challenge is heard; it does not cancel the extradition request.

— What else the judge ordered He instructed that the prisoner stop being held incommunicado at the Altiplano federal prison.

— The contrast Days earlier a different judge threw out a similar challenge brought by another accused cartel figure.

A federal judge in Mexico City has stopped the handover of a senior cartel figure to the United States for the second time this year. The court also ruled on how he is being held.

A federal judiciary building in Puebla. Federal district courts across Mexico hear the constitutional challenges used to contest extradition orders. (Photo: “Palacio de Justicia Federal del Sexto Circuito, Puebla” by CUTI1, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)
