A federal judge in Mexico City has again blocked a handover to the United States. The Mexico extradition of a senior cartel figure known as El Jardinero is suspended.

The order came from judge Alberto Ávila Muñoz. He sits at the Sixteenth District Court in criminal matters in the capital.

El Siglo de Torreón reported the ruling on September 2, 2026. Infobae carried it two days later.

The measure is called a suspensión de oficio y de plano. It is an immediate, automatic pause granted by the court itself.

Who El Jardinero Is, and Who He Is Not

El Jardinero is Audias Flores Silva. He is described in Mexican reporting as a high-ranking lieutenant of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, or CJNG.

Reporting has also described him as a possible successor to Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes. Oseguera, known as El Mencho, has led the CJNG for more than a decade.

A note of caution is needed here, because two names are often mixed up. El Jardinero is not Ricardo Ruiz Velasco, who is known as El Doble R.

Ruiz Velasco leads a CJNG unit called Grupo Élite. In August 2026 the United States offered a reward of US$10 million for information leading to his arrest or conviction.

The two men are separate people facing separate proceedings. Conflating them has been a recurring error in coverage.

Why the United States Wants Him

The American charges against Flores Silva are drug and weapons offences. They were filed in the federal court for the District of Columbia.

They cover conspiracy to manufacture and distribute cocaine, heroin and methamphetamine for import into the United States. A money-laundering conspiracy count is included.

There is also a firearms count. It covers the use of weapons, including an explosive device, in furtherance of drug trafficking.

None of these charges has been tested at trial. A Mexico extradition decides transfer, not guilt.

The Zócalo and National Palace in Mexico City. The district court that issued the suspension sits in the capital. (Photo: “Plaza de la Constitución – Zócalo de la Ciudad de México – 4” by ProtoplasmaKid, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

How the Case Reached This Point

The file has moved back and forth since spring. On April 30, 2026 judge Azucena Lazalde Íñiguez granted the first suspension against the transfer.

A judge later dismissed one of the constitutional challenges in June. That dismissal did not survive.

The Sixth Collegiate Tribunal in criminal matters reversed it. It ordered the challenge to be admitted and heard properly.

The new suspension follows from that reopening. It is the second time this year that a court has stopped the same Mexico extradition.

The Other Half of the Ruling

The judge did not only address the transfer. He also ordered that Flores Silva stop being held incommunicado.

The prisoner is held at Altiplano, the maximum security federal prison in the State of Mexico. Incommunicado detention means being cut off from contact with lawyers or family.

Mexican courts treat that as a constitutional question rather than a prison management one. An amparo is the standard remedy.

An amparo is a constitutional challenge available to anyone in Mexico. It is the same instrument used to contest tax bills, expropriations and, here, extraditions.

Not Every Challenge Succeeds

The contrast came days earlier and is instructive. On September 1, 2026 a judge threw out a similar challenge brought by another accused cartel figure.

Infobae, El Financiero and Excélsior all reported that dismissal. His transfer was not paused.

So the courts are not blocking extraditions as a matter of course. They are deciding case by case, and the two outcomes landed in the same week.

That pattern is easy to lose in headlines. One suspension does not mean the system has closed.

The Wider Picture on Transfers

Mexico extradition and transfer numbers have been high in recent years. El Financiero reported in May 2026 that 178 people had been sent north in under two years.

Several of those transfers were handled as group operations rather than individual extraditions. That route bypasses the ordinary court process.

Individual extradition, by contrast, gives the prisoner a lawyer and a judge. That is exactly what is happening in this file.

The tension between speed and process is the whole argument. Washington wants defendants in American courtrooms, and Mexican judges are applying Mexican constitutional procedure.

What Happens Next

A suspension is temporary by design. It holds the position while the substance of the challenge is decided.

If the challenge fails, the transfer can proceed. If it succeeds, the extradition order itself may have to be reissued or corrected.

Neither outcome is likely to be quick. The file has already been through a district judge, a dismissal and an appeals tribunal in five months.

For now the position is simple. Flores Silva stays in Mexico, and the Mexico extradition request stays unresolved.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the judge decide?

Judge Alberto Ávila Muñoz of the Sixteenth District Court in criminal matters in Mexico City suspended the extradition of Audias Flores Silva to the United States, reported on September 2, 2026.

Who is El Jardinero?

Audias Flores Silva, described in Mexican reporting as a high-ranking lieutenant of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel and a possible successor to its leader.

Is El Jardinero the same person as El Doble R?

No. El Doble R is Ricardo Ruiz Velasco, who leads a separate CJNG unit and carries a US$10 million American reward. They are different people in different proceedings.

Does the suspension cancel the extradition?

No. A suspension pauses the transfer while a constitutional challenge, known as an amparo, is decided. The underlying extradition request remains in place.

Have other extradition challenges succeeded this month?

Not all of them. On September 1, 2026 a judge dismissed a similar challenge brought by another accused cartel figure, and that transfer was not paused.

Sources: El Siglo de Torreón, Infobae, El Financiero, Excélsior, Univision, Proceso, US Department of State, US Department of the Treasury, Rio Times.

World.title: Costa Rica Renters Face Major Barriers to Buying a Home
World.content:
More than eight out of every 10 Costa Rican households that rent would face serious income barriers if they tried to finance even a relatively modest home, according to a new study showing how far property prices have moved beyond many local salaries. The report, Balance and Trends in the Housing Sector 2025, estimates that 81.4% of renter households face either complete exclusion from formal home financing or significant restrictions because of their income. That represents approximately 279,890 families.

The study was produced by the University of Costa Rica’s Graduate Program in Architecture, the Federated College of Engineers and Architects and the organization Gestionando Hábitat. It was released on August 20 but keep in mind the figure does not mean banks have rejected mortgage applications from 81.4% of renters.

Instead, researchers compared household incomes with the financial requirements for purchasing a model home priced at ₡76.5 million, or approximately $170,000. That amount corresponds to the maximum price used in the study for a property classified as social-interest housing.Researchers reviewed financing conditions offered by 26 institutions authorized under Costa Rica’s national housing finance system. They then compared those conditions with the average incomes of households currently renting.

The first major obstacle is the down payment. Depending on the lender, buyers could be asked to provide between 5% and 20% of the purchase price. For the model property, that would mean finding between ₡3.8 million and ₡15.3 million, or roughly $8,500 to $34,000.

Legal fees, property valuations, bank commissions and other closing expenses could add another ₡1.5 million to ₡3.1 million, approximately $3,300 to $6,900. Even buyers who qualify for financing covering 95% of the property could still need between ₡6 million and ₡7.3 million, or $13,300 to $16,200, before completing the purchase.

Monthly payments create another hurdle. Financing about ₡72.7 million over 30 years would produce estimated payments ranging from nearly ₡393,000 to ₡585,000 a month, or approximately $870 to $1,300, depending on the interest rate. Under the study’s most flexible calculation, households would need monthly incomes ranging from approximately ₡786,000 to ₡1.17 million to keep the mortgage payment below half of their income.

Using a more cautious limit of 35%, the required income increases to between ₡1.12 million and ₡1.67 million, or about $2,500 to $3,700 a month. Households in Costa Rica’s two lowest income groups fall below those requirements. Families in the middle group might qualify only under the lowest interest rate and most flexible debt limit. Even households in the fourth income group would not automatically qualify under the more cautious calculation.

Previous debts can make the situation worse since banks consider credit card balances, vehicle loans, personal loans and other obligations when deciding how much a household can borrow. Independent and informal workers may face an additional obstacle if they cannot document their income through tax returns, bank records or official payment receipts.

The problem is not limited to obtaining a mortgage. The study also found a large gap between local incomes and the prices being asked for homes in the Greater Metropolitan Area. Researchers examined 4,338 houses and apartments offered for sale and 1,824 rental properties, using listings collected by the UCR Real Estate Observatory in late June 2026.

They found that 47% of the properties for sale were priced beyond the estimated purchasing ability even of households in the country’s highest income group. For rentals, 56% of the properties in the sample exceeded the estimated spending limit for that same group. Among the lowest 60% of households, only 17% of the homes for sale and 6% of the rentals analyzed were considered financially accessible.

The researchers cautioned that cheaper homes advertised through informal channels or without real estate agents were probably underrepresented. The percentages therefore describe the properties in the study’s sample, not every home available across the region. Even with that limitation, the findings point to a widening mismatch between property prices, household earnings and the amount banks are willing to lend.

For many Costa Rican families, renting is no longer simply a lifestyle choice. It is the only realistic option. Foreign residents may have different incomes, savings or access to financing, particularly if they buy with cash. However, the report helps explain why property prices that appear reasonable to some international buyers remain out of reach for much of the local population.

World.title: How El Nino is choking the Panama Canal
World.content:
The Panama Canal will restrict the number of vessels transiting the crucial waterway from Friday for the second time ever due to drought caused by the El Nino climate phenomenon. Five percent of global trade passes through the canal that connects the Pacific Ocean with the Atlantic.

The waterway is set to reduce daily traffic from 36 to 32 ships a day in an effort to conserve water amid a severe drought likely to last until mid-2027. Canal authorities are also reducing the permitted draft of vessels — how deep they sit in the water — from 15.24 to 14.63 meters.

Panama has declared an emergency over El Nino, which raises surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean and causes global changes in winds and rainfall as well as erratic weather conditions. The canal’s incoming administrator Ilya Espino de Marotta has acknowledged the current “challenging” conditions.

Nothing without water

The 80-kilometer (50-mile) canal draws on freshwater that comes mainly from rainfall and is stored in artificial lakes. Without water, its locks that lift and lower ships at the beginning and end of the journey would not function. Each transiting ship requiers about 200 million liters of water, which is then discharged into the sea.

Water “is the most important resource for operations,” but “between April and August the accumulated rainfall deficit was 35.8 percent below the historical average,” the canal’s water manager Erick Cordoba said. And there are “no signs of recovery in the short term,” Cordoba added.

No signs of recovery

Forecasts indicate that the 2027 dry season, normally between January and April, will start a little earlier than usual and extend into May. In 2023 and 2024, El Nino forced a reduction in daily transits to 22 and the maximum draft to 13.41 meters.

That led to 20 percent fewer vessels and a 17 percent drop in tonnage, not to mention longer lines of ships queuing up. Further restrictions could follow those imposed on Friday. “If we don’t manage to fill the lakes in November, we’re going to have to tighten our belts,” former canal administrator Jorge Quijano said.

Worldwide repercussions

Long-lasting restrictions will lead to “higher shipping costs and longer waiting times” and therefore higher prices for consumers, Rebecca Bill Chavez, president of the Inter-American Dialogue said. A ship loses around 200 containers for every 30-centimeter draft decrease, according to Quijano.

That amounts to hundreds of units for large vessels that can carry up to 16,000. “We’re going to see a significant impact on the container sector,” which is the canal’s biggest source of revenue, he said. But Danish shipping company Maersk believes it is still “too early” to “speculate” about the impact.

The route mainly connects China, South Korea and Japan with the United States — the origin or destination of seven in ten containers that pass through the canal. Rising costs could “potentially affect US trade,” said analyst Natasha Lindstaedt of Britain’s University of Essex. If he wanted to, US President Donald Trump could argue “that trust and reliability in the channel have been lost,” Lindstaedt said.

The US-Israel war on Iran has pushed up traffic in the Panama Canal given the standstill the conflict caused in the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world’s oil and gas normally travels. The difficulties on both routes “put real pressure on global supply chains,” noted Bill.

Future-proofing

The canal authority plans to build a new 4,600-hectare reservoir on the Indio River to the west as a way to limit the effects of future droughts on operations. But this project would not be ready before 2031.

The canal’s watershed also supplies drinking water to half of Panama’s 4.6 million inhabitants via infrastructure that was designed almost a century ago.

World.title: Guanacaste Bakes While the Caribbean Floods in Costa Rica’s Split August
World.content:
August gave us two very different versions of Costa Rica’s rainy season, with unusually little rain falling around Liberia while parts of the Caribbean recorded some of their wettest conditions in decades. Liberia, the capital of Guanacaste and a major gateway for tourists visiting the northwestern Pacific coast, received just 26.2 millimeters of rain during the entire month, or a little more than 1 inch.

At the other end of the spectrum, Canta Gallo in the northern Caribbean recorded 1,781 millimeters, or about 70 inches, during August. The Canta Gallo total made August 2026 the wettest month recorded there during the station’s 30 years of data, according to figures from Costa Rica’s National Meteorological Institute, known as the IMN and Canta Gallo was not alone.

Limón recorded 1,031 millimeters, or about 40.6 inches, making it the wettest August there in 27 years of records. Farther south, Manzanillo received 769 millimeters, or about 30.3 inches, its wettest August in 28 years. The Manzanillo total was roughly double the previous record for the month.

The Caribbean’s unusually wet month was driven by a combination of tropical waves, the position of the Intertropical Convergence Zone and moisture carried into Costa Rica by Caribbean trade winds. This combination repeatedly produced heavy rain over the Caribbean and northern area in August and some of the most intense weather came in the middle of the month.

For example, on August 15 and 16, the IMN counted 20 records for maximum rainfall over a 24-hour period. Mountainous areas of the Caribbean received between 200 and 360 millimeters, roughly 8 to 14 inches, in just 48 hours. Nine weather stations in the northern and southern Caribbean also registered their wettest August 16 on record, with the IMN reporting that the affected stations had at least 10 years of historical data.

By August 17, some stations had already received more rain than they would normally expect during the entire month. In some locations, accumulated rainfall had reached between 100% and 170% of the normal August amount before the month was even two-thirds finished. The situation in Liberia could hardly have been more different.

Only 26.2 millimeters (about 1 inch) fell there during August, showing how sharply rainfall can vary across Costa Rica even during the same weather systems. The northwestern area of Guanacaste and the Caribbean coast often experience very different weather patterns because of the country’s mountains and the direction from which moisture arrives.

The contrast is especially notable for anyone traveling here on vacation since someone spending August along Costa Rica’s Caribbean coast could have experienced days of intense tropical rainfall, while someone staying around Liberia and parts of northern Guanacaste may have encountered considerably drier conditions.

The August numbers also show why broad descriptions such as “rainy season” can be misleading in Costa Rica. Weather can vary dramatically between the Pacific, Central Valley, northern region and Caribbean, sometimes over relatively short distances.

The IMN continued to report unstable conditions in the Caribbean toward the end of August. On August 28, for example, Canta Gallo recorded as much as 110 millimeters of rain in a matter of hours, while forecasters warned that the Intertropical Convergence Zone remained close to Costa Rica and that trade winds were continuing to push moisture toward the country.

August 2026 will therefore go into Costa Rica’s weather records not because everything was exceptionally wet or dry, but because opposite extremes were occurring at the same time.

World.title: ‘Don’t tell your boyfriend’: Man allegedly exposes himself to friend’s girl, apologizes and promises not to do it again in police mediation
World.content:
‘Don’t tell your boyfriend’: Man allegedly exposes himself to friend’s girl, apologizes and promises not to do it again in police mediation

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Ladyville man accused of exposing himself to a 20-year-old woman who is his friend’s girlfriend has apologized for his actions and agreed to stay away from her following a police-mediated settlement.

According to police information, a 20-year-old woman visited the Ladyville Police Station on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, and reported that she was at her boyfriend’s home on Stuart Street earlier that evening when an unknown man repeatedly approached the house.

She told police that the man initially asked for her boyfriend and later for her brother-in-law. She alleged that he subsequently stood near the doorway and peeped into the bedroom before approaching her again.

During the encounter, the man allegedly asked if he could show her something and told her not to tell her boyfriend. The woman reported that the man then took out his penis in front of her.

She said she immediately went inside and locked the door because she feared for her safety before contacting her boyfriend. The couple later visited the Ladyville Police Station and gave statements.

Police identified the man as a 22-year-old man from Ladyville. He visited the police station the following morning, where he was informed of the indecent exposure report, cautioned, advised of his constitutional rights and detained.

However, the woman had indicated that she did not want court action and instead requested mediation.

Police conducted the mediation on Wednesday night between the woman, her boyfriend and the accused creep. According to the police report, the accused was strongly warned to discontinue the behaviour and to stay away from the woman and her boyfriend.

The man apologized for his behaviour and reportedly promised that it would not happen again.

Police say the couple was satisfied with the outcome and agreed not to pursue court action. The parties reached a mutual agreement and the matter was settled.

World.title: The ghost of the age, the one thing Belize needs before any policy can work
World.content:
The ghost of the age, the one thing Belize needs before any policy can work

By Horace Palacio:

Today I want to give Belize a German word, because we need it more than any loan.

Zeitgeist. Zeit means time. Geist means spirit, or ghost. The spirit of the age. The ghost of the times.

Let me define it at the kitchen table. A zeitgeist is the background music of an era, the invisible weather of the mind, the set of assumptions a whole people carries without ever discussing them. Nobody votes on a zeitgeist. Nobody signs it into law. Yet it decides more than any law, because it decides what a people believes is possible, what they attempt, what they tolerate, and what they laugh at. Fish do not discuss water. Nations do not discuss their zeitgeist. They just swim in it.

And here is the claim I will now prove beyond disagreement. The spirit of an age matters more than the resources of an age, and Belize’s current spirit, not its size, not its budget, not its politics, is the heaviest thing this country carries.

First, the proof that spirit beats resources. Florence, in the 1400s, was a city of perhaps sixty thousand souls, smaller than the Belize District, with no oil, no empire, no scale. But it caught a ghost, a shared conviction that man could build, paint, bank, and reason magnificently, and that little town produced the Renaissance and bent the direction of Western civilization. Postwar Japan and Germany stood in literal rubble, poorer than we have ever been, and rebuilt into industrial giants within one generation, because the ghost of those years said one thing, we rebuild. Singapore’s swampy island caught a survival-to-excellence spirit and out-built continents.

And the clincher sits in our own family album. Between 1950 and 1981, a colony of people fewer and poorer than us caught a ghost. The Price generation’s zeitgeist said, we are becoming a nation, so build. And they built, the party structures, the credit unions from seventy five cents, the institutions, the independence itself, with almost nothing in their pockets but the spirit of their age. Same soil as today. Same smallness. Different ghost, different results. So let no Belizean ever again say spirit is soft talk. Spirit is the operating system every other program runs on.

Now the diagnosis, and I ask you to run this test honestly on your own last week of conversations.

What is the default dream of a young Belizean? Departure. The visa is the vision. What is the default explanation for anything broken? Politics, corruption, them. What is the default reaction when a neighbor rises? Suspicion, the claw, must be connections. What is the default posture toward the future? Waiting, for the government, for the season, for the rescue. And what is the default verdict on the country itself? Belize too small, nothing ever changes, da so it go.

That, my friends, is our current zeitgeist, and it has a name. Resignation, wearing realism’s costume. It sounds wise. It is merely tired. And here is its cruelest property, a zeitgeist is a prophecy that hires its own evidence. Believe nothing changes, and you attempt nothing, and nothing changes, and the belief collects its proof. The ghost feeds itself. Every column I wrote this year about the crab bucket, the waiting, the blame, the excuse anthem, was really one column about one ghost.

But now the pivot, and this is where the argument closes every exit.

Zeitgeists are not weather. They are made. Made by people, spread mouth to mouth, and, this is the crucial part, made fastest in small places. The same smallness that spreads gossip through Belize in a day can spread a creed in a season. Georgia changed its national spirit in a decade. Estonia did. Price’s generation did it right here without internet or budget. The stadium-sized cast I wrote about last time, the eleven thousand builders this country needs, is also exactly the size of crowd through which a new ghost travels at the speed of conversation.

So what is the zeitgeist Belize needs right now? I will name it plainly.

The Builder’s Zeitgeist. The spirit of the age whose first question, in every room, is not who do you blame, but what are you building.

Write its creed in contrasts, because a spirit is best seen against its opposite. From who you know, to what you can do. From suspicion of the climber, to study of the climber. From waiting for rescue, to working the problem. From the visa as the vision, to Belize as the project. From announcements, to receipts. From mi tired, to not yet.

And mark what this spirit is not, because I refuse to sell naivety. It is not optimism, optimism is a forecast, building is a verb. It is not blindness, the Builder’s Zeitgeist keeps every receipt this column ever published, the blackouts, the deficits, the scandals, all of it. It is the spirit that reads the whole report card, and then reaches for the hammer anyway. Earned hope, with a tool in its hand.

Now, the part I promised, why no honest reader can disagree. Strip away every jersey you wear, party, church, district, class, and answer one question. Would you rather raise your children among people whose daily question is what did you build, or among people whose daily question is who do you blame? There is one answer, and every human being alive knows it. Red knows it and blue knows it, the believer and the skeptic, the wealthy and the woman on 975 a month. Nobody, anywhere, prefers to live inside resignation. Which means the only possible objection left is the cynic’s, Belizeans will never change. And listen closely to that sentence, because it is not an argument. It is the old ghost itself, speaking through the objector, offering itself as evidence. The disagreement proves the diagnosis. The trap has no exit, only a door marked build.

And the new ghost, understand, is not a fantasy awaiting birth. It is already flickering, this very year, in the record. Public officers risked everything to press send. Belizeans oversubscribed the Hydro Belize share offer, queuing not for handouts but for ownership. The credit union movement crossed a billion dollars of pooled seventy-five-cent faith. Insiders broke decades of silence to argue numbers in public. Young creators built audiences from bedrooms. The new spirit exists, scattered, unnamed, waiting for a country to say its name out loud.

Which brings us to the mechanics, and to you, because a zeitgeist has no ministry. It is broadcast conversation by conversation, and every Belizean is a station with a daily audience. Every question you ask, every success you celebrate or claw, every excuse you accept or refuse, is a vote for the spirit of the age. Change your three household questions, what are you building, how can I help, what did we learn, and you have changed the weather within your reach. Enough weather, changed in enough kitchens, and the historians will do what historians do, look back at Belize in the mid-2020s and write, that is when the ghost changed.

The spirit of the age is not assigned, Belize. It is adopted.

The old ghost had its forty five years.

Adopt the builder. Starting with the very next sentence out of your mouth.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Belize City mechanic charged in fatal Phillip Goldson Highway accident that killed 77-year-old Erleen Gillett
World.content:
Belize City mechanic charged in fatal Phillip Goldson Highway accident that killed 77-year-old Erleen Gillett

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 58-year-old Belize City mechanic and supervisor has been arraigned on three traffic-related charges stemming from last week’s fatal road traffic accident that claimed the life of 77-year-old Erleen Elizabeth Gillett of Burrell Boom Village.

Gregory Nicholas appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Thursday, where he was charged with manslaughter by negligence, causing death by careless conduct, and driving a motor vehicle without due care and attention.

No plea was taken because the charges are indictable.

There was no objection to bail, and Nicholas was granted bail in the sum of $6,000 with one surety of the same amount. As conditions of his bail, he must surrender his passport, cannot leave the jurisdiction without permission from the court, and must report to the Belama Police Station every two weeks on a Friday.

He is due back in court on October 9, 2026, for disclosure.

The charges arise from a fatal collision at about 11:00 a.m. on Thursday, August 27, along the Phillip Goldson Highway near Enriquez Martinez & Sons Ltd.

Police allege Nicholas was driving a gold Dodge Caravan toward Belize City when Gillett, who was crossing the highway, stepped from the median divider into the path of the vehicle. She was struck and reportedly hit the windshield before falling onto the pavement.

Gillett was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where she was pronounced dead on arrival.

Nicholas was subsequently detained, his vehicle was impounded, and a blood sample was obtained. Police also served him with a Notice of Intended Prosecution.

A post-mortem examination conducted on September 1 determined Gillett’s cause of death to be multiple blunt force trauma injuries due to a road traffic accident.

World.title: ‘What if something happens?’ Parents blast school policy leaving children outside locked gate before 7:30 a.m. at Raymond Sheppard Primary
World.content:
‘What if something happens?’ Parents blast school policy leaving children outside locked gate before 7:30 a.m. at Raymond Sheppard Primary

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A group of concerned parents is calling on the administration of Raymond Sheppard Nazarene Primary School in Roaring Creek Village to reconsider its morning drop-off policy, arguing that children who arrive before 7:30 a.m. are being left outside the school compound without supervision.

The concern was raised in a letter sent to Breaking Belize News on Friday morning. According to the parents, the school recently circulated a notice advising that the gate will remain closed until 7:30 a.m., with the school bell reportedly ringing at 8:00 a.m. The notice lists the official drop-off time as 7:30 a.m. and pickup between 2:30 and 3:00 p.m.

The parents say the arrangement creates difficulties for those who must report to work early and have little choice but to drop their children off between 7:00 and 7:30 a.m.

One parent alleged that on Thursday morning several children were waiting outside when a teacher arrived, opened the gate to allow herself and her own children onto the compound, and then locked the gate again, leaving the other students outside.

“This raises a serious question: Who is responsible for the children who arrive before 7:30 AM? What happens if something happens to a child while they are waiting outside the locked school gate?” the parents wrote.

They are asking the school to consider opening the gate at 7:00 a.m. or establishing a safe, supervised area where students who arrive early can wait.

“Children should not be left outside a locked school gate without supervision. Their safety should always be the priority,” the letter stated.

Raymond Sheppard Nazarene Primary is a government-aided primary school located in Roaring Creek Village, Cayo District, according to the Ministry of Education’s school directory.

BBN has not independently verified the allegation involving the teacher, and no response from the school administration was immediately available.

World.title: “The timing is not right”: Mahler pushes back on hotel tax increase
World.content:
“The timing is not right”: Mahler pushes back on hotel tax increase

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Minister of Tourism Anthony Mahler says the announcement of a proposed increase in the hotel accommodation tax came out too early, and that discussions on it have been running for nearly two years.

Speaking to 7 News, Mahler said he met with the Belize Tourism Board’s Board of Directors before taking a Cabinet paper, and that both major industry organisations were present.

“There has been negotiations and discussions about this for almost 2 years,” he said. “In fact, private sector individuals have met with the Ministry of Finance, the Prime Minister and other people without the BTB there, and they knew it was coming.”

Mahler said he personally does not believe the timing is right and has told both the BTIA and the Belize Hotel Association as much.

He tied the proposal directly to sargassum.

“We have a significant problem in sargassum. It is killing us on the coastal communities that are important for our tourism product. How can we fund this?”

Mahler said around $20 million in equipment is needed to fight it, and that BTB has funded the effort alone so far.

“I had always opposed new taxes on the tourism industry, always, and that is a fact.”

World.title: Two charged after 625 pounds of seafood seized on Hattieville-Boom Road
World.content:
Two charged after 625 pounds of seafood seized on Hattieville-Boom Road

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Belize Fisheries Department has seized a substantial quantity of seafood suspected to have been illegally imported into the country.

Fisheries officers, with assistance from the Belize Police Department, intercepted a pickup truck along the Hattieville-Boom Road following a brief pursuit during an early morning enforcement operation on Thursday.

An inspection of the vehicle turned up 290 pounds of tilapia fillets, 335 pounds of jumbo shrimp and 14 octopus.

The vehicle and the seafood were seized and secured.

Two adult males were detained and charged with offences relating to the alleged illegal importation of fisheries products. They are expected to appear before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday.

The Fisheries Department reminded the public that importing fish and fisheries products into Belize requires the appropriate permits and full compliance with applicable laws.

The Department said unauthorised importation poses food safety and phytosanitary risks, and undermines legitimate local businesses that follow the regulatory requirements.

The Department thanked the Belize Police Department for its assistance.

World.title: $100,000 unaccounted for at a government school
World.content:
$100,000 unaccounted for at a government school

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): An audit has been completed at Louisiana Government School after reports that roughly $100,000 went missing over several years.

Minister of Education Francis Fonseca confirmed the audit is done, and that the next step is meetings with the principal, the bursar and others working in finance at the school.

Whether those meetings have happened, he could not say.

“I haven’t gotten any feedback if they’ve had the meeting yet,” Fonseca said.

He was clear on what should follow if the audit found what it was looking for.

“If there are any misappropriation that took place, they would make sure that those who were involved would be held responsible.”

Government schools operate on tight budgets, funded by taxpayers and supplemented by fees and fundraising that parents contribute to. A sum of that size, missing across multiple years, is money that did not reach classrooms, supplies or students.

Nothing has been made public from the audit itself and nobody has been named.

We will keep following the story.

Should the audit findings be made public?

World.title: “It was just time”: Espat explains Gamboa’s transfer after 11 years at SPU
World.content:
“It was just time”: Espat explains Gamboa’s transfer after 11 years at SPU

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Minister of Home Affairs Julius Espat says the transfer of Superintendent Aaron Gamboa from the Special Patrol Unit came down to management, not misconduct.

Gamboa led the SPU for 11 years, possibly a record for any police unit in Belize. He was moved with immediate effect on Monday.

Speaking to 7 News via Zoom, Espat said Gamboa is already officially retired and had been serving on an extension.

“He has been officially retired for, I think, six months now, if I’m not mistaken, and he was given an extension,” Espat said. “But if you have to plan for the future, you have to be able to look at things and bring in new people.”

He said the Commissioner recommended the transfer to a more administrative position.

“SPU for 11 years, that’s a good run. And we need other people now to have an opportunity.”

Espat was clear on his reasoning.

“There’s no bad intention in this move. But change is necessary, especially in the Police Department, it’s necessary to not have a commander in one position for too long.”

World.title: Gift from the heart
World.content:
Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton (second right) checks out specialised equipment donated to the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI) by Abigaye Smythe (second left), founder and managing director of I Have a Heart Foundation, on Thursday, as consultant cardiothoracic surgeon Dr Sunil Stephenson explains its function. Sharing in the moment is chief executive officer at UHWI Dr Sydney Powell. The equipment will give surgeons at the hospital the ability to perform minimally invasive open-heart surgeries. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

A cardiac patient facing her sixth surgery this December has donated US$4,000 in specialised equipment to the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI), directly upgrading its training resources and capabilities for minimally invasive open-heart surgery.

Speaking at the handover ceremony of the medical equipment at UHWI on Thursday, Abigaye Smythe, founder and managing director of I Have a Heart Foundation, revealed that leading this initiative is her life’s purpose.

Describing her connection to the project as lifelong, Smythe shared that she has battled heart disease since the age of seven, when she first began experiencing symptoms.

At 19, Smythe was delivered life-altering news when she was diagnosed with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy — the same disease that took her mother’s life. The rare genetic condition causes fat and scar tissue to replace healthy heart muscle, disrupting electrical signals and triggering abnormal heart rhythms.

Since her diagnosis, the philanthropist has undergone five surgeries at UHWI, making this donation a profoundly personal milestone.

“Because of my own journey, and understanding the fact that cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in Jamaica, I don’t advocate for heart disease patients from a distance. I understand what it means to be one [a cardiac patient], and I understand what it means to lose one. So this is my purpose. And that is why today is so meaningful,” she said.

“I’m not simply donating equipment to a hospital, I’m giving back to an institution that has cared for me, from testing and diagnosis in 2011, through five surgeries between 2012 and 2019, several emergency room visits and hospitalisations in-between, and an institution that will care for me again in December when I undergo my sixth heart surgery. I am investing in my fellow heart disease patients. I’m also investing in my country, in Jamaica,” added Smythe.

The donation builds on a partnership between the I Have a Heart Foundation, the Organisation for International Development, and a medical team from New York’s Montefiore Einstein Hospital. Since 2019, this partnership has provided more than $120 million in free open-heart surgeries at UHWI for 60 financially vulnerable patients.

Smythe noted that while this collaboration has been highly beneficial for both the patients and UHWI, she realised the hospital still lacked the capacity to perform minimally invasive open-heart surgeries without foreign assistance. She highlighted this gap as the driving force behind her efforts to lobby for and secure the new equipment.

“During the 2025 cardiac mission, the international medical team brought their specialised tools to perform minimally invasive open-heart surgery, and this resulted in the first such procedure being performed at UHWI, and possibly the first in Jamaica. They returned [home] and so did their equipment. And they came back in March 2026, for the mission. And when they performed the surgeries, and when they left, so did their equipment again,” she explained.

“So I said, ‘Okay, I want us to be independent, I want us to have our own, I want us to be able to perform minimally invasive open-heart surgeries outside of the mission’. And that is where the begging began. Thanks to our sponsors, we were able to raise the money, and we turned that vision into a reality, and purchased the equipment,” Smythe explained.

Looking ahead, she hopes this contribution will elevate care at UHWI, arguing that the island has no shortage of medical skill or talent but requires some help securing the tools to match that expertise.

“I’m excited to see how this capacity, this capability, will continue to grow. Today is not simply a handover, it is an investment in Jamaican lives, in our health care system, our medical professionals, and the future of cardiac care. My hope is that one day a Jamaican will never have to ask, ‘Can this procedure be done in Jamaica?’ They will simply know that it can be done here, and it can be done here at the University Hospital of the West Indies,” she said.

Expressing gratitude for the donation, Dr Sunil Stephenson, consultant cardiothoracic surgeon at UHWI, told the Jamaica Observer that the equipment was a necessity as the hospital continues to observe an increase in cardiac patients yearly.

“For a year, we perform about 80 to 90 heart surgeries. As a matter of fact, most deaths… in Jamaica are caused by cardiovascular diseases. So we do see quite a bit of patients who require our services and it’s mainly related to lifestyle illnesses. Some are genetic but most of what we do see is related to chronic non-communicable diseases. So there’s definitely an increase,” said Dr Stephenson.

He added that the equipment gave patients greater access to minimally invasive surgery which, he noted, offered significant advantages.

“The benefit in the sense that there’s less pain, they recover much faster. There’s still a shorter time in the ICU, and they need less time on the ventilator. So they recover much quicker and they’re more comfortable. And for females, they prefer the fact that they don’t have an incision in the middle of the chest because they’re very concerned about how the scar would look. So these instruments will actually help us to be able to do these procedures, and extend these procedures to the entire Jamaica, because that’s the population that we serve,” said the doctor.

For his part, Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton thanked Smythe and her team for the donation, and expressed confidence in the quality of staff at UHWI, adding that he had no doubt that the equipment would be put to good use.

“I just want to embrace the concept of ongoing effort to improve, and to make the services more efficient, embrace the concept of volunteerism and charity and gifting, and just say that for health, we have to see ourselves as a community and work together as a community. So thank you again, we appreciate it, and we certainly wish you the very best in terms of your own struggles and work, both as a foundation but also individually,” Tufton said.

World.title: Fit for purpose
World.content:
Mico CARE Centre interventionist Collette Demetrius (right) shows one of the centre’s retrofitted classrooms to (from left) permanent secretary at the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth, and Information Dr Kasan Troupe; The Mico University College President Dr Asburn Pinnock; and portfolio manager, education and special needs, Digicel Foundation Jamilia Crooks Brown at Thursday’s official opening of the facility that caters to children with special needs. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

AFTER more than four decades of supporting children with special needs, The Mico University College’s Child Assessment and Research in Education (CARE) Centre has upgraded its learning environment, unveiling renovations to five classrooms aimed at creating better spaces for students to learn, develop, and thrive.

The project, valued at approximately $24 million, was done in collaboration with Digicel Foundation and partners and provides classrooms with specialised sensory and occupational therapy equipment designed to aid concentration, emotional regulation, and physical engagement.

“The classrooms before were just regular classrooms. The rooms were very old, wooden floors, old aluminum windows, and so on, which are from the 1980s. Renovating these rooms makes the learning space more modern, more accommodating. So what we’ve done, we have looked at the needs of the clients that we serve,” Micro CARE Centre Director Dr Sharon Anderson-Morgan explained after the official handing over and ribbon-cutting ceremony on Thursday.

“So the rooms are now fit for purpose, they’re not just a regular classroom. We have children who are fidgety, for example, because they have attention-deficit disorder or any kind of disorder that causes them to want to move all the time. So we have the kick bands on the chair, they can put their feet on the chair. We have the wobbly things at the end of it, so they can rock and can move,” she added.

Anderson-Morgan pointed to several challenges faced by the institution prior to its renovation.

“The rooms were very, very hot. When you have spaces that are hot and you have bodies moving around, people are going to get a little agitated sometimes. So we’ve had children who react terribly to the heat. For example, we had some of our kids with autism and it gets hot and they would just start screaming,” she said.

“Also, we could not move the furniture as we would like to, because the old furniture did not allow for us to. If you’re going to move the chairs, it’s going to scrape the floor, some children are sensitive to that. They didn’t fit together the way these fit together,” Anderson-Morgan said, adding that the lighting at the facility was also an issue.

“We had these old fluorescent lights that also affected some children. There were children who would look up because they’re hypersensitive to visual stimuli. They would get scared because they think they’re seeing patterns in the ceiling. I remember one day we had to cover a portion of the ceiling with paper because the child kept looking up there because he thought he was seeing something else,” said Anderson-Morgan.

She underscored that the renovations will not only benefit students who enter the facility through its intervention programme, but also those who come in for assessment.

“Sometimes children come here for assessment and they are dysregulated. The clinicians now have the centre space to take them, calm them down before they can assess them, because before, sometimes they can’t get to assess them unless they come back because a child is screaming, running all over the place,” Anderson-Morgan said, adding that the centre assesses close to 1,000 children yearly.

She hastened to add that despite the centre being known to conduct assessments, its services extend beyond that.

“We do assessment, we do intervention, not just academic, because we have speech therapy. And we have occupational therapy, behaviour therapy, we have behaviour therapy for one group, and that’s only because we don’t have an on-site behaviour therapist, so we have to bring in the service. And we also have counselling services, we have a counselling centre up there, where even some of our kids in the intervention programme, they also receive counselling as needed, and sometimes their families need it as well,” she explained.

Permanent secretary in the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth, and Information Kasan Troupe welcomed the upgraded facility and lauded Digicel Foundation and partners for their investment in the special needs sector.

“We’re going to have a room that teachers will be exposed to improve opportunities to train and integrate technology because it is technology-enabled. We’re going to have a room that will build confidence in learners because here they have a safer space, a modern space that they can make mistakes, learn and grow and be strong because they are fully supported with specialists that can train them and support them in the way they should grow,” she said.

“You’re going to have learners who cannot communicate confidently. You’re going to have learners who will learn new skills so they can transform their whole realities in the future. That’s the promise of this investment,” Troupe added.

The Mico University College CARE Centre states on its website that it was established in 1980 as a centre of excellence, dedicated to child assessment and research in education. It was formed through a partnership between The Netherlands and Jamaican governments.

World.title: Malie Donn releases debut album Golden Child
World.content:
Malie Donn.

Dancehall artiste Malie Donn today released his debut studio album, The Golden Child, marking a major milestone for the entertainer who has steadily carved out a place among dancehall’s new generation.

The 21-track project, released through VP Records, follows several years of building his name with songs including Van Cleef, Body Tea, V6, Dirty Mirror, Suspect, Crook and many others.

“The Golden Child represents everything that brought me to this point: the pressure, the growth, the wins and the lessons,” Malie Donn said. “This project gives people a chance to hear more of who I am as an artist, where I want to take the music next and the versatility I bring.”

On Thursday, Malie Donn released the album’s title track, Golden Child, featuring fellow dancehall artiste Squash. The collaboration pairs Malie Donn’s melodic delivery with Squash’s distinctive style, while exploring themes of confidence, ambition and resilience that also run through the wider project.

The official music video for Golden Child also premiered on Thursday, providing the final lead-in to the album. Born Kimalie Hylton, Malie Donn is originally from Jones Avenue, Spanish Town, St Catherine, but grew up in Waterford, Portmore.

His passion for music dates back to his days as a student at Waterford Primary School and developed further while he attended Bridgeport High School. Malie Donn has emerged as one of the acts in dancehall’s newer wave, building a catalogue that has helped expand his audience locally and internationally.

The Golden Child also continues his relationship with VP Records. In 2024, he released The Grand Rising EP through the label, followed by the Leak the Hard Drive EP in 2025.

The album was preceded by Holiday, which arrived on August 7 alongside its official music video and offered listeners an early glimpse of a different side of Malie Donn’s artistry.

For Malie Donn, the release of his first full-length album represents an opportunity to present a more complete picture of himself beyond the individual songs that first brought him attention.

World.title: GOJ TAPS MARKET FOR US$1B
World.content:
The Government of Jamaica (GOJ) has gone to the international capital markets to raise a US$1 billion ($157.62 billion) unsecured bond to support its liability management strategy and budgetary objectives.

The prospectus was published on Wednesday through the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), three weeks after GOJ filed its registration statement to issue debt securities. According to a roadshow document seen by the Jamaica Observer, US$600 million is to be used to fund a tender/exchange offer, with the balance earmarked for general budgetary purposes. A source close to the matter also indicated that the new bond is expected to mature in 2037.

At the same time, GOJ launched the tender/exchange offer for holders of the three existing global bonds, tying the new borrowing directly to its wider effort to manage the country’s external debt.

“The Invitation is part of a broader program of Jamaica to proactively manage its external public debt,” stated the tender invitation to holders of the old bonds/notes.

The Government currently has US$837.53 million outstanding on its April 2028 notes, which carry a 6.75 per cent interest rate. The 2036 and 2039 notes have US$250 million and US$1.24 billion outstanding, respectively.

International Financing Review (ifre.com) reported that GOJ began holding fixed-income investor meetings on September 3, likely in connection with the new bond issuance, which will be listed on the Euro MTF Market of the Luxembourg Stock Exchange. Citigroup Global Markets Inc. and Scotia Capital (USA) Inc. are serving as deal managers and joint lead underwriters for the transaction.

If the value of bonds tendered exceeds GOJ’s maximum purchase amount, the government can determine how much of each series it will accept, applying different proration factors where necessary. This means it could accept less than the full amount tendered by holders of any of the eligible notes.

The new tender offer opened on September 2 and will expire on September 9, unless extended or terminated at GOJ’s discretion. Settlement is expected to be completed by September 17.

“The invitation is not conditioned upon any minimum participation of any series of Old Notes but is conditioned on, among other things, the pricing and closing of an international capital markets transaction in an amount and on terms and conditions acceptable to Jamaica,” stated the GOJ release.

The Government last executed a transaction of this nature in October 2023, when it spent US$237.4 million to redeem three notes with a nominal value of US$233.2 million. At the time, GOJ repurchased approximately US$99.7 million in two separate 2025 notes and US$165.15 million of the April 2028 notes. The tender on the 2028 notes represented 11.6 per cent of the amount outstanding before the GOJ offer.

That tender offer coincided with Jamaica’s first Jamaican dollar (JMD)-linked bond issuance on the international capital markets, worth $46.6 billion, or US$300 million. The instrument carried a 9.625 per cent interest rate and matures in November 2030.

Through the new tender offer, GOJ can extend the maturity profile of its foreign debt and reduce the amount that will need to be refinanced in the near term, in keeping with its broader debt management strategy.

The transaction, however, comes against the backdrop of a difficult start to the government’s 2026/27 fiscal year. According to the central government accounts for April to July 2026, revenue and grants came in eight per cent below budget at $353.84 billion for the four-month period. That was despite $18.04 billion in new taxes being implemented for the current fiscal year, with one company reporting that it paid $454 million in special consumption tax on sweetened drinks for May and June.

The revenue shortfall was largely driven by tax collections coming in $21.32 billion below budget, including a $13.27-billion shortfall in taxes on companies. Expenditure was also six per cent below budget at $387.27 billion. The Government recorded a fiscal deficit of $33.43 billion, wider than the budgeted $30.89 billion.

An overall surplus of $10.28 billion was recorded, compared with a budgeted deficit of $57.86 billion, largely because loan receipts of $130.62 billion were twice the budgeted amount. Based on the roadshow document, a successful bond raise would leave US$400 million, or approximately $63.05 billion, available for general budgetary purposes in the 2026/27 fiscal year.

“The effects of this natural disaster may continue to adversely affect the development and performance of key sectors of the country’s economy,” GOJ’s prospectus stated, regarding the impact of Hurricane Melissa.

The warning was included among the risk factors outlining Jamaica’s exposure to external shocks, including risks to the tourism sector.

The prospectus added that volatility in global energy prices may also contribute to higher domestic energy costs for Jamaica and could place upward pressure on inflation.

“While the full extent of the impact of these conflicts remains to be seen as of the date of this prospectus supplement, the effects of such conflicts could negatively affect Jamaica’s economic growth, inflation and fiscal revenues,” it said.

Final pricing details, including the interest rate on the new GOJ bond, are expected to be revealed in the coming days. Until then, recent sovereign issues elsewhere in teh Caribbean ofer some indication of where borrowing costs have been landing. Trinidad & Tobago refinanced a US$1-billion bond in January at 6.50 per cent for 10 years before issuing a US$800-million bond at 6.20 per cent for 12 years. Trinidad currently carries a higher international credit rating than Jamaica, although S&P Global Ratings has assigned it a negative outlook, compared with Jamaica’s stable outlook.

World.title: ELITE COMPANY!
World.content:
Oblique Seville (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

WORLD champion Oblique Seville will be gunning for his first Wanda Diamond League title when he lines up in the men’s 100m on the opening day of the two-day Diamond League athletics final at King Baudouin Stadium in Brussels, Belgium.

Seville is one of nine Jamaicans down to compete today with another eight set for Saturday.

He is coming off a confidence boosting win in Poland on August 23, and is hoping to join 100m sprinters Usain Bolt, Asafa Powell and Ackeem Blake as Jamaican men who have won the Diamond trophy.

Following his win in Poland, in which he clocked 9.83 seconds to break the meet record, Seville had said he was focused on ending the season on a high.

“I am just having fun. There are great things ahead of me. Many sprinters ran under 10.00s, that is really special. For the rest of the season I would like to keep winning and the next win should be in Brussels.”

He will have his hands full and will need to be at his best as he lines up against a tough field that includes Nigeria’s Kayinsola Ajayi, who has beaten the Jamaican twice this year, Commonwealth Games champion Emmanuel Eseme of Cameroon, Akani Simbine of South Africa and Trayvon Bromell of the United States.

Jamaicans have won at least one Diamond League title in the 16 years that the global series has been contested.

Today, Rushell Clayton, in the women’s 400m hurdles; Orlando Bennett, in the 110m hurdles; Tajay Gayle and Wayne Pinnock, in the men’s long jump; Romaine Beckford, in the men’s high jump; Roje Stona, in the men’s discus throw; Danniel Thomas-Dodd, in the women’s shot put; and Ackelia Smith, in the women’s triple jump, will be hoping to add their names to the list.

Clayton, who is coming off a win at the prestigious ISTAF Berlin on Sunday, has been consistent through the Diamond League series.

The event in Brussels could be decided between points leader Emma Zapletalova of Slovakia, who lost in the series for the first time after she hit a hurdle in Zurich as world leader Anna Cockrell sped to victory.

Veteran American Dalilah Muhammad, who has announced she will retire at the end of this season, and Belgium’s Paulien Couckuyt are expected to challenge for podium places.

Bennett, the World Athletics Championships medallist, is to take on a handful of Americans, led by world record holder Ja’Kobe Tharp in the 110m hurdles.

Tharp’s compatriots Jamal Britt and Trey Cunningham will be expected to give him competition,

Former world champion Tajay Gayle will be hoping to continue his late season improvement after he jumped a season’s best 8.43m in Zurich. There, he challenged world leader Miltiadis Tentoglou of Greece before falling just short.

Gayle and Pinnock will hope to provide robust competition for Tentoglou, who has lost just once in 15 outdoor meets this year.

Beckford is enjoying his best season as a professional and cleared 2.29m in Poland, just off his season’s best 2.30m. He is down to take on world leader JuVaughn Harrison of the United States, Gianmarco Tamberi of Italy, and Oleh Doroshchuk of Ukraine, all of whom have cleared 2.32m this year.

Stona is set to meet world leader Matthew Denny of Australia on Australia in the men’s discus throw, Mykolas Alekna of Lithuania, and Kristjan Ceh of Slovenia, all of whom have thrown over 72.00m this season.

Thomas-Dodd faces two of the best women’s shot-putters in the last decade or so, Jessica Schilder of Netherlands and Chase Jackson of the USA, both of whom have thrown beyond 21 metres this season. Back-to-back Commonwealth Games champion Sahara Mitton of Canada is also expected to feature.

Ackelia Smith is to line up in what is expected to be an explosive women’s triple jump that will see four jumpers who have gone over 15 metres.

World leader Thea Lafond of Dominica will hope to end the series on a high, but will be challenged by Cubans Davisleydi Velazco and Leyanis Perez Hernandez and Senegal’s Saly Sarr.

World.title: ATL Automotive drives  into Ocho Rios
World.content:
ATL Automotive’s new location at the Ocho Rios Bypass Plaza, St Ann, was officially opened on Friday, August 28.

The ATL Automotive Group opened its ninth location on Friday, August 28, at the Ocho Rios Bypass Plaza, St Ann.

“My late incredible father grew up about 1,000 feet east of where we are in this incredible town, and as a youngster his mother, my grandmother, ran a retail store here. And the genius of what became ATL 58 years later was consummated right here in the town of Ocho Rios. So, being here 58 years later, opening a brand new facility, I want to recognise my dad, and all the people that have worked for ATL all those years and that have gotten us to where we are,” Adam Stewart, executive chairman, ATL Automotive Group, told guests at the grand opening event.

Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda, who is the Member of Parliament for St Ann North Eastern, welcomed the investment in the constituency.

“This evening is a night to congratulate and to mark a particular milestone. It is good to see commerce return to Ocho Rios in this way,” said Samuda.

Sloane Jackson, general manager, ATL Ocho Rios, was also on hand to reiterate the further economic contribution the new showroom will make.

“Almost 20 of the people that work for me come from St Mary or from St Ann. We’re hiring locally. We’re training local talent, and we’re using that local talent to bring the goods and services of ATL to the customer,” explained Jackson.

Pointing out that the showroom had been functional since April, Jackson said, “We’ve been selling cars in May, June, July, August, so we’ve been operational for four months. We’ve also been servicing for that time.”

The brand new facility will host sales, service and parts for nine of the ATL Automotive Group’s brands — Honda, Kia, Porsche, Audi, MG, Omoda Jaecoo, Foton, and BYD. The 3,150-square-foot showroom can accommodate six display cars, plus one space for customer delivery, while up to 12 models can be kept externally. The parts and service bays are of similar size to the main showroom.

“Our staff complement is 24. We’re looking to grow that to 30 before the end of the year, and with our continuous growth, it might get to 40 by the end of next year,” said Jackson.

The four service bays are set up to handle the Kia and Honda brands at a collective 16 units a day. Service support for BYD, MG, and Foton is expected to arrive at the end of the year.

Jackson explained that the showroom eases the burden on customers in the north-western side of the island, as they will no longer have to make the long trek to either Montego Bay or Kingston to view a unit, purchase one of the nine brands, or have general service done on their ATL Automotive vehicle.

“In the month of September we’re starting with a discount of 15 per cent on parts and labour,” said Jackson.

The site will also house an Appliance Traders Limited store, replacing the Newlin Street, Ocho Rios, location.

World.title: How Dis Mek? From bean to brew – Jamaican Blue Mountain coffee
World.content:
Jamaica’s Blue Mountain coffee, recognised among the finest coffees in the world, is a staple for many locals. But, how do we get the yummy aromatic drink from sweet red fruit?

This week, the Jamaica Observer travels high up into the Blue Mountains to hear from the Managing Director of the Mavis Bank Coffee Factory, Dr Norman Grant, who details ‘How Dis Mek!’

World.title: UPDATE: Robert Morgan orders investigation into MoBay perimeter road death
World.content:
A police vehicle at the scene where a engineer died while died while working on a section of the Montego Bay bypass.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Minister with Responsibility for Works Robert Morgan says he is deeply saddened and has ordered an investigation following the death of a supervising engineer at the Montego Bay Perimeter Road Project on Thursday.

“On behalf of the Government, the ministry and our implementing agencies, I extend sincere condolences to the family, loved ones and colleagues of the deceased. We share their grief at this profoundly difficult time,” said Morgan.

The statement comes hours after the engineer died from injuries he sustained after being run over by a truck while carrying out his duties along a section of the roadway, also referred to as the Montego Bay bypass in St James.

READ: Engineer dies after being crushed by truck while working on MoBay bypass

In acknowledging the incident, Morgan said an investigation has been opened.

“I have directed that a thorough investigation be conducted into the circumstances surrounding the incident. The contractor, China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), is required to cooperate fully with all relevant authorities and ensure that the facts are established promptly and transparently.

He expressed deep regret at the death of the engineer.

“A tragedy of this nature should never occur on any of our worksites. No deadline, project target or operational consideration is more important than the safety and life of a worker,” he stressed

“The protection of every person working on our infrastructure projects is non-negotiable. We remain resolute in our commitment of ensuring the safety of every worker,” Morgan concluded.

World.title: France downplays SpaceX, Blue Origin snub of ‘worst Macron-organized’ summit
World.content:
Six participants with first-hand knowledge of the summit's organization described it to POLITICO as a poorly coordinated event with an unclear outcome. They were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.

“It’s falling behind schedule, it hasn’t really been coordinated with the major players in the European space sector, and it’s not entirely clear what its purpose is,” said a senior space expert involved in the summit’s preparation.

“And now that the White House has effectively decided to use it against Emmanuel Macron, it’s becoming even more awkward — it shows that, from a diplomatic standpoint, they didn’t do what they should have done,” they added.

Next week’s event aims to gather the international community — including leaders, large corporations, startups and researchers — to discuss issues including the regulation of space activities, competitiveness, security and defense, and space exploration.

Macron is keen to ensure that France and Europe remain credible space powers, with an independent launch capability and their own global satellite communications system, in an effort to reduce dependence on U.S. technology.

The French president's office insisted Friday that the absence of SpaceX and Blue Origin — two of the world's leading space companies — will have little impact on the summit.

World.title: Witkoff and Kushner set to visit Moscow then Kyiv on Sunday
World.content:
Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff listen as Vice President JD Vance speaks during a news conference. | Pool photo by Jacquelyn Martin/Getty Images

The men have been key U.S. mediators in the stalled Ukraine peace talks.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s special envoys Steven Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Moscow and Kyiv in the coming days in an apparent attempt to restart stalled negotiations to end the Ukraine war, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Telegram.

“We discussed today that Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Moscow and then Kyiv on Sunday,” the Ukrainian president wrote.

No details about the substance of the meetings have been released, but a U.S. official told CNN Friday that Witkoff and Kushner intend to press for a diplomatic solution to end the conflict.

World.title: Farage-Bardella show of unity tries to paper over immigration sticking points
World.content:
The document Farage and Bardella signed is only binding if the two parties come to power, and it says France will “will ordinarily accept” migrants intercepted in the Channel — potentially leaving wiggle room for Paris to reject them in some cases. Farage called the line “legalese” at a press conference alongside Bardella.

“As Australia proved in 2012, once you provide no incentive to pay a trafficker money to be taken across a stretch of water, in very very short order, the business model will be broken,” Farage said.

But Farage was not asked about the fact that the phrase does not even appear in the French version of the agreement. A National Rally official, granted anonymity to discuss the agreement’s finer points, said the French translation is the “final” version of the agreement.

The memorandum in both languages says the French will be responsible for deporting migrants to their countries of origin, and that the costs of policing operations will be assessed later. It adds that that France will do “its upmost” to stop departures.

“If France gains control of its borders there will be no departures [from French shores],” Bardella said in a speech at the conference. “If we end up doing pushbacks, it would be a failure of our government, it would mean that we have let dozens of thousands of people enter France illegally,” he added.

And the National Rally has long vowed to submit its immigration plans to a referendum in France, which is a lengthy and uncertain process that could get derailed even Bardella’s mentor, Marine Le Pen, wins the presidential election next year. Polls have consistently showed she is the front-runner.

World.title: Farage plans fall visit with Le Pen in France
World.content:
The official added that Farage plans a series of other visits to leaders on the European right before the end of 2026.

Farage has had a long association with Marine Le Pen and interviewed her for his radio show in 2017. He said Friday that while he would not have struck a deal with the National Front founded by her father Jean-Marie Le Pen, her rechristened party had moved away from “extreme elements.”

The relationship has not always been so harmonious. Farage said in 2024 that RN’s economic policies would be a “disaster” for France and “even worse for the economy than the current lot.”

However, the two parties have forged closer links over their hard line on immigration issues. Le Pen is the favorite in the first round of voting in France’s 2027 presidential election, while POLITICO’s Poll of Polls now has Farage’s Reform UK one percentage point behind the ruling Labour Party ahead of the next general election, due by 2029.

Farage alluded to a return visit from the conference stage in Birmingham after Bardella’s speech, which he gave in English — a rare move for him in public. Farage said: “The only downside is I think they’re going to invite me to go to Paris and I’ll have to speak in French, but never mind, we’ll get there.”

World.title: Russian drone strike hits security service headquarters in Kyiv
World.content:
Smoke rises above the Kyiv skyline following a drone strike on Sept. 2, 2026. | Sergei Supinsky/AFP via Getty Images

Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked the SBU acting chief to prepare an attack that would “mirror, if possible” the strike on his office.

A Russian drone attack on Friday afternoon struck the central Kyiv headquarters of the Security Service of Ukraine, the state’s top counterintelligence agency, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

The attack “directly” targeted the office of Oleksandr Poklad, the acting head of the SBU, Zelenskyy wrote on his Telegram channel.

Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko separately said that nine people had been injured in a fire following a drone strike “on a non-residential building in the Shevchenkivskyi district,” where the SBU headquarters are located. Zelenskyy said on Telegram that he spoke with Poklad after the attack, while Ukrainian Pravda reported that he was not in his office at the time of the strike.

World.title: French government promises €1B for drought-stricken farmers
World.content:
Three schemes account for the bulk of the government’s spending under the new plan.

France will speed up payments under its “national solidarity” scheme designed to compensate for crop losses. It will be topped up to a total of €520 million, provided the country's 2027 budget is duly adopted.

An “agricultural recovery fund” of €235 million aims to provide targeted support for the hardest-hit and most vulnerable farms across the produce, cereal and livestock sectors.

Finally, a targeted tax relief scheme on unbuilt land will cut €330 million in tax revenue for the state. The government is also considering extending a program helping farmers to purchase fertilizer and non-road agricultural diesel.

Genevard also suggested that the retail sector could "play its part" by keeping price rises in check.

Part of her plan is already funded for this year, but more cash will need to be allocated in next year's budget, which is set to be presented by Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu at the end of September.

World.title: Nigel Farage: Departing aides guilty of only ‘loose pub talk’
World.content:
The Reform UK boss said his party has done nothing wrong, but also that the comments captured in an undercover video were ‘human error.’

BIRMINGHAM, England — Two top Reform UK aides forced to step down amid an undercover donations sting were guilty of untrue boasts and “loose pub talk,” party leader Nigel Farage claimed Friday.

“There was certainly human error here,” Farage acknowledged during a press conference alongside National Rally vice president Jordan Bardella, invited to celebrate a joint policy rollout on migration. “It should not have happened.”

Dan Jukes, Farage’s long-term media chief, and James Orr, his senior policy adviser, stepped down Friday morning after Channel 4 broadcast footage apparently showing them agreeing to take donations from a foreign benefactor via a middle-man in the U.K. Experts allege taking the cash and then seeking to hide its provenance could be a breach of U.K. electoral law.

World.title: Le Pen rivals seize on National Rally’s Ukraine divide
World.content:
"We turn off the tap," Aliot said of aid to Ukraine in a television interview, pointing to France's fiscal overstretch and problems in financing areas like health and education. He stressed his party's strong support for Ukraine and condemned Russia for its invasion, but underlined: "Who pays for the war?"

Philippe and Attal — fighting to become the main center-right presidential candidate — both fired back.

"Cutting off aid to Ukraine means playing into Russia’s hands," Philippe posted on X. "The National Rally has changed its position on just about everything, except for its support of Putin’s regime — a stance that runs counter to French and European interests."

"You’ve just heard the 'foreign-backed' party speak ... The National Rally is once again demonstrating its subservience to Russia," echoed Attal.

Le Pen, who's currently leading in opinion polls, responded: "Since Russia's aggression against Ukraine, I have been demanding that France urgently convene a major conference for peace in order to contribute, not to the prolongation of a bloodbath, but to a diplomatic resolution of this abominable war."

However, she didn't repeat Aliot's comments on France's inability to continuing to provide military aid to Ukraine.
