World.title: Bond yields are surging globally but why aren’t equities falling?
World.content:
The 30-year US Treasury yield remains above 5%, near levels last seen in 2007.

 

At the same time, government borrowing costs have climbed to multi-decade highs across Germany, Japan and the UK.

By almost any conventional measure, this should be bad news for equity markets.

Higher bond yields raise borrowing costs, pressure equity valuations and give investors a more attractive alternative to shares.

Yet equities have barely blinked.

The S&P 500 is up roughly 13% this year and sits less than 1% below its 13 August record. Europe’s STOXX 600 has gained about 9.5%, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 has surged more than 27%.

That leaves investors with a puzzle: if higher yields are supposed to hurt stocks, why are equity markets still so resilient?

The answer may lie not in how high yields are, but in why they are rising.

Higher yields can be a symptom of economic strength

New York Fed President JohnWilliams offered an unusually important clue this week.

Speaking to CNBC, Williams said the rise in long-term yields was largely being driven by economic strength and investment in artificial intelligence and data centres.

“What’s driving it…is really a strong U.S. economy and a strong economic outlook fuelled by big investments in AI and data centres and technology in general,” Williams said.

That changes the equation for investors.

If yields rise because investors expect stronger growth, companies may also generate stronger revenues and profits.

Higher financing costs become a headwind, but rising earnings can offset part of that pressure.

Williams made the distinction even clearer. He said it was not necessarily a case of financial conditions weakening the economy.

“It’s more about the economy affecting financial conditions,” he said.

Kevin Warsh sees an economy still absorbing the pressure

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh made a version of the same argument at Jackson Hole on 28 August.

Warsh said real consumer spending had increased by more than 2% over the previous four quarters. Private domestic final purchases, a measure combining consumption and investment, had risen at almost a 3% annual pace during 2026.

He also highlighted a labour market that remains relatively stable.

“The jobless rate, at 4.1 percent, remains low by historical standards and has not changed much for a couple of years,” Warsh said.

More importantly for the bond-equity debate, Warsh said:

“On balance, I would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive.”

That is a remarkable statement in an environment where long-term borrowing costs have risen sharply.

It suggests that higher yields have not yet translated into the kind of financial tightening that would normally threaten the economic cycle.

The earnings boom is giving stocks a cushion

The strongest support for equities is arithmetic, and it comes from company results.

According to FactSet's Earnings Insight published on 28 August, with 97% of the S&P 500 having reported second-quarter results, 86% beat earnings estimates and 77% beat on revenue, both above their five-year and 10-year averages.

Blended earnings growth for the quarter stands at 52%, which would be the fastest since the second quarter of 2021.

Revenue grew 15.5% and the net profit margin reached 17%, the highest FactSet has recorded since it began tracking the measure in 2009.

Even the bond vigilantes are not panicking yet

The most interesting voice in this debate may be Ed Yardeni, a well-known Israeli-born American economist and the president of Yardeni Research.

Yardeni coined the term “bond vigilantes” in 1983 to describe investors who pressure governments through the bond market when they believe fiscal policy has become irresponsible or monetary policy too timid against inflation.

He is not sounding the alarm.

The 10-year Treasury yield remains broadly within his 4%–5% “old normal” range, which he says characterised the period between the pre-financial-crisis years and the pandemic. He also notes that the yield remains below nominal US GDP growth.

“We’ll worry about the government’s debt when the Bond Vigilantes do,” Yardeni wrote.

That does not mean investors should ignore rising yields.

It means the critical threshold may not be a particular number such as 5%.

The bigger warning would come if yields continued rising while economic growth weakened, earnings estimates fell and inflation expectations accelerated.

That would create the combination stocks fear most: higher discount rates and lower profits.

The real test is what happens next

For now, the evidence points to a market facing higher rates with unusually strong earnings support.

The lesson of 2026 so far is that the level of yields matters less than what sits next to them.

That does not make equities immune to rising yields but it does suggest that investors may be asking the wrong question.

Instead of asking whether higher bond yields are automatically bad for stocks, they should ask what is driving them.

If yields rise because productivity, investment and economic growth are strengthening, equities can potentially absorb the shock.

If yields rise because governments are losing control of inflation and debt markets are demanding compensation for greater risk, the story changes completely.

The next test comes on 16 September, when the Federal Reserve meets for the first time since Warsh told the world that policy is not restrictive.

If he means it, bond investors may finally get the answer they have been demanding.

World.title: From giant TVs to 'James Bond glasses': TCL's vision for the future
World.content:
At IFA 2026, TCL is presenting its latest display and connected home technologies under the theme "AI Inspired Life," with artificial intelligence playing a central role across many of the products on show.

 

The company's exhibition ranges from large-format Mini-LED televisions and smartphones to AR glasses and connected home appliances.

Under the name NXTHOME, the company is bringing together displays, household appliances and other connected technologies in an attempt to show how different devices could work together in people's everyday lives.

Euronews spoke to Stefan Streit, chief marketing officer at TCL Europe, to find out what role AI plays in that vision and how the company aims to balance increasingly immersive entertainment with technology designed to reduce unnecessary digital distractions.

AI for 'purposeful solutions'

AI is increasingly becoming part of the infrastructure behind connected devices. But for TCL, Streit says, simply adding AI to a product is not enough.

"Our philosophy is, when we talk about consumer products and implement AI, AI needs to solve a problem or needs to have a concrete purpose. We don't want to just put in AI for the sake of AI. So [we] really try with AI [to] solve something which we couldn't solve before."

What TCL is aiming for are what Streit calls "purposeful" AI solutions. One example is air conditioning, where the company uses AI to adjust how the system operates depending on conditions in the room.

"We save energy for up to 37% thanks to AI. Because AI can also monitor the room. For example, when you're sleeping and you're sleeping deep and not moving, it starts to increase a little bit the temperature. If you would move around, it starts lower, et cetera. So there are really purposeful AI solutions."

Euronews TCL air conditioning and connected home technologies at IFA 2026 in Berlin.

Better screens, fewer distractions

Many of these technologies are also finding their way into the product category TCL is still best known for televisions. The company has been expanding its presence in the European TV market, with larger screens and Mini-LED technology forming an important part of its strategy.

For Streit, TCL's position in the market is closely linked to its focus on manufacturing and developing much of its technology in-house.

"Our products are super competitive, so we can drive that, and therefore you see the market is also growing more in the big size TV and mini LED [sector], and that's where we are the experts. So we have a very strong product, and people see that, of course we try to make it with a good value for the consumers."

But with screens extending across an increasing number of devices, TCL is also looking at ways to make them less distracting. One example is its NXTPAPER technology, which allows users to switch their smartphone into a simplified e-reader mode.

Streit says the technology is designed to filter out much of the blue light emitted by conventional displays and reduce eye strain. The e-reader mode also switches off some functions, reducing notifications and other interruptions while potentially extending battery life.

"When you want to read on a weekend, you don't want to have the disturbance of every app that gives you a notification," Streit told Euronews.

Displays are everywhere

Even though entertainment plays a prominent role in TCL's presence at IFA 2026, the company's broader vision ultimately goes beyond televisions and screens, with the connected home at its centre.

That raises a question: for a company still widely associated with televisions and display technology, why should consumers turn to TCL for other parts of their home?

For Streit, expanding beyond entertainment and into the wider connected home is a natural next step.

"Today, almost everything has a display, right?"

That includes not only televisions, smartphones and tablets, but increasingly other devices around the home. Streit argues that TCL's experience in developing and manufacturing displays gives the company a foundation for bringing screens and connected technology into a wider range of products.

TCL showcases its latest home appliances at IFA 2026 in Berlin. Euronews

"But you know all the other categories... this is just at the beginning," he continued.

"For all of these displays, they come from TCL CSOT, which is the leading display manufacturer in the world. So, get directly at the source of technology, supply chain, innovation. So we really can bring this visual experience in all of these products."

James Bond glasses

How varied those applications can be is a central part of TCL's exhibition at this year's IFA. One example are the company's AR glasses, which Streit jokingly refers to as "James Bond glasses".

"It actually projects the pictures in my natural field of view and you don't see it, but I will get some information. I can use this for translation or navigation."

TCL's AR glasses on display at IFA 2026 in Berlin. Euronews

For Streit, the glasses are another example of how TCL is looking beyond conventional screens and exploring different ways of integrating displays into everyday products.

"So we look at these visual experiences or how we can use displays in all kind of shapes and formats or use cases, how we bring this in different products."

World.title: Bardella signs pact with Farage to stop small boat crossings 'forever'
World.content:
On Friday, Jordan Bardella of the far-right National Rally party signed a "memorandum of understanding" with Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, aimed at stopping the boats "forever" — should their parties come to power — at the party's annual conference in Birmingham.

 

Farage and Bardella signed the agreement which vows to end irregular migrant crossing on stage. The Reform UK leader hailed the deal as a "genuine new entente cordiale" between the two countries and political parties.

Bardella — who is hoping to become France's next Prime Minister — said that "the United Kingdom must not be the destination for illegal immigrants entering France. They must be sent back to their countries of origin.”

Delivering his speech in English, something he rarely does, he accused French President Emmanuel Macron of "failing" to protect France. Switching to French for the press conference that followed his speech, Bardella argued that “if France managed its borders better, no one would leave Calais.”

Bardella and Farage's meeting followed the French President's trip to London on Thursday, where he met with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to discuss how to "scale up" efforts to tackle illegal crossings and strengthen the UK's relationship with Europe.

Britain's Labour government said this week that the UK had recorded the lowest number of boats carrying migrants and asylum seekers across the Channel from France to England this summer since 2019.

Tense past relations with the National Rally party

Farage and Bardella last met in December last year at a private members' club in London. But despite their shared eurosceptic views, Farage has not always had a smooth relationship with the National Rally Party — or with Le Pen.

In 2014, Le Pen accused Farage of "aggression" against her party, after he refused to form an alliance with the National Rally party (which at the time was known as the National Front) in the European Parliament due to what he described as the party's "anti-Semitism and general prejudice."

When questioned about his past ties to the National Rally party by the press, Farage conceded on Friday that he had been “nervous” about the National Front, founded by Jean-Marie Le Pen, when he began his career as a member of the European Parliament in 1999.

“When Marine took over, I observed the situation; I didn’t get involved right away. What she has accomplished, namely ridding the party of those extremist elements and bringing it into the mainstream is a considerable achievement", said Farage.

Reform UK led national polls in the UK for over a year until July, but the party's standing has slumped in recent weeks amid multiple scandals involving allegations of irregular political funding.

On Friday, hours before Reform's conference was set to begin, Farage's Reform UK was reported to the Metropolitan Police and the Electoral Commission over alleged illegal donations.

This followed an undercover investigation aired by British broadcaster Channel 4 News, in which an investigative group called Verbatim posed as a wealthy American financier and his UK-based son. Under UK law, donations from foreign investors are illegal.

World.title: Senior EU officials retierate need for new Europe-wide taxes in next budget
World.content:
Senior EU officials are doubling down on the need for substantial new EU-level taxes to finance the bloc's long-term budget, pushing back against scepticism from the so-called "frugal" member states.

 

The question of new own resources, part of the Multiannual Financial Framework, the bloc's €2 trillion long-term budget for 2028–2034, dominated the informal meeting of European Affairs Ministers in Dublin on Thursday and Friday.

"The issue of own resources is an absolute prerequisite for us to adopt this budget," Benjamin Haddad, the French Minister for European Affairs, told reporters on the margins of the meeting on Thursday.

"Our priority, once again, is to adopt a package of own resources which is in line with what the European Commission initially proposed. We are discussing own resources that essentially rely on actors outside the European Union to generate the funds needed to finance this Multiannual Financial Framework," Haddad said.

Pressure for an ambitious budget backed by substantial new taxes has intensified since negotiations resumed after the summer recess, following a gathering of the "frugal" countries in Berlin last week.

Besides pushing for an overall reduction in the budget's volume, the frugals – a group made up of the EU's largest net contributors – remain sceptical that own resources would generate significant revenue.

That scepticism is rejected by member states including France and Spain, as well as by leading EU institutional figures who are pushing for an ambitious budget underpinned by own resources.

"The European Union must have genuine and new own resources that can help raise the level of ambition of the budget" said Spain's Secretary of State for the EU, Fernando Sampedro, "but it must also consider the rollover of The Next Generation EU."

"The challenges are bigger than in the past. We cannot do more with less. It is time to deliver, and that involves an ambitious budget. The way to do it would be with own resources, new joint debt and the rollover of the current debt."

The bloc is expected to reach a deal on the MFF by the end of the year, avoiding a postponement of talks into 2027, an election year for France, Italy, Poland, Finland, Greece, Spain, Slovakia and Estonia.

"The message to all stakeholders is clear, and I think increasingly from all stakeholders, we need to reach an agreement on the next long-term EU budget by the end of the year," Irish Minister for European Affairs Thomas Byrne said at a press conference on Friday.

"A balanced and ambitious package of so-called new own resources, the new revenue streams for the European Union, will be an essential part of an overall agreement," European Council President António Costa said during a visit to Cyprus on Friday.

The European Parliament, meanwhile, is calling for a 10% increase to the budget's main headings and wants repayment of the recovery fund, the loans used to fund the bloc's recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic, kept off-budget.

"It's very important to try to work on new own resources to have the conditions to support the new priorities that we have in the European Union, such as competitiveness, security, and defence, and the traditional policies, like cohesion, agriculture and fisheries," MEP Carla Tavares (Portugal/S&D) said on the margins of the meeting in Dublin.

The European Commission proposed a set of own resources in its original budget proposal, which has since faced significant opposition from several member states.

"Today, we need a transformation of the whole of the European economy. If we as Europeans want our continent to determine its own destiny Also in the future, we must have strong economy and we need to invest into our competitiveness," European Commissioner for the budget Piotr Serafin said in a press conference on Friday.

The Commissioner has repeatedly stressed that own resources are needed to power ambitious budget which could encourage investment in both strategic and traditional sectors.

The European Parliament has floated three alternative ideas, which the Commission estimates could yield up to €11 billion a year.

Costa is currently touring Europe to discuss the budget with member states. In the first two weeks, he met leaders from Slovakia, Estonia, Lithuania, Latvia, Czechia, Luxembourg, Croatia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Greece, Cyprus and Slovenia.

Next week, the European Council President will meet leaders in Poland, Germany, Malta, Spain, Portugal and Finland. He will not visit Sweden, which is heading to the polls on 13 September, possibly leading to an even more fiscally hawkish government.

The tour is intended to sound out countries' "red lines", helping Costa gauge how far the budget negotiations can go.

The Irish government, which currently chairs discussions among member states in Brussels, is expected to propose a new compromise text before mid-October, when EU leaders gather in Brussels for the European Council.

That compromise is expected to include a package deal on own resources, Euronews understands. To reach a final deal, all 27 member states must agree on the budget, with the consent of the Parliament.

World.title: TAP privatisation: Portuguese government opens talks with Air France-KLM and Lufthansa
World.content:
The Minister of the Presidency, António Leitão Amaro, announced on Friday that the Portuguese government is to open talks with the two groups bidding to buy TAP Air Portugal, Air France-KLM and Lufthansa, which submitted binding offers at the end of July.

 

Quoted by the Lusa news agency, Leitão Amaro said that the bids, although different, have an "overall valuation that is very close", which he believes justifies an "effort to negotiate" in order to obtain improved proposals from both contenders and allow the government to move towards "a single bidder for the very final negotiation".

Parpública, the holding company that manages the Portuguese state's stakes, delivered its report on the two binding offers for the privatisation of TAP to the government for analysis on 1 September.

Two binding offers

Air France-KLM and Lufthansa submitted their bids on 29 July, the last day of the deadline, binding offers to acquire 44.5% of TAP Air Portugal. Parpública then had 30 days to assess the documentation and submit a report to the Portuguese government. Once the bids had been evaluated, the government could invite one or both of the bidders that had submitted binding offers to negotiate and table a new final proposal.

The partial sale process for the national airline, relaunched in 2025 by Luís Montenegro's government, was reduced to two bidders after the withdrawal of International Airlines Group (IAG) - owner of Iberia - leaving Air France-KLM and Lufthansa still in the running.

The decree-law approved by the government a year ago provides for the sale of up to 49.9% of TAP to private investors, of which 5% is reserved for employees, while the state remains the majority shareholder.

The Minister for Infrastructure, Miguel Pinto Luz, has already said that the chosen investor could take on joint management of the airline as early as 2026, alongside the current board, but that the actual capital injection is only expected to take place in the summer of 2027.

World.title: Passport for a newborn: Birth tourism as part of Russia's new emigration
World.content:
Following the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine and the subsequent wave of emigration, one notable trend has been the rise of so-called "birth tourism".

 

Thousands of Russian women, unwilling to tie their children's future to a country that started a war and concerned about Russia's growing isolation, began looking for opportunities to give birth abroad.

The main goal is not only to access quality healthcare, but also to obtain a second citizenship for the newborn, which can potentially open the way for the entire family to emigrate, study, work and travel freely around the world.

Countries that apply the principle of jus soli ("right of the soil"), under which citizenship is granted to every child born on the country's territory regardless of their parents' citizenship, have become particularly popular.

However, the growing number of such trips has already prompted several countries to reconsider their policies due to an "influx of applicants".

Argentina: From dreams of a new passport to tighter rules

Argentina became the most popular destination for Russian women after 2022. The country offered a unique combination of advantages: visa-free entry for Russians, relatively affordable healthcare, automatic citizenship for the child, and the possibility for parents to eventually obtain Argentine documents.

For many families, the main attraction was not only the newborn's passport, but also a broader range of related benefits. A child born in Argentina automatically became an Argentine citizen and received all the rights provided by law, including access to state social programmes and child benefits. Parents could apply for permanent residency and later for citizenship.

Obtaining residency status made it possible to legally live and work in the country, run a business and enjoy most of the rights available to permanent residents. Another advantage was the possibility of subsequently legalising the status of other family members through family reunification and naturalisation procedures.

The Argentine passport itself was also a significant advantage, providing broad visa-free access around the world. Russians were not required to give up their Russian citizenship. The absence of compulsory military service in Argentina was another factor.

Birth tourism agencies actively promoted this combination of benefits in their advertising. Potential clients were offered not simply assistance with arranging childbirth abroad, but effectively a ready-made emigration pathway for the entire family, with agencies promising help with paperwork, obtaining residency and eventually securing citizenship.

Maxim Levoshin and his wife Yekaterina Gordienko pose for a photo with their newborn son Leo in Buenos Aires, Argentina, on Saturday 18 February 2023. Natacha Pisarenko/Copyright 2023 The AP. All rights reserved

According to Argentine authorities, around 10,500 pregnant Russian women arrived in the country in 2022 alone. Many arrived shortly before giving birth and left the country soon after obtaining documents for their child. Authorities estimated that around 7,000 of these women left Argentina almost immediately.

According to The Wall Street Journal, by mid-2024, the total number of Russians who had moved to the country since the start of the war had reached around 75,000, with several neighbourhoods in Buenos Aires already forming a "Little Russia".

Argentine authorities eventually began openly raising concerns about abuses of the immigration system. Agencies selling Russians comprehensive service packages — including arrangements for childbirth, assistance with paperwork and support in obtaining citizenship — came under investigation. Advertising materials often emphasised that having a child in Argentina could be the fastest way to obtain a second passport and lay the groundwork for the entire family to relocate.

After President Javier Milei came to power, the rules were significantly tightened. Parents of a child born in Argentina can no longer use their child's birth as a fast-track route to obtaining citizenship themselves. Naturalisation now requires at least two years of legal residence in the country. At the same time, access to free healthcare was restricted for foreigners without legal status, and additional requirements were introduced for people entering the country.

The impact was significant: while Russians submitted more than 7,000 applications for residence permits in Argentina in 2023, by mid-2025 the number of such applications had fallen to fewer than 2,000.

Russian nationals Alla Priglovkina and Andrei Ushakov spend time with their son Lev Andres, who was born in Argentina, in the bedroom of their home in Mendoza, Argentina, 14.02.2023. Natacha Pisarenko/Copyright 2023 The AP. All rights reserved

Brazil becomes the new magnet

As the Argentine route closed, Russian families, particularly in 2026, shifted their attention to Brazil. According to Deutsche Welle, the number of Russians travelling to Brazil increased significantly after Argentina tightened its migration rules.

The Brazilian passport is considered one of the "strongest" in the world: it allows visa-free travel to 161 countries, including countries in the Schengen area and the United Kingdom, and also allows holders to apply for a US visa valid for up to 10 years.

A child born in Brazil automatically receives Brazilian citizenship and a birth certificate. At the same time, the child can also obtain their parents' citizenship through the relevant consulate, becoming a holder of two passports.

Older children in the family can obtain Brazilian citizenship through a simplified procedure within their first year of residence in the country. This opportunity is unique to Brazil.

The newborn's parents, as well as their grandparents, are entitled to a residence permit with the possibility of later naturalisation. For parents, one year of residence in the country and proof of Portuguese language proficiency are sufficient to obtain citizenship, while grandparents must live in Brazil for four years.

For many Russian families, Brazil is becoming more than just a place to give birth; it is part of a long-term emigration strategy. Statistics also reflect this trend: 477 Russians obtained Brazilian citizenship in 2024, rising to 613 in 2025. More than half of the new citizens were women.

Chile, the US, Canada and other destinations: What attracts Russian women

In addition to Argentina and Brazil, Russian families are considering a range of other countries where having a child can offer additional immigration advantages. The choice depends not only on the possibility of obtaining citizenship, but also on the quality of healthcare, the cost of services, how quickly documents can be processed and the prospects for the family to subsequently obtain legal status.

Chile holds a particularly prominent place among these countries. It has long been considered one of the most attractive destinations for birth tourism in Latin America. A child born in Chile receives citizenship, while the parents can benefit from simplified procedures to legalise their stay. The Chilean passport is also considered one of the strongest in the region and provides visa-free access to a significant number of countries around the world.

Another advantage of Chile is its well-developed healthcare system. Private clinics in Santiago and other major cities are often compared with medical centres in the United States and Western Europe in terms of their facilities and quality of care. At the same time, the cost of pregnancy care and childbirth is generally significantly lower than in the US.

It is this combination of high-quality healthcare, political stability and relatively moderate costs that makes Chile an attractive alternative for families who are not prepared to pay US prices but want a comparable standard of care.

A doctor examines a five-month-old girl during a routine appointment at UCSF Benioff Children's Hospital on 16 March 2011 in San Francisco, USA. Lea Suzuki/San Francisco Chronicle

The United States has also remained a popular destination and is perhaps the best-known destination for birth tourism in the world. Under the 14th Amendment to the US Constitution, a child born on US territory automatically receives American citizenship regardless of their parents' status.

However, the cost of this option is significantly higher than in Latin American countries. The total cost of childbirth, accommodation, insurance and legal assistance can run into tens of thousands of dollars.

In recent years, US authorities have also stepped up efforts to combat organised birth tourism, paying increased attention to cases in which foreign nationals use tourist visas solely for the purpose of giving birth in the country.

A similar principle applies in Canada, where a child also automatically receives citizenship by virtue of being born in the country. Canada is chosen for its high level of safety, well-developed healthcare system and reputation as a country with a strong social welfare system. However, the financial costs are also relatively high, while waiting times for some medical services can be longer than at private clinics in Latin American countries.

Among the less obvious but increasingly popular destinations is Mexico. The country grants citizenship to children born on its territory, while its geographical proximity to the United States makes it attractive to those seeking a second passport for their child at a more moderate cost. In addition, the cost of medical services at private clinics in Mexico is often significantly lower than in North America.

For wealthier families, Switzerland remains another option. Unlike countries in the Americas, it does not grant citizenship by birth, but is considered one of the world's leaders in the quality of maternity care. Giving birth there is therefore seen more as a premium medical service than as a means of obtaining a second passport.

How countries are tackling "birth tourism"

Many countries have previously faced an influx of foreigners travelling specifically to obtain citizenship for their children.

Ending automatic citizenship

The most radical approach has been to end unconditional birthright citizenship.

Ireland, Australia and New Zealand have taken this approach. In Ireland, following a 2004 referendum, a child no longer automatically receives citizenship solely on the basis of being born in the country. Today, in most such cases, at least one parent must be a citizen of the country or have the right to permanent residence.

The United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand previously adopted a similar approach.

Restricting benefits for parents

Against this backdrop, Argentina has taken a less restrictive approach. Children still receive citizenship, but authorities have removed parents' ability to quickly obtain their own documents on the basis of their child's birth. This measure has significantly reduced the popularity of Argentina as a birth tourism destination.

A mother hugs her newborn baby in hospital shortly after giving birth. Natalia Deriabina, Shutterstock)

Visa restrictions

The US has retained birthright citizenship, which is guaranteed by the Constitution, but has begun tackling birth tourism through other means.

Since 2020, US consular officers have been able to refuse tourist visas if they believe the primary purpose of a trip is to give birth in the country in order to obtain US citizenship for the child.

In recent years, authorities have also stepped up action against intermediaries and begun revoking visas on a large scale for people involved in such schemes.

Checks at borders and maternity hospitals

Hong Kong offers a notable example, after authorities faced a large influx of pregnant women from mainland China. Mandatory advance registration at maternity hospitals, quotas for foreign women and tighter border controls were introduced. As a result, the number of such cases fell sharply.

Debate in Canada

Canada still maintains unconditional birthright citizenship, but the political debate over restricting birth tourism is becoming increasingly heated.

Canadian studies show that more than 5,400 births to non-residents were registered in the country during the 2024-2025 financial year. Against this backdrop, politicians are increasingly calling for the rules to be reviewed.

War as a driver of new migration

Russia's war against Ukraine has reshaped the migration strategies of thousands of families, with giving birth abroad becoming a way to secure citizenship and new opportunities for their children.

But as birth tourism grows, countries often tighten their rules. Argentina has already done so following an influx of pregnant Russian women, and Brazil could face similar pressure if the trend continues.

World.title: Inside the quiet luxury revival of the Venice Lido – home to the glittering film festival
World.content:
The crème de la crème of the world of cinema has been jetting into Venice for the 83rd edition of its International Film Festival.

 

The glittering event is centred on the Lido island, a narrow strip of land a short water bus ride from the historic centre.

The island has a character all of its own; a summer resort of beach establishments and historic hotels beloved by Venetians but often overlooked by international tourists.

That is, apart from when it transforms into a global hub of the silver screen for 11 days each September.

But there have been some signs that the quiet isle of Belle Époque architecture that gives way to campsites, pine forests and nature oases may be undergoing a revival with luxury in mind.

Its most famous hotel, where the film festival was originally hosted, has undergone a full revamp, while another storied establishment is set for renovation and a new four-star superior resort opened last year.

Film festival’s starriest hotel gets an upgrade

The Hotel Excelsior Venice Lido is the film festival’s most prestigious address, having hosted the inaugural edition in 1932 on its sea-facing terrace.

Since the property’s opening in 1908, it has become a favourite of royalty, politicians and, of course, film stars.

Greta Garbo, Audrey Hepburn and Elizabeth Taylor graced its Moorish-inspired interiors in the past, while current icons like George Clooney and Nicole Kidman continue to base themselves there during the festival.

The hotel’s reopening in May this year unveiled a series of stunning renovations to the storied property of domes, arches and minarets.

One of the most significant upgrades is to its Palm Court, an interior lobby of lush greenery restored to its former glory as the social heart of the hotel.

The space now features archival photography of royalty, famous directors, and Hollywood legends who stayed at the property over the last century.

As for accommodation, more than half of the 198 rooms and suites have been refreshed with soft Mediterranean colour palettes and custom Murano glass.

There is also a new signature terrace restaurant, pool bar and beach club with 299 cabanas, called Amù Venice. It combines Riviera flair from where the brand was born on the Côte d'Azur at the rooftop of the Fairmont Monte Carlo with the gastronomic traditions of the Veneto.

New four-star resort opens on Venice Lido

Last year saw another example of the Lido’s iconic 1920s architecture revived as a four-star superior resort.

Meliá Venezia Lido is far less extravagant than the Excelsior, but it adds an elegant and more affordable accommodation option to the island.

The communal spaces are flooded with the clear light off the Adriatic sea, while several of the 60 rooms have sweeping views over the lagoon to the historic centre.

There is also a restaurant, AcquaRiva, with an Art Deco-inspired design and fusion Mediterranean-Venetian dishes.

Storied Lido hotel to undergo €200 million restoration

The sprawling Grand Hôtel des Bains once also welcomed cultural icons and film greats. Author Thomas Mann stayed at the property in 1911, inspiring his novella Death in Venice.

The grand, Liberty-style hotel closed in 2010, but last year plans were announced for its reopening.

A €200 million investment will see the property and its beachfront restored and modernised as a high-end resort.

The sprawling Grand Hôtel des Bains once also welcomed cultural icons and film greats. Serge Le Strat

“This is more than a restoration – it is a revival of European legacy through modern excellence,” said Mohamed Alabbar, Chairman and founder of Eagle Hills, a real estate development company based in Abu Dhabi, which is financing the project along with the urban regeneration COIMA ESG City Impact Fund.

“Venice has always been a bridge between worlds, and we are proud to be part of its future, bringing our experience in luxury hospitality to one of the most symbolic hotels on the continent.”

World.title: Germany's alliance against the far right
World.content:
Trade unions, churches and human rights activists are worried about the rise of the far-right AfD. How can civil society protect people who are threatened by far-right extremism?

Fighting for democracy and human rights in Germany today means mustering up a lot of courage. For Felix Pankonin , locking and checking all doors and windows around the house has become practically second nature. Sometimes a hot-tempered lawmaker from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party shows up on his property; his bicycles have been vandalized; and other times he receives threats that something will happen to his animals. Most recently, his partner was physically assaulted.

Pankonin is the project director of educational programs on political issues, Jewish history and antisemitism at the Hillersche Villa in Zittau, in the eastern German state of Saxony.

The situation is similar for Keerthana Kuperan, who works as a political advisor at DaMOst , the umbrella organization for migrant groups in eastern Germany. Yes, says Kuperan, whose parents are from Sri Lanka, right-wing extremism has had a major impact on her work over the past three years.

"We have completely different security protocols now. After 6:00 p.m., no one is left alone in the office, and when putting up posters in rural areas, security measures are put in place beforehand."

Her work is primarily focused on ensuring the safety of activists. Another aspect of her work involves dealing with challenges from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which files parliamentary information requests, often on migration, in order to delay political proceedings and highlight issues that should not really be controversial.

Ahead of the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, numerous business owners with a background of migration went on strike against racism and fascism, and in support of a free and democratic society Image: Peter Gercke/dpa/picture alliance

In Saxony-Anhalt, a federal state with a very low proportion of foreigners, state legislative elections will be held on September 6. DaMOst observes that the political landscape has shifted to the right. This has led to the discrediting of democratic networks, which has affected their funding and job opportunities.

Green Party politician becomes target of hostilities

Miriam Zeller, a councilwoman in Stendal (a city of 37,000 in Saxony-Anhalt), is a member of the environmentalist Green Party and is running in the state election on September 6. Zeller told DW that the hostility was even more intense when the Greens were in power.

Her daughter stopped being invited to birthday parties, and she herself was viciously accused of being a warmonger. From the very beginning, the Greens had declared their solidarity with Ukraine after it had come under attack from Russia.

"It can't get any worse than this," says Zeller.

However, she pointed out that, fortunately, as a teacher, she is a civil servant and therefore cannot lose her job.

For others, the specter of losing one's job — should the AfD come to power — is very real.

Miriam Zeller, a Green Party candidate, is feeling the impact of the shift to the right in her private life as well Image: Miriam Zeller

Alliance for Democracy: Educating people on how to defend themselves

People like Pankonin, Kuperan and Zeller need more protection. The Together for Democracy alliance aims to support individuals or institutions that are being attacked or threatened by far-right extremists.

The aim of the group's Solidarity Agreement — which over 80 groups have signed, including labor unions, the major Christian churches, sports organizations, human rights groups as well as social and environmental organizations — is to ensure that anyone who is targeted for their commitment to democracy will not be left alone. The groups joined forces in 2024 to form an alliance against the far right when it became clear that attacks on democracy were intensifying.

Now, alliance members want to also offer help and support in the event of attacks on youth or cultural centers, hate campaigns against people who speak out publicly, or when volunteers are threatened — whether through public expressions of solidarity or by providing legal or financial support. The alliance includes powerful actors such as the German Trade Union Federation (DGB) and environmental organizations like Greenpeace.

Yasmin Fahimi, the head of the DGB, which has over five million members, took the opportunity to present the new agreement in Berlin. When asked by DW whether the AfD, in the event of an election victory, could actually fire all public employees, Fahimi was clear.

"This fantasy of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt — to carry out a complete personnel shake-up in government agencies, ministries, courts and the police — is completely unlawful," Fahimi said. "We are making it clear to our members that they can fight back against this. It is also a manifestation of an authoritarian mindset to believe that one can simply issue a decree and do as one pleases. That's not how our democracy works."

That is why the DGB is training its members both in constitutional law and civil service law so they can defend themselves, Fahimi said. The trade union leader calls for more commitment from politicians.

"We must ensure — especially in regional areas, but also within our institutions — that people cannot simply be forced to comply with unlawful orders. I believe it would be good for the Conference of Interior Ministers to discuss how to provide clear information, seminars and workshops on these issues, so that public servants, ministry employees and staff at institutions governed by the rule of law are not left to fend for themselves," Fahimi told DW.

Threats, abuse to German mayors hurting local government To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hope for help for queer people following the Berlin attack

"Of course, this alliance can mean more protection for queer people who are active on the ground," says Andre Lehmann, from the Queer Diversity Association (LSVD+) — a civil rights organization that has represented the interests and concerns of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans* and intersex queer people (LGBTQ+) since 1990.

"Right now, we're seeing a lot of attacks on Pride events all over Germany. In some cases, local organizers don't even know what to do in such situations. That's where an alliance like this can step in," Lehmann said in an interview with DW.

The Islamist attack on the Pride event in Berlinhas deeply unsettled the queer community, said Lehmann. On top of that, many democracy projects are being financially bled dry right now of all times.

The alliance will hardly be able to make up for the lack of funding for democracy projects that has resulted from the federal government's cuts and restructuring. However, teaming up with other organizations helps build strength, says Sophie Lampl, who works for Greenpeace.

"That is certainly one of the strengths we can bring as an environmental organization: our ability to campaign. To provide support when civil society organizations or individuals are attacked, to publicly stand up for them and to bring this injustice to light," Lampl argues.

Will the alliance also be able to help in rural areas?

Felix Pankonin has often helped the Together for Democracy alliance — by providing legal advice, funding for security and moral support. Pankonin would like to see more involvement from major organizations in rural areas.

Green Party politician Miriam Zeller reports that she has also received aid from small local networks. She believes that a large network, with its newfound solidarity, can make a big difference and could be a vital source of support, even in rural areas.

Andre Lehmann sounds determined: "We will defend our democracy and, if necessary, guide our local people through this valley," he says.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Nigeria: Suspected oil thieves dead after inhaling fumes
World.content:
A Nigerian environmental group says that at least 37 people died trying to siphon crude oil off a ship illegally. Police acknowledged a fatal incident but gave fewer details, saying investigations continued.

A Nigerian environmental NGO says that at least 37 people died in an attempt to tap oil from a loading vessel in the south of the country illegally.

Most of them died as a result of inhaling hazardous fumes, the Youth and Advocacy Centre said.

Nigerian authorities were yet to issue a death toll but had acknowledged a fatal incident in which people were killed, apparently while trying to steal crude oil.

What do we know about the case?

The incident took place overnight on Thursday in Okrika in Rivers State in the oil-rich Niger Delta in the south of the country.

The environmental group said it happened at a jetty as a vessel was loading oil from the Indorama Eleme Petrochemical through the Port Harcourt Refinery. The people who died were "suspected oil thieves" trying to siphon the commodity off into boats at an "illegal tapping point."

The Youth and Advocacy Centre NGO said that other people were still missing, potentially lost in the water, quoting a network of volunteers.

Police acknowledged an incident but said they continued to investigate the details.

"The Rivers State Police Command can confirm the deaths. The victims were allegedly attempting to steal crude oil," said spokesperson Blessing Agbabe.

Africa's fuel crisis: Is Dangote the answer? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Oil theft is fairly common in the Niger Delta region of Nigeria, Africa's biggest oil producer, with oil mining areas hotspots for poverty and environmental degradation.

The Nigerian government estimates that oil theft causes losses worth several billion dollars annually and has been trying to clamp down on the practice.

The tapping process can also cause leaks and environmental damage.

If confirmed this would be the worst fatal accident on record connected to attempted oil theft since at least October 2023.

However the Nigeria Security and Civil Defense Corps said that the casualty figures circulating remained unverified, saying it was working with other security agencies to clarify the details.

World.title: Germany, partners aim to finalize 'return hubs' by year end
World.content:
German Interior Minister Dobrindt said "technical discussions" were underway with non-EU countries to establish controversial "return hubs." Rights organizations have questioned the legality and morality of the plans.

Germany and other European Union countries are aiming to finalize so-called "return hubs," detention centers outside the bloc where they wish to send migrants whose asylum requests have been rejected, by the end of the year.

The European Parliament in June approved tougher migration rules that paved the way for the creation of "return hubs."

"We want to reach an agreement with third countries this year," which would then enable the establishment of so-called "return hubs," said German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt after a meeting with his counterparts from Denmark, Greece, Austria and the Netherlands in Copenhagen on Friday.

He added that "technical discussions" were currently underway with countries outside the EU, but did not name such countries.

What did the EU ministers say on 'return hubs?'

The five EU countries whose ministers attended the Copenhagen meeting are seeking a deal with an undisclosed non-EU country to host the "return hubs."

Uganda and Rwanda in particular are seen as possibilities —two autocratically ruled countries.

"Around New Year, we expect to have a common understanding with a partner country outside of the European Union," said Danish Migrations Minister Morten Bodskov.

Both the Greek and Danish migration ministers said they wished for the "return hubs" to become operational by 2027.

"We do not accept that foreigners staying illegally in Denmark should be rewarded because of our difficulties in returning them," Bodskov said in an earlier statement.

How the far right hardened Europe's migration stance To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The controversial scheme had already been briefly adopted by the United Kingdom under the former conservative government, but has since been scrapped after the social democratic Labour Party came to power.

In Italy, the right-wing government of Giorgia Meloni reached a similar deal with Albania which currently faces legal challenges.

Are EU 'return hubs' legal?

The legality of the plans for the so-called "return hubs" remains unclear under EU law.

A legal appraisal issued by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) in April concluded that the controversial Italian deportation centers in Albania do not violate European law.

EU law does not in principle prohibit member states from establishing such centers outside their own territory.

However, it stipulates that deportees continue to receive legal counsel and linguistic support, and are able to maintain contact with their families and the relevant authorities.

Andreas Grünewald, a migration expert with the German evangelical charity Brot für die Welt (Bread for the World), questioned the feasibility of the plans, calling them "practically difficult to implement and highly problematic in terms of human rights."

He said ministers risked running into "political dead ends."

Rights organizations criticize EU 'return hubs'

The highly controversial plan has been met with wide rejection from rights groups, including children's charities and church organizations, who have criticized the plans for what they see as the "criminalization of migration."

Marta Welander from the International Rescue Committee (IRC), a global humanitarian aid, relief and development NGO, said the plans risk "normalizing detainment in prison-like facilities" and warned that deportees may face "persecution, torture or worse" in their destination countries.

Caritas, a Catholic charity operating in Germany, Austria, Switzerland and Slovakia, said that migrants risked becoming trapped in a "legal grey area" if "arbitrarily and indefinitely detained" in the hubs.

Spain's Ceuta grapples with aftermath of border chaos To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Florian Westphal, CEO of Save The Children Germany, warned of the risks faced in particular by children and young people.

"The planned return centers in third countries are places of uncertainty and carry the risk of massive violations of children's rights," he said.

"Transferring children to states with which they have no connection, and where they face the risk of deprivation of liberty and are cut off from key figures in their lives, cannot be in their best interests. Children deserve unconditional protection, no matter where they come from or where they live."

World.title: Nepal flood disaster puts climate justice under spotlight
World.content:
The devastating Himalayan glacial floods have raised broader questions about who should bear the costs and responsibility for the impacts of climate-related disasters.

Days after devastating floods swept through Nepal's Bhotekoshi-Trisuli river basin, the true scale of the disaster is still emerging.

More than 1,250 people have been confirmed dead and almost 4,000 are still missing.

Buildings, bridges, roads and more than a dozen hydropower facilities have been destroyed, causing an estimated $2.6 billion (€2.24 billion) in damage to public and private infrastructure, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).

Search and rescue operations for missing people remain underway, with families still hoping for their safe return.

The exact cause of the glacial collapse remains unclear, but experts say climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.

Nepal floods trap hundreds in hydropower tunnels To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A global responsibility?

For Nepal, the disaster has raised a question that goes beyond rescue and reconstruction.

It's about climate justice and who should bear the costs and responsibility for such environmental disasters when the Himalayan nation contributes only a tiny fraction of global greenhouse gas emissions yet faces increasingly severe climate-related risks.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said responding to the catastrophe is a "global responsibility."

"As we work tirelessly to address the damage caused by this sudden and massive disaster, a deeper question has also emerged: How did this destruction happen to us?" Shah asked while addressing Parliament this week.

"Mitigating and managing its impacts is regarded as a shared responsibility of the international community," he stressed.

Kathmandu is planning to raise climate justice issues in the upcoming United Nations General Assembly session in New York, where Prime Minister Shah himself is likely to lead the Nepali delegation.

"We will make our case about the impact of climate change and seek global support and moral obligation to tackle it," Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told DW. "We will also take the initiative of building a coalition of climate-vulnerable countries to raise our collective concerns."

After Nepal floods, survivors return to ruins of their homes To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Highly vulnerable to climate impacts

Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people, has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming.

The country accounts for just 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions and emits about 0.5 tons of CO₂ per person each year, making it a "negligible contributor to climate change," according to the World Bank.

But the landlocked Himalayan nation is highly vulnerable to the effects of climate change, with flooding, landslides, glacier-related hazards and other environmental risks threatening lives and livelihoods.

Nepal's leaders say the country needs long-term international support to adapt to a rapidly changing mountain environment.

The country's government estimates that implementing adaptation priorities between 2025 and 2035 could require as much as $18 billion to $20 billion. And Kathmandu wants international climate finance to provide most of these funds.

Nepal has spent years arguing in global climate forums that vulnerable mountain countries need greater support for adaptation and resilience.

In December 2009, Nepal held a historic Cabinet meeting at Kala Patthar, near Mount Everest base camp, at an altitude of 17,192 feet, to highlight the threats that climate change and glacial melting pose to Nepal and other mountainous nations.

Bimala Rai Paudyal, a former Nepali foreign minister, said the latest disaster meant "this is an opportune time for us to highlight glacier melting and climate justice issues in international climate forums."

"Earlier, we were only advocating about climate impacts. Now, we are heavily suffering from it," she told DW.

Paudyal believes Nepal is well positioned to lead an alliance of vulnerable countries, given its exposure to climate risk as well as its expertise and contribution to the climate justice effort.

In Nepal, families cling to hope as thousands still missing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An opportunity for global climate action?

Kathmandu has formally approached the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)-backed "Loss and Damage Fund" for assistance over the latest floods.

But the fund, set up by the UN in 2025 to aid the impacts of climate change, has not yet begun distributing its limited cash.

The fund also relies on voluntary contributions and lacks legally binding commitments under current international climate agreements, leaving major emitters such as China, India and the US under no direct obligation to compensate for climate change impacts.

Still, some observers and climate advocates believe Nepal can present a strong case for urgent global climate action.

"Nepal can turn this tragedy into an opportunity for global climate action," Dinesh Paudel, professor of sustainable development at Appalachian State University in North Carolina, told DW. "For which, Nepal needs to build a consensus among national stakeholders and maneuver cautiously, considering geopolitical factors."

According to him, Kathmandu can create an ethical movement for climate justice by highlighting the recent flood. This could then lead to creating an effective and legally binding mechanism to deal with climate impacts in the future.

Ashok Swain, professor of peace and conflict research at Uppsala University and also UNESCO Chair on International Water Cooperation, shares a similar view.

"Nepal should not be left to pay for a climate crisis it did little to create or for regional non-cooperation over which it has limited influence," he said. "This is not a question of charity. It is fundamentally a question of climate justice and a fair distribution of responsibility."

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

World.title: How can African retailers compete with Shein and Temu?
World.content:
Shein and Temu are expanding across Africa with low prices and vast product ranges. Businesses and unions warn the growth could come at a cost for local jobs.

A T-shirt for a few dollars, along with jewelry, shoes and accessories — all delivered straight to your door. For many young people in African cities, shopping no longer starts in a store.

They scroll through Instagram or TikTok, see influencers showing off their latest purchases, and place an order with just a few clicks.

This combination of extremely low prices, a huge selection and aggressive social media marketing has made Chinese company Shein one of the world's most successful online fashion retailers.

Temu, also from China, follows a similar model with an even broader range of products.

For Africa's young, urban consumers, the appeal is obvious. But as more purchasing power flows directly to Asia through these platforms, another question is becoming increasingly important: What happens to local retailers, manufacturers and jobs?

South Africa shows the impact

South Africa is currently the clearest test case. Shein launched there in 2020, followed by Temu in 2024.

According to a study commissioned by the Localization Support Fund, the two platforms generated around 7.3 billion rand (about $405 million) in 2024. That represents 3.6% of the total market for clothing, textiles, footwear and leather, but already around 37% of online sales in the sector.

The study also estimates that 2,818 manufacturing jobs and 5,282 retail jobs failed to materialize during that period, a combined impact of about 8,100 jobs. By 2030, more than 34,000 additional retail and manufacturing jobs could be at risk under the study's modeled scenarios.

China's fast-fashion giant Shein opens first store in Paris To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Simon Eppel, a research director with the South African Clothing and Textile Workers' Union (SACTWU), sees this as a growing threat to the domestic industry.

He says Shein and Temu have gained a significant market share in a short period of time and put local manufacturers under pressure.

"They sucked up billions of rands […] in sales, and undercut local manufacturers," Eppel said.

The union is calling for stricter controls.

"In fact, we propose to ban these apps in South Africa," added Eppel, noting that the SACTWU sees such a move as one possible measure to counter the effects of the price pressure.

Aggressive price competition

Industry experts have cautioned that online giants such as Shein can operate at a speed that is difficult for a small African retailer to match.

Digital data shows which products are in demand, while influencers, discounts and a constant stream of new offers encourage consumers to buy.

For users, the line between entertainment and shopping is becoming increasingly blurred. But price is a crucial factor for many consumers.

Tsonam Cleanse Akpeloo, chairman of the Association of Ghana Industries, Accra chapter (AGI Accra), stresses that the offers are particularly attractive in price-sensitive markets.

"Their prices are attractive in price-sensitive economies where consumers naturally look for products that fit their budgets," he told DW.

Local business owners say that problems arise when they can no longer compete on price.

Companies that rely on high-quality materials and higher standards are put at a competitive disadvantage.

In Ghana, Akpeloo has observed similar developments in sectors such as aluminum and hardware.

Nigeria: Cheap imports for urban youth

Nigeria is also an important market for the major Chinese online retailers. Temu has a dedicated platform for the market there, while Shein is building its reach primarily through influencers and fashion content.

The appeal is clear: a wide selection, low prices and access to international trends. But Nigeria has already experienced what cheap imports can do to a local industry.

For governments, therefore, the issue is not just fashion. It is also about the conditions under which local businesses can compete with global platforms.

New tariffs on low-cost goods from China To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Shein and Temu do not have a direct presence everywhere in Africa. Their strongest presence so far is in countries such as South Africa and Nigeria, and to some extent in Ghana and Kenya. But their products also reach customers indirectly in many other African countries.

So-called freight forwarders play an important role. They provide customers with a delivery address in a country where Shein or Temu delivers directly. The package is initially sent there and then forwarded to other places across Africa.

This is how it works for Mariama Sow from Guinea-Bissau. She orders shoes, accessories and human hair for hair salons from Shein. She uses a freight forwarder in Portugal, which then forwards her orders to Guinea-Bissau.

"Underwear, shoes, clothes and school supplies, and above all the human hair, live up to their promise," Sow said.

At the same time, she says she has heard complaints from other customers about poor quality or incorrect sizes. Another problem, she says, is that local retailers are losing customers, particularly younger ones.

The tax dispute shows the political dimension

For governments, the issue is also about taxes and fair competition. South Africa has therefore tightened the rules governing small online imports. The government wanted to prevent international platforms from enjoying a tax advantage over local retailers.

For a local retailer who pays rent, staff costs and taxes, such differences can be significant.

The conflict is therefore not simply a matter of China versus Africa. It is about whether local businesses can compete under comparable conditions.

Akpeloo from AGI Accra is also calling for better controls.

"We need stronger action against smuggling, better enforcement of customs and quality standards," he told DW.

Goods entering the market without the required duties and taxes can put additional pressure on local businesses.

Beyond cheap imports

Despite all the criticism, it would be too simplistic to portray the platforms solely as a threat.The key question is where the economic value is created.

A delivery driver earns money from an order placed in China. A textile worker, by contrast, can support an entire local value chain — from the fabric producer to the sewing factory and retailer.

For African governments, the challenge will therefore be to provide access to affordable products and digital commerce without weakening their own industrial base.

The real competition is no longer just between Shein, Temu and local retailers. It is also over the shopping habits of a young generation — and over whether Africa will remain primarily a consumer in the new digital economy or become a producer itself.

World.title: How vulnerable is Germany's infrastructure?
World.content:
The growing number of attacks on substations and railway lines in Germany is raising concern. Experts say that people will have to get used to the likelihood that such incidents will continue.

On Tuesday morning, unknown perpetrators attempted to attack the power supply near the coal-fired power plant at Jänschwalde in the eastern state of Brandenburg, partly succeeding in their objective. Then, later the same evening, a substation near Cologne suffered a disruption in what is believed to have been an act of sabotage.

On Wednesday, an explosion occurred near the railway station in the Bavarian city of Augsburg, caused by a hand grenade, according to investigators.

In the early hours of Thursday, several incendiary devices were thrown onto a construction site in Munich, close to a number of defense companies. Then, on Thursday evening, a suspicious object was discovered at a power substation in Dormagen, between Cologne and Düsseldorf. Investigators say a claim of responsibility has since been received.

While it remains entirely unclear who was behind the attacks in Jänschwalde, Cologne and Augsburg, investigators in Munich have arrested at least two suspects, reportedly Bulgarian nationals.

Already 160 attacks on critical infrastructure this year

What all these incidents have in common is that they appear to have targeted so-called critical infrastructure: energy facilities, the rail network, companies of strategic importance to national security and defense contractors.

Taken together, these sites can hardly be protected in their entirety. According to media reports citing an internal document, the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) has recorded 160 potential acts of sabotage and more than 700 suspicious drone sightings so far this year.

People in Berlin express concern over Russia

Even if the exact circumstances of each incident remain unclear, their rapid succession has created a growing sense of constant threat among the public. To find out how people are reacting, DW spoke to residents on the streets of Berlin.

One woman described her immediate reaction: "Fear. I was just talking about it with a colleague. It makes me feel very uneasy. I think about it a lot, and yet no one really talks about it. Maybe it's because people are afraid and would rather push it out of their minds?"

One man added: "We first need to recognize that something is happening, that we are under attack. I have very close ties to Russia and very close Russian friends, and it is very, very painful to see what is happening."

Is Germany's civil defense prepared for crisis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A freeze in German-Russian relations

The fact that Russia is the first thing that comes to many people's minds when they hear about the recent wave of attacks is hardly surprising. On Tuesday, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), both members of the governing alliance with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), appeared before the press. They announced that the German government is convinced Russian actors were behind the attempted drone attack on Halle/Leipzig Airport on August 4.

The government responded by closing Russia's consulate general in Bonn and ending the lease on the Russian House in Berlin. Moscow, in turn, retaliated by shutting down the Goethe-Institut in Moscow. Relations between Germany and Russia are now at their lowest point in years.

"We are no longer at peace, but neither are we at war," Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) remarked last year.

The reality is that since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in the spring of 2022, Germany has been among Ukraine's strongest supporters, both financially and militarily. That holds true even though successive German governments, including the current one, have consistently maintained that the country is not itself a party to the war.

Germany's support for Ukraine as a motive?

Since then, the Bundeswehr, after years of continuous downsizing, has undergone rapid rearmament, driven in part by concerns that Russia could pose a threat even to central Europe.

Neither at war nor at peace: Sönke Marahrens, a colonel in the German armed forces and a security expert at Kiel University, believes Germans would be well advised to prepare for this new form of confrontation, whoever may be responsible for it.

He told DW: "Hybrid warfare and hybrid activities are, in my view, essentially the same thing because they rely on the same methods. Foreign states or organizations pursue their strategic interests without resorting to diplomacy. This can take the form of sabotage, disinformation or attacks on critical infrastructure."

At the same time, the researcher stresses that it would be difficult to describe the situation as a state of war.

Private firms urged to strengthen infrastructure security

But it would be too simplistic to attribute every such incident immediately and unequivocally to Russia. Earlier this year, for example, an attack on a cable bridge in southwest Berlin caused a power outage that lasted several days. Hundreds of thousands of people were affected in freezing temperatures. In that case, which remains unsolved, suspicion has fallen on far-left extremists.

A debate has long been underway in Germany over how best to prepare for such attacks in the future. This spring, the government passed legislation known as "KRITIS," aimed at strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure, although the law has yet to enter into force.

Herbert Reul (CDU), the interior minister of the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, noted in an interview with public broadcaster ZDF that critical facilities, including those operated by private companies, can already be monitored through video surveillance. Responsibility for securing the surrounding areas, however, lies with authorities such as the police.

As Reul put it: "In Germany, we are sensitive when it comes to video surveillance and, more generally, to measures that affect civil liberties or data protection."

Reul argued that companies themselves need to invest more in protecting their facilities. The German Police Union (DPolG) takes a similar view. Its chairman, Heiko Teggatz, said that safeguarding critical infrastructure is not primarily the responsibility of the police, but first and foremost of the operators themselves.

"Those responsible for the security of their facilities must also invest in their protection," Teggatz said.

What is lacking, he argued, is not technical capability but a consistent willingness to invest.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Romania prosecutors indict Andrew Tate for trafficking minors
World.content:
The social media influencer has also been indicted for money laundering and sex with a minor. His brother Tristan has been indicted for complicity.

Prosecutors in Romania on Friday officially indicted social media influencer Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan on trafficking charges, years after investigation into the brothers' activities began.

Andrew Tate was indicted for trafficking minors, money laundering, sex with a minor and witness tampering. His brother has been indicted for complicity.

The brothers hold dual US and British citizenship.

They were arrested in Miami in late July, following a British request for their extradition on rape charges.

Andrew Tate is one of the most prominent faces of the "manosphere", a male-centered social media movement rooted in anti-feminist discourse.

How misogynists take over social media To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did the Romanian prosecutors say about the Tates' indictment?

The Tate brothers have been mainly based in Romania since 2017, where they have been under criminal investigations since December 2022 on charges including human trafficking.

Romanian prosecutors said the Tates recruited their victims by falsely claiming to be seeking a relationship or marriage. They would then force them to produce pornographic content for a webcam business from which they mostly kept the profit.

The Romanian anti-organized crime prosecuting unit DIICOT said one of Andrew Tate's victims was only 15 when he seduced her in Britain in 2012, then moved her to Bucharest.

He then went on to exercise physical violence and mental intimidation to force her to produce pornographic content for social media sites.

Tristan was an accessory in the sexual exploitation committed by his brother, DIICOT said, using physical aggression to coerce the victim.

According to prosecutors, the Tates kept $1.25 million (roughly €1 million) from the camshow income generated by sexually exploiting the victim, which amounts to some 80% of her gains. They then tried to launder the funds by buying four luxury cars.

Misogyny on social media To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Can the Tates be extradited to Romania?

The spokesperson for DIICOT said it was not immediately clear whether the unit will seek the brothers' extradition from the US.

While they can be tried in absentia in Romania, the trial will not start immediately. Romanian laws stipulate that the indictment be sent to a preliminary court chamber for a judge to ensure the legality of the case files.

The preliminary chamber judge has 60 days to finalize the report, as per the law, but indictments tend to take significantly longer.

Andrew Tate, who is a self-proclaimed misogynist, and his brother have denied any wrongdoing.

"We ‌will examine every aspect of [the indictment] with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process," a Romanian lawyer for the Tates, Eugen Vidineac, said in a statement.

Edited by: Zac Crellin, Natalie Muller
