World.title: Hungary faces EUR 1 million-a-day migration fine: Brussels responds to PM Magyar’s plea
World.content:
The European Commission says it is in close and constructive talks with the Hungarian government over the country’s huge migration-related fine, as Prime Minister Péter Magyar seeks a way to stop the daily EUR 1 million penalty without abandoning Hungary’s strict border policy.

Brussels responds to Hungary’s request

According to Index, the European Commission has confirmed that it is in contact with the Hungarian authorities over the EUR 1 million-a-day fine imposed on Hungary for breaching EU asylum rules. A Commission spokesperson said on Thursday that discussions with the Hungarian side were taking place “closely and very constructively” when asked about Hungary’s options for resolving the dispute.

The statement came after Prime Minister Péter Magyar repeatedly called for help from Hungary’s European partners over the financial penalty. At the same time, the Hungarian government has made clear that it does not intend to abandon the country’s border fence or significantly loosen its migration policy.

The Commission spokesperson stressed that the fine stems from a ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU). Therefore, Hungary and the court must consider what steps can be taken to resolve the underlying dispute.

Asked whether the fines already imposed on Hungary could potentially be compensated through the EU’s next seven-year budget, the spokesperson again pointed to the need for Hungary to address the concerns identified by the European court.

Photo: Anadolu/Dursun Aydemir

Péter Magyar wants to keep Hungary’s tough border policy

Speaking at a government press briefing on Thursday, Magyar said that the issue of the migration fine had been discussed with numerous European partners since his government took office. The prime minister described the treatment of Hungary as “extremely unfair”, arguing that the circumstances surrounding migration policy had changed significantly since around 2016.

He also acknowledged that some of the Hungarian legislation challenged by the European Commission had been adopted under the previous government, but argued that EU asylum and migration rules have since become stricter across the bloc.

Magyar said Hungary was not prepared to ease its migration policy, but wanted to find a solution that would comply with European law while maintaining strict border controls. He also said his government wanted to recover the roughly EUR 1 billion that Hungary has already lost through the penalties.

Hungary’s state of emergency expires next week

Another major decision is approaching for the new government. The previous Orbán government extended Hungary’s “state of crisis caused by mass immigration” until 7 September 2026, meaning the measure is due to expire within days.

The emergency regime was first introduced in March 2016 and has been repeatedly extended ever since. The new government must now decide whether to maintain it or allow it to expire. The Hungarian Helsinki Committee has called for the measure to be terminated, arguing that there is no longer a sufficient legal basis for maintaining it.

The organisation stressed that ending the state of crisis would not mean abandoning border protection. It would not require the removal of Hungary’s border fence or the uncontrolled admission of migrants, it said.

Instead, the organisation argues that authorities could return to what it describes as standard, lawful border and immigration procedures, including identifying people, checking their status and examining asylum applications individually.

World.title: Tragedy at Hungary’s Ambulance Service headquarters: Worker dies after fall from 7th floor
World.content:
A worker at Hungary’s National Ambulance Service headquarters has died after falling from the building’s seventh floor in Budapest. Police say there is currently no suspicion of foul play, while the circumstances of the fatal incident are being investigated.

A tragic incident occurred at the headquarters of Hungary’s National Ambulance Service (OMSZ) on Thursday, when one of the organisation’s employees fell from the building’s seventh floor and died.

The incident was first reported by ATV, which contacted the National Ambulance Service for information. The organisation confirmed the death but said that the exact circumstances were still being investigated.

“The circumstances of the incident are currently being clarified. The National Ambulance Service stands by the family of our deceased colleague and the ambulance service community, and will provide them with all necessary support.”

The organisation did not disclose further details about what happened before the fatal fall.

Police rule out foul play for now

The Budapest Police Headquarters (BRFK) told Telex that there is currently no suspicion of foul play in connection with the death. Police are investigating the circumstances of the incident as part of an administrative authority procedure. No further details have been released at this stage.

It is therefore not yet known whether the death was the result of an accident or whether other circumstances contributed to the fatal fall. The National Ambulance Service has meanwhile expressed its support for the deceased employee’s family and colleagues following the tragedy.

Investigation continues

Authorities are expected to establish the exact circumstances of the incident as their investigation progresses. For now, officials have provided no information about what happened immediately before the employee fell from the seventh floor.

Unfortunately, this was not the first fatal accident recently. Last week, a seven-year-old boy died after falling from the tenth floor of a block of flats in Szeged. Police are also investigating the circumstances of that incident. The investigation into the death at the National Ambulance Service headquarters remains ongoing.

World.title: Hungary’s agriculture faces major crisis: Less than 3% of arable land is irrigated
World.content:
With drought causing increasingly serious damage to Hungarian agriculture, less than 3% of the country’s arable land is currently irrigated. A new policy study argues that the answer is not more tariffs or government intervention, but a broad reform of the rules surrounding irrigation, innovation, employment and agricultural subsidies.

The study, titled A New Dawn for Hungarian Agriculture, was authored by Bill Wirtz, Senior Policy Analyst at the Consumer Choice Centre, at the request of the Free Market Foundation.

According to the report, Hungarian agriculture is facing several challenges at the same time. Alongside increasingly severe droughts, high production costs, labour shortages, limited food-processing capacity and weaknesses in export logistics are undermining the sector’s competitiveness.

“Hungary should not seek to protect the past of its agricultural sector, but make its future competitive. This requires less protectionism, more predictable rules, greater innovation, and the allocation of subsidies independently of political influence,” said Bill Wirtz.

Drought adaptation among the most urgent priorities

The study identifies adapting to drought as one of the most pressing issues facing Hungarian farmers. The record drought of 2022 alone caused more than HUF 1 trillion in damage to the country’s agricultural sector.

Wirtz recommends reforming Hungary’s water-use system, removing barriers that make irrigation investments more difficult and speeding up the adoption of drought-resistant crop varieties.

The report also highlights the potential of New Genomic Techniques (NGTs). It argues that Hungary could follow Denmark’s example and position itself as one of Europe’s leading centres for developing crop varieties that are more resistant to drought while requiring fewer resources.

Stay up-to-date with our Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

No tariffs on grain imports, study argues

The report also rejects the idea of introducing tariffs or further import restrictions on the grain market. Instead, it recommends helping farms on the Great Hungarian Plain adjust to changing market conditions, including by moving towards livestock farming and horticultural production.

According to Wirtz, restricting imports would ultimately push up food prices for consumers rather than solving the underlying problems facing Hungarian agriculture.

Labour shortages and food processing need reform

Labour shortages are another major obstacle. The study recommends making it easier for Hungarian farms to employ seasonal workers from outside the European Union.

In the food-processing sector, the report calls for fewer licensing requirements and lower administrative burdens. It also argues that Hungary could improve the competitiveness of its agricultural exports by strengthening transport connections towards Croatia and Slovenia and increasing competition in rail freight.

If you missed it: Another severe food price surge is taking shape: prices could start rising in the autumn, with 2027 bringing the greatest pain

Agricultural subsidies should be independent

The study identifies the independent allocation of agricultural subsidies as one of the key conditions for successful reform.

“The independence of the subsidy system is not merely a question of fairness. Without it, it is difficult to build an agricultural sector in which investment decisions are driven by performance and market opportunities rather than political connections.”

Ultimately, the report argues that the success of Hungarian agricultural policy should be measured by whether it can ensure affordable and reliable food supplies, encourage innovation and make Hungarian producers more competitive.

With climate pressures intensifying and Hungarian farmers facing growing economic challenges, the study suggests that protecting existing structures may no longer be enough. Instead, it calls for fundamental changes aimed at making the country’s agricultural sector more resilient, innovative and competitive.

World.title: Netopia Payments expands license to include money remittance services after Romania’s Central Bank approval
World.content:
Romanian payments and technology platform Netopia Payments is entering a new stage of development after it received the authorization of the National Bank of Romania (BNR) to expand its payment institution license to include money remittance services, the company said.

The company, which processes more than RON 10 billion annually, is preparing new embedded finance solutions and developing an integrated financial platform for merchants, it said.

The company aims to expand its portfolio of services for merchants beyond traditional online payment processing and toward a comprehensive financial ecosystem.

At the same time, it is preparing to diversify the payment methods it accepts, including through the integration of account-to-account (A2A) solutions such as RoPay, and to expand financing options offered through partners, including merchant cash advance products.

Netopia’s priorities for the coming period include operationalizing its newly licensed activities, developing new financial products, and expanding its technology and operational infrastructure.

“Obtaining the license from the National Bank of Romania validates our security and compliance standards, but more importantly, it provides the foundation on which we are building Netopia’s future. Our vision is to become a comprehensive growth partner for entrepreneurs in Romania,” Raluca Micu, CEO of Netopia, said.

In the medium term, the company aims to build a one-stop shop model for merchants, a unified platform integrating multiple payment methods, rapid funds collection, automated transaction reconciliation, and complementary financial services.

Netopia Payments is a Romanian payments and technology platform for merchants, providing digital payment infrastructure and financial solutions to thousands of companies. Since 2023, private equity fund Innova Capital holds a majority stake in the company.

(Photo: the company)

simona@romania-insider.com

World.title: Romanian construction company Concelex appoints Daniel Spiridon, Carol Șerban to strategy and transformation roles
World.content:
Romanian construction company Concelex announced it was strengthening its management team by bringing in two professionals with international backgrounds in strategy and transformation.

Daniel Spiridon, with over 20 years’ experience in management consulting and executive leadership, has joined Concelex as Deputy CEO Strategy.

Carol Șerban, a construction engineering graduate with international experience in strategic consulting, has joined as Director of Strategy and Transformation.

The two appointments “support Concelex's current phase of accelerated growth and strengthen the company's capabilities in strategy, organizational transformation, and business development,” the company said.

Daniel Spiridon (in opening photo) spent more than 15 years at McKinsey & Company, where he rose through every stage of his career to become Managing Partner of the local office. He subsequently joined eMAG as VP Business Development and Strategy and, as CEO, led eMAG's operations in Hungary. A graduate in economics, he also holds a Master's degree in International Business and Finance from BI Norwegian Business School. As Deputy CEO Strategy, he will oversee the implementation of Concelex's strategy, develop the Strategy and Transformation function, and be involved in developing and optimizing the company's business portfolio, with the goal of strengthening its competitiveness and profitability.

Carol Șerban

Carol Șerban brings a construction engineering educational background paired with experience in international strategic consulting. A graduate of the Technical University of Civil Engineering Bucharest, he holds a Master's degree in Structural Engineering from the University of Manchester and an MBA from the University of Oxford. He began his career in the UK, where he spent seven years in civil and structural engineering and project management, before joining Kearney's Romania office. He has also held the position of Commercial Director at Glovo Romania. As Director of Strategy and Transformation at Concelex, he will coordinate organizational transformation programs, with a focus on optimizing business processes, accelerating digitalization, and identifying strategic initiatives to support the company's performance.

“Concelex has reached a stage where the scale of the projects we manage and the company’s accelerated growth prospects require us to continuously strengthen our leadership team. Daniel and Carol bring complementary experience and a valuable perspective on how we build, organize, and prepare for the next stage of growth. They are professionals with a solid track record in their fields, and I am confident they will make a significant contribution to Concelex's development in the coming years," Radu Pițurlea, chairman and CEO, Concelex, said.

World.title: Central Romania: Restored castle in Covasna reopens to the public
World.content:
The Miko Castle in the village of Olteni, Covasna County, which has been restored with EU funding, is set to reopen its doors on Saturday, September 5, Agerpres reported.

Built in 1827 by Count Miko Miklos, the castle is notable for the murals discovered on its interior walls during the restoration work. The paintings depict scenes from the social life of the period, as well as scenes from the Napoleonic Wars.

The property was returned to the descendants of Count Miko in 2007. Seven years later, they sold it to the Covasna County Council and the Bodoc Local Council.

The restoration was carried out as part of a project worth approximately RON 20 million, co-financed by EU funds through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR).

The castle will house the Székely Equestrian Museum, a section of the Székely National Museum in Sfântu Gheorghe.

The castle is also set to become part of the Transylvanian Manor Houses Route, one of 12 national cultural tourism routes financed through PNRR, the Covasna County Council said.

The reopening will also be marked by a screening of the Italian film Vita mia, directed by Edoardo Winspeare, which features several scenes filmed inside the castle. Other events for the opening weekend include a tour focusing on the history of the castle, and a guided tour of the Székely Equestrian Museum.

(Photo: Consiliul Județean Covasna)

World.title: Swedish man wanted over Stockholm shooting apprehended in Romania
World.content:
Romanian organized crime prosecutors have apprehended a Swedish citizen wanted by authorities in his home country over his alleged involvement in a shooting targeting two people in Stockholm. The suspect had lived in Romania for approximately three years, according to the Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT), as reported by Biziday.ro.

Prosecutors searched two properties in Bucharest and nearby Otopeni as part of an investigation into organized crime and aggravated murder.

According to investigators, several individuals tried to kill two people at a Stockholm address in September 2024. One of them allegedly fired at the building, with bullets passing through the entrance door and entering the home.

DIICOT said the suspect helped those involved in the attack, with his actions considered serious illegal threats aggravated by the use of a firearm.

Swedish authorities issued an arrest warrant for the man. He will be brought before a judge at the Bucharest Court of Appeal, with Romanian and Swedish law enforcement agencies cooperating in the case through Eurojust.

During the searches, authorities seized an air gun, a gas pistol, a bulletproof vest, quantities of plant material, data-storage devices, and bladed weapons.

According to DIICOT, another Swedish citizen suspected of belonging to a rival organized crime group was located in Romania in late July. A Romanian court ordered his detention pending extradition in connection with an alleged conspiracy to commit murder.

World.title: Estée Lauder Romania renews SkyTower lease, moves to new office
World.content:
Estée Lauder Romania has extended its lease at Bucharest’s SkyTower for a third time and relocated its headquarters to a newly fitted-out space on the building’s ninth floor. The beauty company has operated from the office tower since 2017.

The announcement did not disclose the duration or financial terms of the renewed lease, nor the size of the new office.

“This extension reflects our commitment to our team and our activities in Romania,” said Adrian Simionescu, country manager of Estée Lauder Romania.

The company also uses SkyTower’s SkyHub and board meeting areas to organize events.

Located in northern Bucharest, SkyTower is owned by Raiffeisen Property Holding International.

The 137-meter building has 37 floors and is Romania’s tallest office tower. Its underground structure extends to a depth of 60 meters and provides parking and storage space.

World.title: Romanian tech group Arobs sells Polish subsidiary to WB Electronics
World.content:
Arobs Transilvania Software, one of the largest technology companies listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange, has sold its entire stake in Arobs Polska to WB Electronics.

Before the sale, the company acquired the 5.66% stake held by Michal Drogosz, enabling the subsequent transfer to WB Electronics of 100% of the share capital of Arobs Polska, the company said in a filing with the Bucharest Stock Exchange. The filing did not disclose the value of the transaction.

The decision to sell comes as the company pursues a focus on “areas where the group has established capabilities, can leverage international synergies and sees the most relevant growth opportunities.” These areas include software and engineering services for the automotive industry, IoT and telematics, enterprise software, life sciences and travel.

Arobs Polska focuses on developing electronic solutions for satellite applications, giving it a distinct profile compared with the group’s core business lines. Its activity is characterized by extended development cycles, projects carried out predominantly under institutional programs, and specific capital and infrastructure requirements, Arobs explained.

The integration of Arobs Polska into WB Electronics will ensure the continuity of ongoing projects and provide the team with access to an industrial platform and a portfolio of programs suited to the specific nature of its activities, the company said.

The transaction does not affect the current operations of Arobs Transilvania Software.

World.title: Romanian court lifts house arrest for mercenary Horațiu Potra in alleged coup plot case
World.content:
Romania’s High Court of Cassation and Justice lifted the house arrest imposed on mercenary Horațiu Potra on Thursday, September 3, allowing him to remain free under judicial supervision while standing trial. The court granted Potra’s appeal against the previous preventive measure, Agerpres reported.

Horațiu Potra is one of the main defendants in a case concerning an alleged plot to destabilize Romania following the annulment of the 2024 presidential election.

The High Court released him from pre-trial detention in mid-June and placed him under house arrest, ordering him to wear an electronic monitoring bracelet. He had been in custody since November 2025, when he was brought back to Romania from Dubai together with his son and nephew.

Prosecutors indicted Potra on charges including attempted actions against the constitutional order, illegal possession of weapons and ammunition, violations of rules governing explosives and pyrotechnic materials, and public incitement. He is being tried alongside 20 alleged members of his mercenary group and former presidential candidate Călin Georgescu.

Prosecutors claim Horațiu Potra and his associates planned to infiltrate protests held after the December 2024 election annulment to provoke unrest and violent confrontations.

According to investigators, Cãlin Georgescu and his associates devised the plan during a meeting at a farm in Ciolpani shortly after the election was annulled. Potra allegedly coordinated efforts to bring a group of mercenaries to Bucharest and escalate the demonstrations into actions capable of destabilizing the constitutional order.

The allegations remain subject to examination by the court, and the defendants are presumed innocent until a final ruling.

(Photo source: Inquam Photos/Octav Ganea)

World.title: Romania’s 2026-2027 school year begins on September 7
World.content:
Students across Romania will return to classrooms on Monday, September 7, for the start of the 2026-2027 school year. The calendar includes 36 weeks of classes divided into five modules, with five holiday periods between them, Digi24 reported.

The school year officially runs administratively from September 1, 2026, to August 31, 2027, but classes begin on September 7. Each school will determine the timetable for opening-day ceremonies, access for parents, and other activities.

The first module will run until October 23, although no classes will be held on October 5, International Teachers’ Day. The autumn holiday is scheduled from October 24 to November 1.

Students will return for the second module on November 2 and continue classes until December 22. The winter holiday will run from December 23, 2026, to January 10, 2027.

Then, the third module begins on January 11, with its closing date varying by county. Local school inspectorates selected a one-week holiday between February 15 and March 7 after consulting students, parents, and teachers.

Classes will subsequently continue until April 23, followed by the spring holiday from April 24 to May 4. The final module will run from May 5 to June 18, with the summer holiday beginning on June 19 for most students.

Graduating high school students will complete 34 weeks of classes and finish on June 4, while eighth graders will end their 35-week school year on June 11. Most students in technological and vocational education will continue until June 25.

One of the main changes this year affects students entering ninth grade, who will be the first to begin the phased introduction of Romania’s new high school curriculum.

The new school year begins amid continued concerns about access to education, particularly in rural areas. According to Education Ministry data analyzed by the Friedrich Ebert Foundation Romania’s Monitorul Social (Social Monitor) project, only 75.2% of children and young people aged 3 to 23 were enrolled in some form of education in the 2024-2025 school year.

The gross enrolment rate in preschool education stood at 86.3% in 2025, but there was a considerable gap between urban areas, at 98.4%, and rural communities, at 74%. Among three-year-olds in rural areas, the rate was only 60.2%.

The divide was even wider in primary education, where the gross enrolment rate reached 98.5% in urban areas but only 71.5% in rural areas. At lower-secondary level, the corresponding figures were 96% and 65.6%, a gap of more than 30 percentage points and the largest recorded over the past five school years.

The overall gross enrolment rate was 85.1% in primary education, 80.7% at lower-secondary level and 78.6% in high school and vocational education. Monitorul Social said participation generally declines as students advance through the education system, while distance, transport costs and limited nearby options can create additional barriers for rural pupils.

World.title: Serbia’s Vucic Slates EU Condemnation of Mladic Tributes as ‘Stupid’
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos cancelled her planned visit to EU candidate state Serbia on Friday, the day after Ratko Mladic’s body was transported on a government plane to Belgrade, where it was met by officials and an army honour guard.

Groups of supporters of the former Bosnian Serb military chief also greeted the motorcade carrying his body into Belgrade with banners praising Mladic, hung from roadway overpasses, with messages such as “Thank you, General” and “Welcome home, General”.

“The return of his remains to Belgrade reminds Europe of the darkest pages in our recent history,” Kos wrote on X.

“The glorification surrounding his death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built … The values that underpin our common future are not negotiable. In this context, I have decided not to proceed with my planned visit to Serbia at this time,” she added.

Her criticisms have been echoed by ministers from several other EU member states.

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic dismissed Kos’s criticism as “extremely brief, but stupid, as usual”.

“‘Glorification’ of General Ratko Mladic, except it doesn’t say who was glorifying anything. And when they can’t find anything concrete, then they deal with underpasses and overpasses [where pro-Mladic banners were displayed]. I suppose we were meant to ban people from showing up, to ban the funeral,” he told the media on Friday.

Mladic’s body was returned to Serbia on Thursday evening on a Serbian government plane.

Ratko Mladic’s son, Darko, confirmed on Friday that the funeral will be held on Monday at the Topcider Cemetery in Belgrade.

Before the funeral, a tribute to Mladic will be held in a church where the coffin will be placed, and on Saturday, a public commemoration will be staged at the Home of the Army of Serbia, in central Belgrade.

Darko Mladic said a procession would be organised on Monday from the church to the cemetery and emphasised that he expects a large turnout.

“This is a people’s funeral, and, as you all know, I do not engage in politics and would not mix politics into this. The only thing I can say is that regarding our requests [to the Hague for Mladic’s conditional release because of illness], of which there were many in the past, President [Vucic] was always there for us, and I would like to publicly thank him for that support in defending General Mladic, which meant a lot to us,” Darko Mladic said.

Neither Darko Mladic nor the Minister of Justice, Nenad Vujic, who was sitting next to him at the press conference, specified whether there would be army or state honours at the funeral.

On August 27, when Mladic died, Vujic initially said Mladic would be buried with state honours. “General Mladic is a general and there are protocols that apply,” he said then.

Mladic held the rank of general in the Yugoslav People’s Army, JNA, during the 1990s but legal experts in Serbia are divided on whether there is any basis for a funeral with state or army honours, given that he was convicted of genocide.

President Vucic has since cast doubt on the idea of a funeral with state honours. Minister Vujic on Friday, when quizzed about state honours, just said that the state would provide all the family was entitled to, out of “respect for the family’s wishes … [and] according to the laws of the state of Serbia”.

Asked whether he will attend the funeral in person, Vucic on Friday pleaded a packed schedule. “I have an official visit from the President of Uzbekistan [Shavkat Mirziyoyev] for the whole day on Monday and Tuesday, scheduled four months ago,” he said.

Several European dignitaries have echoed EU commissioner Kos in criticising the glorification of Mladic.

Belgium’s Foreign Minister, Maxime Prevot, wrote on X on Friday that “it is shameful and disrespectful to the victims and their families to reserve such honours for his funeral.

“It’s a step distancing Serbia from EU’s fundamental values of respect for human dignity, human rights and the fight against impunity – going in the opposite direction of what is expected from a EU candidate country,” Prevot said.

Ireland’s Minister for European Affairs and Defence, Thomas Byrne, told media on Friday that it was “not acceptable” if there were “senior figures from government memorialising that man”.

World.title: Kosovo Charges Serbian Security Officers Over Jashari Compound Massacre
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Blerim Isufaj (C), Chief Prosecutor at the Kosovo Special Prosecution, with prosecutor Valdet Gashi on September 4, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Kosovo’s Special Prosecution announced on Friday that it has filed an indictment charging 35 suspects with involvement in the murder of 26 civilians at the compound of Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA commander Adem Jashari in the village of Prekaz in Skenderaj/Srbica in March 1998.

“After years of work, we have succeeded in finalising the investigation into the Prekaz case by filing an indictment. We have managed to substantiate the well-founded suspicion that the accused committed the criminal offence of war crimes against the civilian population – specifically on March 5, 6, and 7, 1998, in the village of Prekaz, more precisely in the Jashari neighbourhood,” prosecutor Valdet Gashi said.

BIRN has seen the indictment which, among others, includes the names of Jovica Stanisic, the former head of the Serbian State Security Service; Vlastimir Djordjevic, a former high-ranking Serbian Interior Ministry official; Sreten Lukic, a wartime head of the Serbian interior ministry’s staff for Kosovo and Milorad ‘Legija’ Ulemek, a former commander of Serbia’s State Security Unit for Special Operations.

“Based on material and testimonial evidence, we have identified 35 accused individuals in this case who held high command positions within the Serbian special police units,” Gashi added.

Serbian police and military forces besieged the Jashari family compound in Prekaz from March 5 to 7, 1998, leaving 59 dead, including the founder of the KLA, Adem Jashari, himself.

The assault caused outrage among Kosovo Albanians and is seen as the incident that encouraged widespread armed resistance against Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic’s regime.

Gashi told media on Friday that the indictment was filed in absentia as the authorities could not secure the presence of the suspects.

Stanisic is currently serving a sentence for war crimes in another case after being convicted by the Hague Tribunal, while Ulemek is in prison for his role in the killing of Serbian Prime Minister Zoran Djindjic. Djordjevic and Lukic have been released after serving war crimes sentences for other crimes.

Chief Special Prosecution Prosecutor Blerim Isufaj highlighted the indictment as “the first one concerning the killing of civilians in the Jashari family compound in Prekaz, Skenderaj”.

In cases concerning war crimes committed during the 1998-99 Kosovo war, legal cooperation between Kosovo and Serbia remains almost non-existent, so it appears unlikely that most of the indictees will be available for trial.

World.title: Serbian President Launches ‘Non-Political’ Podcast as Election Looms
World.content:
Ahead of elections expected in the next few months, Serbia’s head of state has started doing podcasts, while promising to give politics a big miss on his show.

The first episode of Vucic’s PodcAVst aired on Friday at noon on his official YouTube channel. In it, Vucic interviewed the basketball coach Miroslav “Muta” Nikolic, introducing him as a “pal” and a “legend of Serbian basketball”.

“When I was a boy, I applied to become a radio reporter. At the time, my dream was to become a sports commentator or reporter. I didn’t make it – Radio Belgrade rightly rejected me because I had a slight speech impediment,” Vucic reminisced in the introduction.

Vucic said he decided to try the podcast format for a simple reason: to have conversations with successful people.

“I’ve missed having conversations with successful people, with people who are different from me, so that I can learn something from them, gain a different perspective and listen to them, rather than having them listen to me,” he said.

“I’ll try not to be someone who argues or disagrees with guests, but instead to be here to learn as much as possible from people working in completely different fields. And there won’t be a single word about politics,” he added.

During the interview, Vucic and Nikolic spoke about basketball strategies, teams, players and coaches. They also reminisced about Vucic’s own sports efforts and his brother Andrej’s life.

Since the podcast premiered live, it had a live chat filled with supportive comments like “Serbia Wins” and “Serbia United”, and emojis including the Serbian flag, a wolf, hearts and flexed biceps. Some presented opposing views, however, such as “The students will win against Vucic”, referencing the wave of student-led protests against his government.

By launching his own podcast, Vucic is following a trend already embraced by political figures in the region, notably Albania’s Edi Rama with his weekly “Flasim” (“Let’s Talk”) podcast, as well as politicians further afield, such as California Governor Gavin Newsom and US Senator Ted Cruz. It has not been announced when Vucic’s next show will be aired.

The podcast’s launch comes amid Vucic’s already extensive presence in traditional media ahead of nationwide elections expected to be held in the coming months.

According to Serbian election watchdog CRTA, by August 18 he had made 64 live television appearances that month, already surpassing his previous monthly record of 61, set in March 2025.

World.title: Week in Review: Ghosts and Guns
World.content:
Bosnian Serb military chief Ratko Mladic died in The Hague at the age of 84 on August 27, having spent his final years serving a life sentence for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. BIRN covered the death of Mladic extensively, with profiles, features, analyses and opinion articles.

Mladic’s death has shown just how far the former Bosnian Serb military chief’s legacy extends beyond the judgments that established his responsibility for some of the worst atrocities of the Bosnian war.

Across Bosnia’s mainly Serb Republika Srpska entity, Mladic supporters took to the streets, lit candles and publicly celebrated Mladic, including in towns where his forces committed crimes, while politicians in both Bosnia and Serbia joined in paying tribute. For genocide survivors, the sight of young people who may not even have been born during the war glorifying Mladic was particularly disturbing, proving that nationalist narratives have passed to another generation.

The reactions have also prompted deeper questions about what justice has achieved. Former Hague Tribunal intern Ahmet Gumusbas observed that Mladic’s conviction established criminal responsibility and an authoritative record of the crimes, but could never end disputes over memory and denial. Journalist Kristina Ljevak Bajramovic reflected on the gulf between Mladic, who was able to grow old, and the thousands of his victims who were denied that chance.

In Serbia, meanwhile, Youth Initiative for Human Rights director Sofija Todorovic argued that official tributes to Mladic demonstrate how the glorification of convicted war criminals has become embedded in Serbia’s politics, media and public life.

World.title: Romania Opens New Human Trafficking Case Against Tate Brothers
World.content:
Andrew and Tristan Tate arrive at court for a pre-trial hearing in Bucharest, February 2024. Photo: EPA-EFE/Robert Ghement.

Romanian anti-organised crime prosecutors on Thursday evening indicted British-American influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate in a new case involving alleged trafficking of minors, according to court records seen by BIRN.

Prosecutors accuse the defendants, together with two Romanian nationals, of trafficking minors and related offences, including money laundering.

The new indictment follows a December 2024 decision by the Bucharest Court of Appeal to return the original case file to prosecutors for the investigation to be redone.

Romania’s anti-organised crime agency, DIICOT, subsequently expanded its investigation and brought additional charges.

According to judicial sources cited by online publication HotNews, some of the allegations have been separated from the broader investigation in order to avoid the risk of statutory limitation.

The brothers have been under investigation in Romania since their initial arrest in December 2022.

They face various allegations, including human trafficking, rape, trafficking of minors, sexual intercourse with a minor and money-laundering.

In June, prosecutors expanded their investigation into Andrew Tate to cover new allegations that he sexually exploited a woman in 2017, taking advantage of her vulnerable situation to induce her to produce sexually explicit content and perform video chat activities – and that he and his brother, Tristan, laundered almost 3 million euros earned from human trafficking via two companies between 2018 and 2022.

The Tate brothers have denied wrongdoing.

Despite being arrested in 2022, the case against them has made slow progress: in late 2024, a court returned the original indictment to prosecutors, saying it was flawed, and in February 2025 DIICOT permitted the brothers to leave Romania, despite the ongoing case.

They are currently in the United States, contesting extradition to the United Kingdom, where authorities have brought nearly 60 charges against them, including rape, human trafficking and sexual exploitation.

Both brothers have described the cases against them as politically motivated and unfounded.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Poland Investigates Arson of Drone Factory as Suspected Russian Sabotage
World.content:
Hungary PM looks to recover ECJ fines; Orban’s son central figure in Chad mission

Statements made by PM Peter Magyar this week indicate that Hungary might not be the kind of pliant partner the EU had hoped for after his predecessor, Viktor Orban, was turfed out of office. Magyar met with Manfred Weber, leader of the European People’s Party (EPP), and European Council President Antonio Costa earlier this week, and made clear he would strongly defend Hungary’s rights and interests during the talks over the next seven-year EU budget (MFF). Magyar said in a Facebook post that his Tisza party would like to become a full member of the EPP, the European political family of centre-right parties that Orban’s Fidesz left in 2021 before being expelled. However, before that can happen, the Article 7 procedure – a punitive measure which removes voting rights of member states – against Hungary would have to be closed, he said. The procedure was launched by the European Parliament in 2018, but needs a formal decision by the Council of the EU to end the process. Magyar also touched on the sensitive subject of the 1 million euros that Hungary is paying daily for failing to comply with EU asylum regulations. The case dates back to the Orban government’s decision to close the controversial transit zones at the border, while making it next-to-impossible to submit asylum applications from inside Hungary. Under the current system, asylum applications can only be submitted at Hungarian embassies in Belgrade or Kyiv. Last year, Hungary received 113 asylum applications and granted refugee status, subsidiary or humanitarian protection to just 35 people. Weber reportedly offered to help in settling the issue, but Magyar stressed the border fence will have to remain in place. Reopening the transit zones would be highly controversial, as the opposition would use it as evidence Magyar is bowing to pressure from Brussels. On the other hand, the fines have already reached around 1 billion euros – a significant loss of revenue for the Hungarian budget. Magyar floated the idea of recovering this money in the framework of the MFF negotiations. In another move likely to be frowned on in Brussels, the Hungarian government blocked Ukraine’s EU accession process for the third time this week, arguing insufficient progress on minority rights.

The family of former PM Orban was back in the headlines this week as documents obtained by news site 444.hu confirmed what had long been suspected – that Orban’s son, Gaspar, was the driving force behind Hungary’s planned military mission to Chad (and not the wild conspiracy theory of Hungary serving Russian interests in the region). The idea originated during a trip to Niger in May 2023 by Orban Jnr and Tristan Azbej, Hungary’s deputy state secretary responsible for helping persecuted Christians. The two initially planned an agricultural project there – a model camel farm supported by the Hungarian University of Agriculture and Life Sciences. Farmers from Niger would have been instructed by Hungarian experts on how to process camel milk and produce dairy products. However, after a military coup in Niger in 2023 attention shifted to Chad, where the project’s aims were significantly expanded. In addition to the planned model farm, it was to include a medical and a military mission involving up to 200 Hungarian soldiers. According to the documents now obtained, Orban Jnr functioned as the pro-forma leader and central coordinator of the project. Virtually all major decisions – from when to buy plane tickets for experts to arranging the shipment of medical equipment – depended on him. In a previous interview, former defence minister Kristof Szalay-Bobrovniczky had tried to defend the mission and Orban Jnr’s role in it: “Gaspar Orban is a military officer… He goes wherever he is ordered to go. I assigned him as a liaison officer.” The newly published documents prove otherwise. In the end, the Chad government lost enthusiasm for the project. Although 27 billion forints (73.5 million euros) were earmarked for the mission in the 2026 budget, the plan was quietly shelved by Orban as the April election approached.

World.title: Under Pressure Over Gaza, Israel’s Defence Industry Expands in the Balkans
World.content:
In recent years, Israel has faced growing international criticism over its conduct in Gaza and its policies and practices throughout the occupied Palestinian territories - and mounting calls for an arms embargo. Several countries have imposed full or partial restrictions on arms trading with Israel, while the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement has received growing support for its campaigns across Europe and beyond.

Yet military ties between Israel and countries across the Balkans have continued to deepen. Greece is one of Israel’s closest military partners in the region, maintaining extensive cooperation and signing several major deals in recent years - most recently to buy an expensive air defence network. But cooperation has extended beyond Athens, with Israeli defence companies expanding their presence around the region through arms sales, joint ventures and technology partnerships.

Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest defence company according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s Top 100 Arms-Producing and Military Services Companies for 2024, has been a major beneficiary of this expansion. The company accounted 34 per cent of its revenue in the second quarter of 2025 from the Israeli market and has signed agreements to establish joint production facilities with local partners, expanding its regional presence.

World.title: Croatia Set to Purchase Powerful Korean Rocket System
World.content:
September the 4th, 2026 – Croatia is set to purchase a powerful Korean rocket system, with the first talks between the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia (MORH) and the South Korean Ministry of Defence on military cooperation actually having begun a year ago.

The government will adopt a decision on the purchase of 18 self-propelled multiple rocket launchers Chunmoo K239, with the accompanying rockets, for 435.2 million euros excluding VAT. As Krešimir Žabec learns for Jutarnji list, with this system Croatia will obtain rockets with a range from 30 to more than 300 kilometres, including ballistic missiles for deterrence.

procurement details

It’s currently expected that Defence Minister Ivan Anušić will soon sign a contract with the South Korean company Hanwha Aerospace. Cooperation will also be contracted with the Polish company WB Group, which will install the command-and-control system (C2). Poslovni reports that according to available information, 85 percent of the contracted system will be delivered by 2028. Payment is planned in the period from 2026 to 2029. As touched on above, the first talks between MORH and the South Korean Ministry of Defence on military cooperation actually began a year ago. Back at the end of 2024, Croatia contracted the purchase of eight HIMARS systems with the United States, but the US, due to the needs of its own army, suspended the delivery of 300-kilometre-range rockets to allies, while a sales ban applies to those with a range of 500 kilometres.

Because of this, Croatia opted for a solution that has already been chosen by Poland, Norway and Estonia. Compared with HIMARS, Chunmoo also offers twice the firepower because it has two rocket containers with a total of 12 rockets, while HIMARS has one with six. Support for the purchase was also given by Prime Minister Andrej Plenković and President Zoran Milanović. Two months ago in Ankara, after the NATO summit, Milanović announced the acquisition of new armaments as a response to Serbia’s purchase of the Israeli PULS system. “We will have to counter that as a state in some way, by equipping ourselves with something similar,” he said at the time.

training and the technical parts

The Chunmoo K239 system consists of a mobile launcher on a truck, a fire-control system and a communication system. Its key advantage is the possibility of using different types of rockets from standardised modular containers. It is the only operational system of this type that can simultaneously use rockets of different calibres on the same launcher.

The commander in the field can thus at any moment fire a rocket adapted to the mission, without the need for modifications. For example, four 280 mm rockets can be placed in one container, and six guided 239 mm rockets in the other. If the most powerful ballistic missile CTM-290 of 600 mm calibre, with a range greater than 300 kilometres, is used, one such projectile is placed in one container. Its trajectory after launch reaches an altitude of between 25 and 40 kilometres before diving towards the target.

The rate of fire depends on the calibre. The system can fire 12 guided 239 mm rockets in less than a minute. The entire system is operated by a three-member crew. The contract covers the launchers and rockets, logistical support and training lasting six weeks. 100 soldiers will be needed to operate all 18 launchers. The largest part of the system will be delivered in 2028, and at this moment it is a secret where it will be stationed within the ranks of the Croatian Army.

World.title: Varaždin to Ban Sale of Alcohol in Shops After 22:00
World.content:
September the 4th, 2026 – The continental Croatian city of Varaždin is set to become to first continental city to introduce a ban on the sale of alcohol in shops and kiosks after 22:00.

Varaždin will become the first continental city in Croatia to introduce a ban on the sale of alcohol in shops and at petrol stations after 22:00, but that isn’t the only ban. Net.hr reports that those who are caught consuming alcohol in public areas outside of the premises of bars, restaurants and cafes could also face penalties, regardless of when they purchased it.

Varaždin residents will no longer be able to get hold of alcohol so easily in the evening hours. Just as some coastal cities have already done earlier, Varaždin is introducing this new measure. “For the reason that our fellow citizens requested it. Constant disturbance of public order and peace, especially around petrol stations, particularly the one in Zrinski and Frankopan Street, daily complaints from people who nevertheless deserve to have peace and a night’s rest – these are the main reasons,” said Neven Bosilj, Mayor of Varaždin. In shops and at petrol stations, the sale of alcohol will not be allowed from 22:00 until 07:00.

the consumption of alcohol in public will also be banned

Drinking alcohol out in public anywhere outside of the premises of bars, cafes and restaurants will also be subject to a ban. Anyone caught by the police and municipal wardens will have to pay a fine of up to 260 euros for the offence. In the night-time hours, alcohol will still be able to be consumed legally only in restaurants, bars and cafes. Many owners of such establishments can now expect higher turnover because of the move.

Whether people are complying with the new rules will be controlled by the police and municipal wardens, of whom there are not enough, so the mayor has announced the following:

“We’re announcing a tender for new municipal wardens because the state has also transferred various powers, since they cannot find people for construction inspections, so they transfer certain jobs to units of local self-government. That’s why we’re strengthening it,” said Mayor Bosilj. After the public consultation is completed, the decision on the restricted sale will be voted on by the City Council, and it is expected to enter into force at the beginning of November this year.

World.title: Value of Fiscalised Receipts Up By 17% in Croatia in August
World.content:
September the 4th, 2026 – The value of fiscalised receipts and invoices was up by 17% in August across Croatia. This was specifically in the provision of accommodation and food prep.

Poslovni reports that in addition to the aforementioned, 274.6 million invoices were issued in total last month, which is 8.9 million or 3.3 percent more than a year earlier. The value of fiscalised invoices rose strongly in August, while the growth in their number was considerably more moderate. Across all activities covered by the fiscalisation system, the value of issued invoices reached 6.56 billion euros, which is 17 percent or 955.3 million euros more than in the same month last year, according to data from the Tax Administration.

At the same time, 274.6 million invoices were issued last month, 8.9 million or 3.3 percent more than a year earlier. The data thus show that the average value of invoices grew noticeably faster than their number. The largest share of turnover relates to wholesale and retail trade and the repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles. In that activity, 169.9 million invoices were fiscalised, 2.6 percent or 4.25 million more than last year, while their value increased by 7.8 percent, or 258.1 million euros, to 3.56 billion euros.

In hospitality and tourism, i.e. the activity of providing accommodation and the preparation and serving of food, the number of fiscalised invoices rose by six percent to 65.7 million euros. Their value at the same time increased by 10.3 percent or 164.5 million euros, reaching 1.8 billion euros. The data refer to the period from the 1st to the 31st of August 2026 and cover all activities included in the Tax Administration’s fiscalisation system.

World.title: Why Diaspora Millennials Should Secure Croatian Citizenship as Early Retirement Safety Net
World.content:
September the 4th, 2026 – Diaspora millennials should see securing Croatian citizenship not only as a way to beat the airport queues and connect with their heritage, but as a future retirement safety net.

For very many decades, the path to obtaining a second passport was viewed by the Croatian diaspora in America through two distinct lenses: a sentimental nod to heritage, or a luxury asset reserved exclusively for the ultra-wealthy. However, a macroeconomic shift is changing this narrative. A growing number of millennial professionals in the US are faced with a relentless cost-of-living crisis, skyrocketing healthcare premiums, and an increasingly volatile political landscape. As a result, they’re viewing corporate life with a raised eyebrow after years upon years of accepting it as the norm for the “American Dream”.

Instead of waiting until the golden age of 65 to finally escape the corporate ladder, forward-thinking Americans with a chance of grabbing Croatian citizenship in their 30s and 40s are leveraging Croatia’s simplified citizenship-by-descent laws to construct an unconventional backup plan: an early, high-quality, low-cost European retirement plan. We’ll call this lifestyle move an “Adriatic Arbitrage”, given that it represents the deliberate act of earning strong US dollars today while securing the legal right to transition permanently to a Mediterranean lifestyle decades ahead of schedule.

taking the “fire” movement across the pond

It’s still a relatively unknown term for Europeans, where the idea of living to work just isn’t ingrained, the Financial Independence, Retire Early (FIRE) movement has captivated millions of American millennials.

The core philosophy of the term relies on ultra-aggressive saving to accumulate a substantial nest egg that sustains a modest life free from full-time employment. Across the pond in the US, achieving FIRE is exceptionally difficult due to real estate inflation and the high cost of basic necessities. By obtaining a Croatian passport, diaspora members immediately unlock a backdoor to financial independence that simply isn’t available to most. Securing citizenship with this in mind eliminates the complex, anxiety-inducing web of visas, income thresholds, and renewal fees that non-EU citizens who don’t hold permanent residence in Croatia face all the time.

It’s true that since joining the Eurozone, prices in Croatia have risen, but a monthly budget that feels restrictive in cities like Austin, New York, or Seattle transforms into a very comfortable lifestyle in coastal regions like Istria, Split, or the islands of Dalmatia. Millennials are realising that they do not need a multi-million dollar American nest egg to retire comfortably, they simply need the legal right to live permanently in a country with a vastly lower cost of living and an incomparably higher quality of life than the USA.

defusing and trashing the us healthcare bomb

The single greatest financial barrier to early retirement in the United States is the astronomical cost of healthcare. For Americans under the age of 65, leaving a traditional corporate job means entering the private insurance market, where catastrophic plans routinely cost regular families thousands of dollars per month in premiums and deductibles. By obtaining Croatian citizenship with the help of dedicated services like CroatianByDescent, applicants secure a lifelong safety net. As Croatian citizens, they gain access to Croatia’s universal, comprehensive healthcare system (HZZO). While healthcare infrastructure in Croatia is socialised and therefore operates differently than the commercialised US model, it provides robust, high-quality care without the threat of medical bankruptcy. For a 35-year-old American planning a future exit from the workforce, securing affordable, accessible healthcare removes the largest financial wild card from their retirement equation.

securing freedom in a profoundly non-american sense

We always hear how America is the land of the free. With the majority of people teetering on the edge of losing their housing quickly if something goes wrong and with crushing medical bills being the norm, I have to admit that it’s difficult for us as Europeans to understand what is so free about it. Outside of the likes of North Korea and Afghanistan (if you’re female), most of the world is free. Croatia is not only free but completely safe. An early retirement strategy serves a dual purpose as “generational insurance” for the diaspora. When an American millennial secures their Croatian citizenship by descent, they aren’t just getting an exit strategy for themselves. Under current regulations, they pass this fluid, borderless EU birthright down to their own children, giving them access to EU education and careers.

In a world where global flexibility is the ultimate currency, giving the next generation the automatic right to live, study, work, and retire anywhere across 27 European nations is an invaluable asset. It is an investment that appreciates over time, offering their family a lifetime of options that money alone cannot buy.

swapping the american dream for the croatian dream

The narrative around gaining the citizenship of another country by descent has fundamentally matured over the decades. While tracing family roots and connecting with ancestral villages remains deeply moving and always a more than good enough reason to pursue that path, today’s applicants are driven by a sharp sense of practical foresight. This is particularly true if you’re a US citizen.

croatianbydescent has turned personal experience into professional guidance

Through the expert guidance of specialised agencies like CroatianByDescent, all of whom are members of the Croatian diaspora themselves, the complex bureaucratic maze of the citizenship application process is streamlined into an accessible project. For stressed American professionals, navigating the paperwork today isn’t just about honouring the past, it’s about funding, planning, and claiming a peaceful, sun-drenched future on the Adriatic, where a broken leg or heart surgery won’t result in bankruptcy.

World.title: This Map Shows Just How Hot Croatia Has Been This Summer
World.content:
September the 3rd, 2026 – This map shows just how hot Croatia has been this summer, with drought and unstable rainfall causing serious agriculture issues.

The State Hydrometeorological Institute (DHMZ) has published an analysis of temperature and precipitation amounts for summer 2026. Index reports that the data shows that almost the whole of Croatia had an extremely warm summer, while parts of the country, especially the east and part of central Croatia, were markedly dry. The mean seasonal air temperature during the summer was noticeably higher than the average for the reference period 1991–2020. According to DHMZ data, deviations of the mean temperature ranged from 1.8 °C in Daruvar and Makarska to as much as 3.3 °C at Puntijarka and Zavižan.

an extremely hot summer for croatia

According to the percentile distribution, summer 2026 has so far been extremely warm across almost the entire territory of Croatia. The only exceptions were Varaždin and Daruvar, where the summer was classified in the very warm category. The DHMZ map shows that very large temperature deviations were recorded throughout the country. In addition to Puntijarka and Zavižan, where the temperature was 3.3 degrees above normal, in Parg, Senj and Gospić the deviation amounted to 2.9 °C. In Osijek the mean summer temperature was 2.8 °C above normal, in Dubrovnik 2.7 °C, and in Zagreb, Bjelovar and Pazin 2.4 °C above the average. Percentiles at numerous stations were very close to the maximum values. In Osijek, at Puntijarka, Zavižan and in Dubrovnik they amounted to 99.9, which shows how unusually warm the summer was in relation to the climatological normal.

droughts caused serious issues for eastern and central croatia

DHMZ also published data on precipitation amounts. Deviations relative to the 1991–2020 normal ranged from only 24.7 percent in Gradište, where 51.2 millimetres of rain fell, to 119.2 percent on Rab, where 193.5 millimetres were measured. The most pronounced precipitation deficit was recorded in the east of the country. Gradište and Slavonski Brod had an extremely dry summer. The map shows that in Gradište only about a quarter of the usual summer precipitation amount fell, while in Slavonski Brod around 37 percent of the normal was recorded.

Very dry conditions were recorded in Osijek, Daruvar and Parg, as well as in the western part of central Croatia, i.e. in the area of Zagreb, Puntijarka, Sisak and Karlovac. In Zagreb and Karlovac around 51 percent of the usual precipitation amount was recorded.

rainfall along most of the coast was relatively normal

It was also dry in the vicinity of Križevci, Ogulin and Gospić, at Zavižan and on Lastovo and Vis, i.e. at the Komiža station. In the rest of Croatia the precipitation amount was within normal limits. This also applies to a large part of the Adriatic, including Rijeka, Senj, Zadar, Šibenik, Split, Makarska and Dubrovnik. Thus, summer 2026 has been one of exceptional temperature terms across all of Croatia, while the distribution of precipitation was considerably more uneven, with a particularly pronounced drought in the east and in part of central Croatia.

World.title: Kaljski dialect Officially Declared Protected Cultural Asset of Croatia
World.content:
September the 3rd, 2026 – The Kaljski dialect from Kali has officially been declared a protected cultural asset of the Republic of Croatia.

The Kaljski dialect, spoken in Kali on the island of Ugljan, has officially become part of Croatia’s protected intangible heritage. By decision of the Ministry of Culture and Media dated the 26th of August, this specific island speech has been entered into the Register of Cultural Assets of the Republic of Croatia under the designation Z-8010. Morski reports that the Kaljski dialect is a distinctive speech that belongs to the Central Chakavian dialect of the Chakavian dialect group. In its explanation, the competent ministry particularly emphasised its unique linguistic structure, as well as the invaluable role it plays in preserving the local identity, rich history, customs and everyday life of the residents of Kali.

This prestigious recognition is the result of many years of effort and dedication by the entire local community. Side by side in the preservation and promotion of the indigenous expression are the “Srdelica” Kindergarten, the Kali Branch School and the parent “Valentin Klarin” Primary School, with strong support from the Kali Public Library, numerous local associations, the Tourist Board and the Municipality of Kali itself.

The particular value of this linguistic story lies in contemporary projects aimed at documenting and transmitting the speech. As part of the Kalipedia project, an extensive online dictionary has been created that today numbers around three and a half thousand words enriched with authentic audio recordings. At the same time, through the Kalamra project, free speech recordings of residents of all generations have been recorded and digitised, while the “Kualjska besida” initiative systematically encourages children and young people to creative and literary expression in their native Chakavian. With the official acquisition of the status of a cultural asset, concrete protection measures have also been secured. In the coming period, detailed documentation, scientific research and the lasting transmission of the Kaljski dialect to new generations will be carried out, with the continued active engagement of the entire local community.

World.title: Around 78,000 People Were Registered as Unemployed in Croatia in July
World.content:
September the 3rd, 2026 – Approximately 78,000 people were formally registered as being unemployed in Croatia back in July, which is a figure that is 0.1% less than in June.

Katarina Kusec reports for Poslovni that Eurostat estimates that 13.5 million people were unemployed across the EU back in July, of whom 11.3 million were in the Eurozone. According to a report by the European statistical office Eurostat, the unemployment rate in the Eurozone and the European Union remained more or less entirely unchanged in July compared with June, while it slightly decreased in Croatia. Specifically, it stood at 6.4 percent across the Eurozone and 6.1 percent at EU level. Compared with the same month last year, the unemployment rate rose by 0.1 percentage points.

Furthermore, Eurostat estimates that 13.5 million people were unemployed across the EU in July, of whom 11.3 million were in the Eurozone. Looking at the situation on a monthly basis, the number of unemployed people fell by 41,000 across the EU, while it remained unchanged in the Eurozone. As for Croatia specifically, the unemployment rate back in July stood at 4.3 percent, which is 0.1 percentage points lower than it was in June and half a percentage point lower than in the same month in 2025. Around 78,000 people were registered as formally unemployed in July, which is 1,000 fewer than the previous month and 8,000 fewer than back in July 2025.

Countries with a lower unemployment rate than Croatia were the Czech Republic (3.3 percent), Poland (3.4 percent), Malta and neighbouring Slovenia (both 3.5 percent), Bulgaria (3.6 percent), Cyprus (3.9 percent), and Germany and the Netherlands (both 4 percent). The highest rates were recorded in Finland (10.5 percent), Spain (10 percent) and Sweden (8.7 percent). For Croatia, Eurostat also publishes quarterly data on youth unemployment. In the second quarter of 2026, that particular rate stood at 16.4 percent, with around 19,000 young people registered as formally unemployed.

World.title: Jadrolinija Extends Sailing Season for High Speed Zadar-Ancona Line
World.content:
September the 3rd, 2026 – Jadrolinija has decided to extend its sailing season for the high speed Zadar-Ancona line until September the 6th.

Jadrolinija has stated that for its very first season of operation, the high speed Zadar-Ancona line has achieved positive results and great interest from passengers on both sides of the Adriatic. Poslovni reports that Croatia’s largest ferry company, Jadrolinija, will extend the first season of the high speed Zadar–Ancona line until the 6th of September due to excellent passenger interest.

“Jadrolinija has extended the sailing season for this line until the 6th of September, with additional trips on Wednesdays, Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays, as well as promotional ticket prices. For adults the ticket costs 80 euros while children aged 3 to 12 travel for 40 euros,” Jadrolinija stated. They recalled that they introduced the high-speed Zadar–Ancona line this year as a new international connection that brings the Croatian and Italian sides of the Adriatic coast closer and enables travel between the two cities in approximately four hours on the vessel Jelena, which has a capacity of 400 passengers.

The strong interest from passengers on both sides of the Adriatic and the good response confirms the importance of fast, simple and direct connections between Croatia and Italy outside of air travel. It also confirms the Zadar-Ancona line’s potential for the further development of tourist and transport links between the two coastlines.

Back in 2025, Jadrolinija carried 12.6 million passengers, which is on a par with the previous record year and confirms stable demand, as well as 3.8 million vehicles, which is two percent more vehicles than the previous year. The growth and trend of these operational indicators are also accompanied by positive financial results. Jadrolinija’s fleet now comprises 58 vessels with an average age of 27.8 years, which is below the European average of around 33 years. Fleet renewal remains the company’s most important strategic project.

World.title: Study: Estonia's climate warming 1.5 times faster than global average
World.content:
When forecasting climate change, scientists usually opt to determine what the climate will look like at a specific point in time, for example in 2050, or in 2100. In a new study, however, researchers linked local changes directly to the prevalence of global warming. "It does not matter whether two degrees gets reached in 2040, according to a more pessimistic projection, or in 2070, or in 2090 according to a more optimistic projection. What counts is what happens to Estonia's climate once that level is reached," explained the study's lead author, Erko Jakobson, associate professor of atmospheric remote sensing at the university.

The principal finding is that Estonia's annual mean temperature has been going up by about one-and-a-half degrees for every one degree rise in mean temperatures globally. At the same time, periods of very cold weather will become increasingly rare, while hot days, tropical nights and heatwaves are to get more frequent. In other words, during the warmer part of the year, climate change can already be observed with your own eyes, not to mention felt firsthand in Estonia alone.

Observable climate change

In order to create a picture of the future, the researchers ran 31 global climate models. Jakobson noted the public's expectations regarding the accuracy of climate forecasts are unfortunately often far in advance of what current science is capable of delivering. "Some local governments want us to tell them, right down to the village level, how the climate will change in this or that location. We cannot do that – even if it were mathematically viable to do it at the county level, it would not be meaningful, and we would essentially be telling lies," Jakobson explained.

The analysis revealed also that Estonia's winters are warming several times faster than its summers. For every additional degree of global warming, Estonia's average winter temperature rises by 1.9 degrees Celsius, while its summer temperature rises by 1.3 degrees Celsius. The number of freezing days falls by 13 percent for every degree of warming. While milder winters help save on heating costs, they may bring issues of their own, not least to winter sports enthusiasts – though currently active skiers are not likely to see completely snowless winters as a rule, in their lifetimes.

"We forecast a decline in the number of cold days, and we do not actually know whether snow will fall during those cold days. In any case, even under the most pessimistic forecasts, Estonia should continue to see snow until the end of the century. But the fact that we used to have long periods without thaws will be but a fond memory for skiers," Jakobson noted. Even more convoluted challenges await farmers, as the milder conditions actually threaten winter crops: The insulating layer of snow will be replaced by more damaging freeze-thaw action.

A warming climate more generally and globally brings intensified precipitation too. For every additional degree of global warming, precipitation in Estonia rises by an average of approximately 31 millimeters, or 4.6 percent.

This precipitation falls mainly in winter and the fall, but the models remained unclear about summer projections. Estonia's location plays a key role here. "We looked at the bigger picture, meaning the entire Baltic Sea region and points south. It clearly emerged that the dividing line runs more or less through our area: In summer, it becomes drier to the south and wetter to the north," the scientist said.

Erko Jakobson Source: Personal collection.

In any case, Estonia's summer hydrological picture is set to become more contrasting. Short, heavy downpours wash soil and nutrients off fields while failing to alleviate drought stress in plants.

"Instead of periods of steady rain, half of the precipitation will often fall within a few hours. That water does not have time to soak into the ground but immediately runs into ditches and rivers, doing more harm than good to fields. The drought problem therefore actually increases," Jakobson warned. The stronger evaporation characteristic of a warmer climate may cause problems for farmers especially in spring and summer.

The dynamics of air masses, however, continue to pose a considerable challenge for climatologists. Estonia's weather is shaped simultaneously by strong Atlantic cyclones and high-pressure systems to the east. Precise changes in atmospheric circulation and wind behavior are therefore difficult to capture with physical models.

"There is a great deal of uncertainty regarding changes in circulation, and I do not see a good prospect of the forecasts becoming much more certain. Our latitude means that our weather is not made here but comes from elsewhere. Everything depends on whether weather coming from the north or the south gains the upper hand," the researcher added.

Because of the uncertainty, it cannot currently be said that Estonia will experience stronger winds and storms in the future. In summer and autumn, average wind speeds may even decrease slightly. "One very widespread belief is that it will become windier in the future. In some ways, that is logical: there is more heat and energy. In our work, we saw that some models show wind speeds increasing, while others show them actually decreasing. We therefore cannot confirm that winds in Estonia will indeed become stronger and storminess will increase," Jakobson said.

Bigger questions

Jakobson stressed the projections in the models are based on continuous trends, but the climate system contains a number of tipping points. "If the Antarctic ice sheet or Siberian permafrost melts significantly, or the Gulf Stream changes substantially, enormous quantities of greenhouse gases could be released. Current climate models have not accounted for such abrupt changes, so there may still be surprises," the associate professor warned.

Jakobson noted that scientific facts and the future scenarios presented by climate models unfortunately tend to become mixed up with day-to-day politics in public debate. Instead of assessing physical reality, people argue over the economic consequences of the green transition.

Scientists' task, however, is to measure the causes and pace of warming, while finding solutions and allocating resources remain the responsibility of society and politicians. "When large sums of money are involved in politics, fraudsters sometimes get involved and things go wrong. But the fact that something goes wrong in politics unfortunately does not mean that climate change does not exist," the scientist said.

The study was first published in the journal Boreal Environment Research.
