World.title: Tajikistan reports socioeconomic progress since independence
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 4. Tajikistan has made significant progress in socioeconomic development during the years since gaining state independence, Trend's correspondent reports.

Tajikistan’s Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Azerbaijan Ilhom Abdurahmon made the remarks in Baku at an event marking the 35th anniversary of Tajikistan’s state independence.

"Over the years since gaining independence, our country has made significant progress in socioeconomic development," the ambassador said.

According to him, the country’s GDP has increased 3.4 times over the past 10 years, while average annual economic growth stood at 7.6%.

I. Abdurahmon said Tajikistan’s GDP reached 173 billion somoni ($18.70 billion) in 2025, while real economic growth amounted to 8.4%.

The ambassador also noted that the country’s population increased from 5.3 million in 1991 to 10.7 million in 2026. According to him, the poverty rate has declined to 19%.

"These indicators reflect the results of consistent state policies aimed at improving quality of life, strengthening social protection and expanding opportunities for citizens," the diplomat emphasized.

World.title: Tajikistan, Azerbaijan deepen cooperation across key sectors, ambassador says
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 4. Tajikistan and Azerbaijan are expanding cooperation across key areas, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

Tajikistan’s Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Azerbaijan Ilhom Abdurahmon made the remarks in Baku at an event marking the 35th anniversary of Tajikistan’s state independence.

"Today, Tajik-Azerbaijani cooperation is steadily developing in the political, trade and economic, investment, transport and logistics, energy, industrial, agricultural, educational, cultural and humanitarian spheres," the diplomat said.

He emphasized that expanding practical cooperation creates additional opportunities to strengthen relations between the two countries.

According to the ambassador, particular importance is attached to developing business contacts, industrial cooperation, mutual investment, as well as cultural and humanitarian exchanges.

"Deepening business ties, developing industrial cooperation, mutual investment and intensifying cultural and humanitarian exchanges will undoubtedly contribute to further strengthening ties between our peoples," I. Abdurahmon said.

World.title: Tajikistan sees scope to expand transit routes through Azerbaijan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 4. Tajikistan is interested in further utilizing Azerbaijan’s transport and logistics capabilities and developing transit routes, including the Middle Corridor, Trend's correspondent reports.

Tajikistan’s Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Azerbaijan Ilhom Abdurahmon made the remarks at a ceremonial event in Baku marking the 35th anniversary of Tajikistan’s state independence.

"There is significant potential to utilize Azerbaijan’s transport and logistics capabilities and develop transit routes, including the Middle Corridor," he said.

The ambassador noted that most transit freight shipments between European countries and Tajikistan pass through Azerbaijan.

"Azerbaijan is an important partner for Tajikistan in transit freight transportation along the existing corridors connecting our countries," I. Abdurahmon emphasized.

According to him, further deepening cooperation in transport and logistics will contribute to expanding economic ties between the two countries.

The ambassador also noted that four direct flights per week operate between Dushanbe and Baku, which, according to him, contributes to the development of tourism ties between the two countries.

World.title: Tajikistan says trade turnover with Azerbaijan rose 84% in 2025
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 4. Trade turnover between Tajikistan and Azerbaijan increased by 84% in 2025, Trend's correspondent reports.

Tajikistan’s Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Azerbaijan Ilhom Abdurahmon made the remarks in Baku at an event marking the 35th anniversary of Tajikistan’s state independence.

"In 2025, trade turnover between our countries increased by 84%, while the volume of strategically important transit shipments grew by 50%," the diplomat said.

According to him, the signing of the Declaration on Strategic Partnership in Baku on May 23, 2024, marked an important milestone in the development of bilateral relations.

"This document brought bilateral relations to a new level and covers virtually all key areas of cooperation," I. Abdurahmon said.

He also noted that the eighth meeting of the Azerbaijan-Tajikistan Intergovernmental Commission on Trade and Economic Cooperation was held in Baku in May 2026. Following the meeting, documents were signed on establishing a Business Council, the mutual allocation of annual education quotas and further expansion of practical cooperation.

The ambassador emphasized that the two countries still have significant potential to expand business ties, industrial cooperation and mutual investment.

World.title: Azerbaijan is one of Tajikistan’s closest and most important partners – ambassador
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 4. Tajikistan’s Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Azerbaijan Ilhom Abdurahmon made the remarks on September 4 in Baku at a ceremonial event marking the 35th anniversary of the state independence of the Republic of Tajikistan, Trend's correspondent reports.

"Azerbaijan is one of Tajikistan’s closest and most important partners, with whom we maintain sincere and friendly relations," the ambassador said.

According to him, the peoples of the two countries are connected by deep historical, cultural and spiritual ties, shared traditions and mutual respect.

The ambassador also emphasized the role of the two countries’ leaders in shaping modern Tajik-Azerbaijani relations.

According to him, this foundation of friendship continues to strengthen today through regular political dialogue and trusted contacts between the leaders of the two states.

World.title: Housing affordability hits all-time low despite falling property prices
World.content:
Housing affordability has fallen to its lowest rate on record, with households earning a typical income only able to afford about one in every 10 homes sold across the country.

According to data from realestate.com.au, a household earning a median income of about $125,000 a year could afford just 12 per cent of all homes (houses and units combined) sold nationally in the last financial year.

Despite recent falls in property values, stronger prices last year and recent hikes in interest rates have powered the result and reversed the "marginal improvement" from the 2025 financial year.

The company's senior economist, Angus Moore, said housing affordability is "challenged" as the central bank has increased the cost of borrowing money and repayments on loans.

"The three RBA interest rate hikes made in February, March and May increased mortgage rates and further constrained household borrowing capacity amid an already difficult cost-of-living environment," he said.

"Looking ahead, affordability may improve marginally if home prices continue to soften, but this is unlikely to be a turning point for many buyers.

" Without a meaningful increase in housing supply, affordability will remain a significant challenge, particularly for lower-income households. "

Housing will take 'generation to fix' Property price declines of 7 per cent will not solve Australia's housing affordability issues, NAB chief economist says.

The figures included in the report were based on a household spending 30 per cent of their gross income on mortgage repayments, with a 2.5 per cent buffer, meaning a household earning just over $125,000 annually could afford to make loan repayments on just 12 per cent of homes sold in the past year.

The data also relies on the median household income instead of the average household income.

For example, if the nation was made up of 99 households ranked from lowest-earning to highest-earning, the amount earned by the 50th one would be the median.

An average figure, however, would add up the earnings of all the 99 and divide them by 99, meaning the result is skewed by some wealthy households. According to analysis of HILDA data by the Grattan Institute, the average Australian household earns $161,000.

Higher property prices, slower income growth and higher mortgage rates have impacted housing affordability. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Victoria the most affordable, but even it slides

The report found that affordability declined in every state in the last financial year, but did not examine the territories.

South Australia became the least affordable state with just 7 per cent of properties sold affordable for median households.

Victoria was the best performer for people seeking a home, with 16 per cent of properties affordable for median households — but even that has fallen.

Even for people not seeking to buy, the data is tough. Mortgage repayments, relative to incomes, are at the highest point since 1989.

That means they are taking up 35.5 per cent of average household income, higher than during the so-called Global Financial Crisis (GFC) when it was 33.3 per cent.

In 1989, the figure was 37.5 per cent.

Back then, interest rates on mortgages were about 15.5 per cent, compared to 6.3 per cent in June 2026. But they were being applied to much lower house prices and the ratio of "annual income to cost of a house" was much lower.

If home loan interest rates were at 1989 levels today, three quarters of an average household's income would go towards repayments on the average mortgage.

Pressure unlikely to subside soon

Economist Luc Redman said despite a recent fall in property prices, the pressure within the market remains.

"Home prices have remained elevated across the sales distribution — despite a softening in the back half of the financial year — combined with higher interest rates reducing households' borrowing capacity," he said.

The problem, however, is what he calls a "clear structural supply problem" when it comes to having enough places to live.

" The country does not have enough homes, particularly in well-located areas. Without meaningful reforms to address supply across levels of government, this will continue over the long term. "

Affordability constraints are likely to remain while housing supply is limited. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Maiy Azize is the national spokesperson for Everybody's Home, a coalition of welfare and homelessness organisations that work on the housing crisis.

She said changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax discounts, which have made it less attractive to be a property investor, were a start.

"The government's tax reforms are a great step, but they will take time to work their way through the housing market. These numbers show we need action in the meantime," she said.

However, she said there needed to be more changes if the situation were to improve sooner.

"Governments should put limits on rent increases to give renters some breathing room. That will help people trying to save for a deposit, as well as the growing number of people who will rent for the long term," Ms Azize said.

"We can't rely on the private market to deliver the affordable homes. These numbers make that clear. That's why the federal government needs to dramatically boost social housing.

"Government can build affordable homes at the scale needed, in the places people need them. It also takes pressure off the rental market because fewer people will be competing for affordable rentals."

Maiy Azize says boosting social housing stock will help improve affordability. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

Borrowers are feeling the pinch

Nadia Harrison is the chief executive of Mortgage Stress Victoria, a legal service that deals with people struggling with housing debt.

She said the body has seen "significant growth in demand" for its services.

Can housing take another hike? Three of the big four banks now think the RBA could hike again this year. What would it do the property market?

"From February 2026, the number of people reaching out for assistance increased by around 30 per cent compared to the monthly 2025 average, and that level of demand has remained steady since," she said.

Ms Harrison advised people who are struggling to meet mortgage repayments should contact their lender for support.

However, that isn't a blanket solution, because not all lenders are legally forced to provide assistance.

Housing affordability will remain a challenge for households even if property prices continue softening. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

Mortgage Stress Victoria wants to see a charter — a broad agreement — that extends hardship provisions to all borrowers.

"At the moment, the rights and protections you have as a home owner in hardship vary depending on the lender you've borrowed from, and the industry code that they subscribe to," she said.

"A mandatory Mortgages Charter which lifts and harmonises hardship protections across the board would go a long way to making mortgages fairer."

World.title: Loretta had a quiet retirement until Elon Musk built a data centre next door
World.content:
American war veteran Loretta Thornton was so confident she had found a peaceful place to retire, she named her house 'Serenity'.

Nestled in wilderness and rustling trees in Memphis, Tennessee, the home offered Loretta the quiet life. She spent 11 years soaking it up after a military career, including deployment during the Gulf War, that left her with PTSD.

But her serenity was shattered when a noisy new neighbour moved in next door.

Elon Musk's SpaceXAI (xAI) quietly developed a data centre inside an abandoned warehouse with little regulatory oversight.

It is now the US' largest, so hulkingly huge it has been named Colossus II.

"When they cranked this up, I thought I was back in Desert Storm," she said.

"I thought I was stuck back in the middle of a war. That's what it sounds like to me."

Loretta Thornton says noise and fumes have affected her quality of life, while her power bill has doubled. (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

Loretta says an aeroplane-like noise drones from the site non-stop. Dozens of gas turbines burp out fumes that, at times, cause her eyes and throat to burn.

"I feel stomach-fold-up-sucker-punched, because I never thought anything like this would move in in my life," she said.

Similar situations are being replicated across the US. An AI arms race is powering a data centre boom, and there are concerns it is outpacing the bureaucracy required to effectively regulate it.

That's led to a national political fight that is dominating election races two months ahead of the critical midterms.

Donald Trump remains an advocate for data centre development, arguing every town in America should want one or risk ending up "backwards and poor".

But his party's candidates are breaking ranks to campaign against them in their districts, fearing Democrats could otherwise ride a rising wave of community anger to easy election victories.

State border battleline

The Tennessee-Mississippi border has become one of many front lines in the battle over data centres' prolific spread.

SpaceXAI is operating or building at least four large centres along the state line.

Residents say lax regulations mean they have gone ahead without public consultation or even a council vote, and locals are now dealing with incessant noise, pollution and even rocketing power bills suspected to be caused by the climbing demand.

The Colossus I data centre straddles the Tennessee-Mississippi state border. (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

"Elon Musk has been here exploiting Memphis on purpose because there are no guardrails in place," said Amber Sherman, who lives close to one of SpaceXAI's other centres, Colossus I, and blames it for a respiratory illness.

" I think that he sees Memphis as a sacrifice zone like a lot of people do. They see us as the path of least resistance and don't think that Memphians are going to fight back. "

Critics say it reflects a concerning national pattern of tech companies taking advantage of outdated city codes and leaving residents in the dark.

"XAI and Elon Musk aren't the first perpetrators, they are just the newest ones, and they are moving at a velocity we have never seen," KeShaun Pearson from Memphis Community Against Pollution said.

SpaceXAI did not respond to questions from the ABC.

Republicans break ranks

Most Americans oppose new data centres in their communities, according to an August YouGov poll.

Only 24 per cent of respondents said the construction of new data centres was good for the US.

More than 200 US jurisdictions have now imposed moratoriums on new centres, according to a national tracker.

Memphis councillors are now considering joining them.

But business leaders argue the developments are needed to power economies global, national and local.

Business leaders say Memphis should benefit from data centre investment in the area. (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

The Greater Memphis Chamber opposes a moratorium and says the centres could bring long-term community benefits if the city leverages its advantages.

"The better path is not to close the door," the business group said in a statement in August. "It is to stay at the table and negotiate harder."

The data centre boom has given the area tens of millions of dollars in property taxes.

Advocates say the money is desperately needed after decades of disinvestment in a city where manufacturing and auto jobs have disappeared and a quarter of the population lives in poverty.

The centres also have an extremely powerful backer — the US president.

Mr Trump has signed orders to fast-track permits, cut red tape and facilitate construction on federal land.

"If I were the mayor of a town or the governor of a state and I had a chance to get a big plant in, an AI plant or a data centre, I would absolutely want it because the jobs are enormous … and the taxes paid are enormous," he said alongside cryptocurrency leaders at the White House in August.

"The only reason that communities throughout the USA should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backward and poor," he posted online.

A lawsuit alleges Colossus II was set up with "no permits, no public input, and no notice to nearby communities". (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

From Michigan to Florida, Republican candidates are now positioning themselves as anti-data centre.

In Texas, the Republican governor, Trump ally Greg Abbott, recently announced a data centre moratorium, which Mr Trump labelled a mistake.

In Wisconsin, the Republican candidate for governor, Tom Tiffany, has started calling his opponent "Data Centre David Crowley".

And a Republican campaign memo about the Senate race in Ohio warned: "More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around [Republican candidate Jon] Husted's neck," Axios recently reported.

"If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one," the memo said.

'A lot of empty promises'

In Tennessee and Mississippi, some residents say community trust in the centres has been eroded further by unfulfilled promises of local investment.

In 2024, Mr Musk promised to build an $US80 million ($111 million) water recycling facility, initially easing concerns about data centres draining the local aquifer.

SpaceXAI said the grey water plant would supply 10 million gallons per day of cooling water for the supercomputer.

Data centre rush doubles in a year The rush of AI data centres is expected to put a larger burden on the electricity grid than previously estimated, with projects in development more than doubling in a year.

Two years on, construction has barely started and that promise has been put on hold.

"Here in the mid-south region, we have some amazing pure drinking water. It also happens to be priced unreasonably cheap and so that is the primary source of cooling for xAI's data centres," Sarah Houston from Protect Our Aquifer said.

She said data obtained by the community group through freedom of information requests was revealing the extent of the centres' water use.

" Just one of their data centres we know is using at least 800,000 gallons of water a day — and that's just one data centre. "

SpaceXAI says work on the water recycling plant will restart in January 2027.

"We're not going to celebrate this water facility until the water is switched from our aquifer to wastewater," Ms Houston said.

"Until then it is a lot of words and a lot of empty promises."

Lawsuits are also proliferating.

The non-profit Southern Environmental Law Center is suing SpaceXAI, alleging it set up dozens of unpermitted gas turbines across its data centre sites that are releasing "smog-forming pollution, soot and hazardous chemicals like formaldehyde" into the air.

The City of Memphis commissioned third-party air quality testing near SpaceXAI sites in June 2025 and found there were "no dangerous pollutant levels" at those locations.

Mississippi resident Taylor Logsdon, who is part of a separate class action over noise concerns, said all other avenues had been exhausted. But she had been criticised by some locals in the Republican area, who had called her 'woke' and a 'libtard', she said.

Taylor Logsdon says data centre noise has left her with no choice but legal action. (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

"A lot of these people here, they've told us all, 'Why don't you just move?'" she said.

" I can't move. I'm a stay-at-home mum and my husband doesn't make that much money. We bought the house at like $70,000 you can't find that no more, there's no way. "

Loretta Thornton fears bringing a legal fight against Mr Musk, the world's richest man, is futile.

"If you start fighting with him, don't you know you'll be dead before it's settled?

"Maybe I can help somebody else by speaking out but I know it's not going anywhere. They're not going to shut that down."

World.title: Fred Hollows built something remarkable but its future is under threat
World.content:
Fred Hollows pioneered life-changing eye care in hundreds of Indigenous communities. ( )

It is almost 60 years since ophthalmologist Fred Hollows first ventured into the Australian outback to restore sight to the blind.

His mission has brought life-changing eye surgery to more than 3 million people worldwide, including tens of thousands of Indigenous Australians.

In the three decades since his death, a devoted group of surgeons, nurses and admin wizards has selflessly carried on his work in remote clinics.

But many are nearing retirement age, and they fear Fred Hollows' vision will not survive unless governments can see past a glaring funding blind spot.

The operating room in the small outback hospital hums with machines and quiet efficiency.

Five women in surgical scrubs barely say a word as they perform their fourth routine miracle of the day — restoring a patient's sight.

During the ABC's visit, Wendy Lindsay lies awake on the operating table under a blue sheet. The only visible part of her is her right eye.

A cataract — clouded, stubborn — is being extracted with the technological sophistication you'd expect of a world-class hospital.

But this single-storey facility in Bourke, in north-western New South Wales, is a dusty nine-hour drive from any metropolitan centre.

And this ophthalmological operating theatre? It only cranks into action 10 times a year when the Outback Eye Service rolls into town for three days.

Surgeon Nicole Lim relies on a camera and a video screen to guide the delicate eye surgery. ( )

Three months earlier, when Ms Lindsay first arrived at the clinic for surgery on her left eye, she was struggling to see through the cataracts that had been gradually robbing her of sight for years.

She says being able to see clearly through her left eye has given her greater confidence to move through her daily activities.

"I can't wait," she says of having sight return to her right eye.

The 84-year-old has travelled 280 kilometres for the surgery from Thurloo Downs Station — a three-hour drive through country so remote her partner insisted his son drive her halfway, where his daughter met them to complete the journey.

Nicole Lim says Fred Hollows' pioneering work inspires her. ( )

Wendy Lindsay rests in the clinic after cataract surgery. ( )

The logistics seem onerous for a simple day-surgery procedure, but they're nothing compared with the alternatives: travel more than 1,000 kilometres to Sydney; join a years-long waiting list in a regional hospital; or, as the service's nurse manager Joanna Barton puts it, "just go blind".

Ms Barton has been running the Outback Eye Service (OES) in NSW since 1995, when she walked into the Bourke hospital and met ophthalmologist Minas Coroneo, who was earnestly trying to keep the service going after its founder, Fred Hollows, had died two years earlier.

Professor Hollows was a fierce advocate for geography not being the arbiter of who could access health care, and the now Professor Coroneo says he did not want to be "the person who stopped that service".

Three decades later, he and Ms Barton — now both in their 70s — are still working together to keep the service going.

But they are worried about its future, as funding remains precarious.

Joanna Barton, left, has been bringing health care to remote communities since the 1990s. ( )

Minas Coroneo performs cataract surgery at the Outback Eye Service in the 1990s. ( )

Outreach and outpatient eye clinics in Bourke, Lightning Ridge, Walgett, Cobar, and Brewarrina, have tested thousands of people over the past 30 years and, with the help of Ms Barton and her tiny team, those requiring treatment have received it.

But it is estimated 30 per cent of the population in these areas — about 40,000 people — suffer from preventable or treatable eye conditions that will lead to blindness without medical intervention.

"I'm nearer the end of my career than the start," says Professor Coroneo, chairman of the Department of Ophthalmology, UNSW, at Prince of Wales Hospital in Sydney.

Minas Coroneo has continued Fred Hollows' work and built his own legacy, including pioneering the use of Trypan blue dye to make cataract surgery safer. ( )

He's been doing this work for longer than Professor Hollows did, and has spent decades alongside Ms Barton and other advocates fighting for funding to guarantee its survival.

Ms Barton describes the financial model supporting the OES as a complex jigsaw.

Funding comes from three main sources, none of which are permanent or guaranteed: The Fred Hollows Foundation charity, and state and federal government grants operating on a year-to-year basis.

“This is our dilemma," Ms Barton says.

"If one of these sources pulled out [funding] tomorrow, we’d all be gone.

“We’ve been trying for years to get recurrent funding. We need to know we are part of NSW Health — that we’re a permanent fixture in the health system.

" Really, it's our dedication and passion — that's the only reason this service is still going. "

Joanna Barton prepares Wendy Lindsay for eye surgery. ( )

NSW Health Minister Ryan Park says the government "will never turn away additional funds" for the OES.

But Ms Barton and Professor Coroneo want certainty.

“Our ask is to please embed us in the public system as an everyday service," Ms Barton says.

Professor Coroneo's view is clear: the health care of Australia's most marginalised people should not be reliant on charity and the generosity of donors.

"It would be catastrophic," he says of the prospect of the service ending.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised this article contains images of people who have died.

Pipe-smoking miracle worker

New Zealand-born Frederick Cossom Hollows could have been buried anywhere.

But he chose the red earth of Bourke, where the work that brought him international recognition really began, as his final resting place.

Fred Hollows is buried in the historic cemetery at Bourke in outback NSW. ( )

Fred Hollows chose Bourke as his final resting place. ( )

Fred Hollows' mission spread far beyond Australia's shores. ( )

His grave is marked with rocks of red sandstone hauled from nearby Mount Oxley and arranged in a dotted outline of an eye around his headstone, which sits in the place of a pupil.

"I think he fell in love with that place," says Olga Collis, now 78, who was an Aboriginal health worker when the then Dr Hollows first visited Bourke in the early 1970s.

"He fell in love with the red dirt and scrub, the people, the surrounds.

" He was a Kiwi, but he loved Australia. And he found his restful place here. "

Olga Collis started working at the Outback Eye Service in the 1970s. ( )

Olga Collis recalls being surprised by Fred Hollows' personality when she first met him. ( )

For years, Dr Hollows worked in Bourke unpaid, on weekends, travelling 10 hours each way from Sydney every few months on some of the roughest roads in the country.

He recognised that Aboriginal communities in the outback needed critical health care, so he walked among them to gain their trust.

Ms Collis remembers the first time she met him. Her supervisor told her she'd be accompanying a doctor who was visiting Alice Edwards Village, a former Aboriginal mission on the outskirts of Bourke.

Before they entered the village, Ms Collis says, Dr Hollows stopped the car, turned to his "very elegant" wife Gabi and told her, in language considerably more colourful than Ms Collis wants to repeat, to take off her makeup, her lipstick and her earrings.

Fred and Gabi Hollows working during the National Trachoma and Eye Health Program. ( )

The Fred Hollows Foundation supports the work Fred and Gabi Hollows started decades ago. ( )

"Don't ever meet people dressed like that," she remembers him saying to Ms Hollows. "Meet them on their own ground."

Ms Collis says she thought: "Is this a doctor? Do doctors speak like this?"

But then she watched him work.

They walked from house to house, with Dr Hollows smoking his pipe and taking the time to sit on the ground and yarn with families.

Loading...

More than 100,000 Indigenous people were screened during the National Trachoma and Eye Health Program, which ran from 1976 to 1979. ( )

Fred Hollows was passionate about meeting people on their own terms and earning their trust. ( )

"I'm Fred," he'd introduce himself without any affectation.

"He spoke the way we spoke, in their tongue, you know. So natural," Ms Collis says.

By the time they had finished their rounds, word had spread that Fred Hollows was in town, and he could fix your eyes.

"It was his approach. The open communication. The respect," she says.

"The seeds were planted and, believe me, those people turned up for the clinic."

Speaking from her home in Sydney decades later, Gabi Hollows, who met Fred during her training as an orthoptist and worked with him on the National Trachoma and Eye Health Program, doesn't remember the exchange in the car as Ms Collis recalls it, but she is not surprised by it.

Gabi Hollows has overseen her first husband's extraordinary legacy for decades. ( )

"Fred was very pragmatic and very matter-of-fact," Ms Hollows says.

" He was really — no bullshit, you know? He'd be very impatient at times. "

Nicknamed "the wild colonial boy" of Australian surgery, he expected excellence from the educated and privileged but was gentle with those who were more vulnerable, she says.

"He was as gentle as he could be with any of the old ladies or any of the old patients who reminded him of his old mum or his grandma," Ms Hollows says.

Loading...

First grandmother, then grandson

Bourke resident Robert Dixon was seven or eight years old when Dr Hollows restored his grandmother's eyesight.

He's 67 now, and the memory remains vivid.

"She had thick glasses," he says, "which she never had to wear after Dr Hollows."

In recent months Mr Dixon has undergone the same cataract surgery at the Bourke clinic.

He has diabetes, a condition that affects a devastating number of First Nations people and places them at greater risk of blindness.

"If you don't get your eyes done, you're going to go blind," Mr Dixon says.

Clear eyesight means Robert Dixon will be driving for years to come. ( )

When cataracts rendered him unable to read the letters below the first two lines on an eyesight test, he lost his licence, which he needed for his job as a hospital security guard.

"When I got one eye done, I could see real good, but they were still trying to take the licence," he says.

"So six months later, I had the other eye done and could read the bottom line on the chart."

He says that without the operation, he'd "be done".

"If I didn't have the operation, I'd be blind now. I wouldn't be able to handle that," he said.

The procedure to remove a cataract and replace it with a clear artificial lens usually takes less than an hour per eye from preparation to surgery to discharge. Then there's a follow-up consultation the next day.

Cataracts develop over several years and can lead to blindness. ( )

The convenience of being able to have the surgery in Bourke, where Mr Dixon lives, meant undergoing the procedure was an easy decision for him.

But it's not so straightforward for others.

Heavy lifting behind the scenes

The logistics of running the mobile clinic are complex, but decades of experience have refined the process.

Dubbo-based Joanna Barton coordinates the service with two other full-time staff based in Sydney. They manage a calendar that stretches a year in advance.

Every surgery trip to Bourke then mobilises staff from across western NSW — nurses from Orange, Coonabarabran, Dubbo and Bourke, anaesthetists from Dubbo and Sydney, and ophthalmologists from the training program at Sydney's Prince of Wales Hospital.

Equipment is ordered, packed and shipped.

Joanna Barton has been coordinating the Outback Eye Service since the 1990s. ( )

The OES treats between 1,200 and 1,300 patients a year, with about 150 undergoing cataract and oculoplastic surgery, and the others receiving treatment for conditions including trachoma, which can lead to permanent blindness.

"Eighty per cent of the work goes on behind the scenes. The surgery and clinics are the icing on the cake," Ms Barton says.

The stakes are higher than restoring vision alone.

"We're talking about [preventing] falls. We're talking about broken hips," Ms Barton says.

" Think about it — $6,000 for cataract surgery to save someone's sight or get their sight back. Or the cost if someone falls over, breaks their hip, and they're in a nursing home for the rest of their lives. "

The Outback Eye Service brings vital health care to Indigenous communities. ( )

Ms Barton says it is essential for the service to be a permanent fixture in the public health system and "definitely not an add-on".

A statement from the Fred Hollows Foundation says that while "charitable funding has helped fill important gaps, essential healthcare services should not rely on philanthropy in the long term".

"We urge the NSW government to commit to sustainable, long-term investment in the Outback Eye Service so communities across western NSW can continue to access the eye care they need, regardless of where they live," the statement says.

Today, the service is run with two full-time equivalent nurse positions funded on a year-to-year basis by the federal Western Primary Health Network at a cost of about $338,000 per year.

Medical staff prepare a patient for cataract surgery at the Bourke operating theatre. ( )

The Fred Hollows Foundation funds one full-time orthoptist position costing $199,000 per year.

NSW Health then covers a range of services and expenses critical to running the OES, including resources from the South Eastern Sydney Local Health District, accommodation, plane flights and hospital facilities.

It also staffs the surgeries through the Western Local Health District, and provides operating equipment.

The Royal Flying Doctor Service also supports the OES.

But none of this support is guaranteed or permanent.

New generation, same vision

Professor Coroneo has developed a relay-style staffing system for the Bourke and outreach clinics that aims to alleviate burnout.

Under this roster, 14 ophthalmological specialists from the Prince of Wales Hospital work at these clinics as part of their training. When they finish, they hand over to the next generation.

Nicole Lim says many people only receive the eye care they need because the Outback Eye Service is in town. ( )

Nicole Lim is inspired by Fred Hollows' legacy. ( )

Nicole Lim trained at the Prince of Wales Hospital under Professor Coroneo and is one of the new generation of ophthalmologists carrying on Professor Hollows' work.

Before starting her training, Dr Lim visited the Tilganga Institute of Ophthalmology in Nepal, run by Sanduk Ruit, who worked closely with Professor Hollows.

"Seeing Fred Hollows' impact on that global scale was very inspiring," she says.

Now, as a junior consultant, Dr Lim also has seen the impact of this work during trips to Bourke and Cobar, where, just before flying home one day, a patient arrived with an eyelid lesion consistent with basal cell carcinoma.

As the next oculoplastic specialist would not be visiting Cobar for six months, Dr Lim did the biopsy on the spot.

"If we didn't travel out there, we'd lose a lot of patients who are actually being reached just by us being present," she says.

A true silver lining

When the ABC reconnects with Wendy Lindsay several months after the surgery on her right eye, she admits it has taken her a while to stop reaching for spectacles she no longer requires.

Having perfect vision has given her a new outlook on life.

"Everything wasn't quite clear before," she says.

Now, in her new home in Dubbo, Ms Lindsay can easily read subtitles on the TV and thread a needle.

She has also been able to return to her favourite hobby of making fine silver jewellery.

With her sight restored, Wendy Lindsay has been able to make fine silver jewellery again. ( )

Without a hint of difficulty, she uses tiny pliers to twist and bead thin strands of precious metal into delicate bracelets and necklaces.

It is clear how much she enjoys this fine, detailed work now that her eyesight has been restored.

"I hadn't done it for quite some time," she says, holding up an intricate bracelet.

Another simple joy is being able to walk confidently in the garden alongside her dog, Miss Toby, without fear of tripping over.

Life is now a whole lot brighter for Wendy, pictured with her dog, Miss Toby. ( )

But without the OES, Ms Lindsay, Mr Dixon and thousands of other Australians living remotely would be needlessly struggling with deteriorating eyesight and a poorer quality of life.

Looking to the future

After years of calling for stable funding, Professor Coroneo's message to governments is clear: fund the Outback Eye Service properly, permanently, or risk losing it when he and Ms Barton retire.

A spokesperson from South Eastern Sydney Local Health District says the "collaborative partnership model … enables additional services, outreach activities, and workforce support to be delivered in communities where access to specialist eye care may otherwise be limited".

"NSW Health acknowledges the important role played by charities in supporting the health and wellbeing of regional communities," the spokesperson says.

"The Outback Eye Service remains an active public health service delivered through appropriate contracts and service agreements.

"Service planning and funding arrangements are regularly reviewed to ensure communities continue to receive access to high-quality eye care and to identify opportunities that support its ongoing sustainability."

World.title: How to keep your kids safe at petting zoos
World.content:
A three-year-old girl has died from a rare illness after visiting a petting zoo in Victoria. She had developed brain damage and kidney failure after spending weeks in intensive care.

The girl is confirmed to have had haemolytic uraemic syndrome, a rare but serious serious condition, caused by infection with a specific type of Escherichia coli bacteria (or E. coli for short). This can be transmitted in a variety of ways, including after contact with animals on a farm or at a petting zoo.

Fortunately, such tragic cases are rare. But they do shed light on bacterial infections harboured by some animals and the need to take hygiene precautions when visiting petting zoos.

I'm a microbiology lecturer, and I'm planning to visit a petting zoo next weekend with my family.

Here's what we know about the infection risk at petting zoos, and what parents can do to help keep their children safe.

What is haemolytic uraemic syndrome?

Haemolytic uraemic syndrome most commonly results from infection with types of E. coli that produce a specific toxin called the Shiga toxin.

Early symptomsof infection are nausea, stomach cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea, which can contain blood.

Girl's death after petting zoo visit 'very rare', health authorities say The family of a young girl who died earlier this week say she may have contracted a bacterial infection while petting and riding animals on a farm.

Warning signs that need urgent medical assessment include bloody diarrhoea, markedly reduced urination, lethargy, pallor (looking pale), unexplained bruising or red-purple spots on the skin.

If a doctor suspects someone has haemolytic uraemic syndrome, they will ask about symptoms and examine the person. Hospitalisation as soon as possible will be necessary. Blood, stool and sometimes urine tests confirm the diagnosis.

The Shiga toxin can damage the lining of blood vessels, which leads to circulatory and kidney problems. This can progress to haemolytic uraemic syndrome, leading to kidney failure, high blood pressure, seizures and in some cases death.

So emergency medical treatment is essential, in a hospital intensive care unit, with dialysis and blood transfusions often needed.

The disease is more common in children.

How is it spread?

These bacteria can can spread to humans by contaminated food and water. Humans can also spread the bacteria to other humans, via faeces, such as when changing nappies.

But the situation most relevant here is the spread via some animals. Bacteria are present on animal fur and wool, so children can come into contact with it when patting or cuddling an animal. But that's not the only way.

Bacteria are also present on manure, bedding, soil, feed, enclosure floors and fences.

The risk lies when people's contaminated hands come into contact with their mouth.

Toddlers are particularly difficult to protect because they often put fingers, toys, food and dummies in their mouths and need help to wash their hands thoroughly.

Are some animals riskier than others?

Cattle and other ruminants, including sheep and goats, are recognised animal reservoirs for Shiga-producing E. coli, as well as some other pathogens.

For example, animal contact can also expose children to Salmonella, Campylobacter and Cryptosporidium, all of which can cause gastroenteritis.

When choosing a petting zoo, favour venues with handwashing stations immediately outside animal areas, with running water, soap and disposable towels. (Unsplash: Clay Banks)

While exposure to these can occur on farms, petting zoos and open zoos specifically have been identified as a risk for these microorganisms. Animals may not always show symptoms.

But petting zoos are great for kids, aren't they?

Petting zoos and farm experiences can provide children with educational experiences involving animals, farming, food production and animal welfare. They're also such a great family activity and educational resource.

The Australian Veterinary Association supports petting zoos where animal health, welfare, public safety and disease-transmission risks are appropriately managed.

Hygiene plans include clear communication about the risks of infection, readily accessible handwashing facilities, and physical separation between animal-contact and food areas.

Parents need to ensure their children are supervised. Most importantly, they need to ensure their children's hands are washed before coming into contact with anything that might go into a child's mouth — a dummy, or food, for instance. Hand sanitiser is not as effective as washing with soap and water for 20 seconds or more.

So when choosing a petting zoo, favour venues with handwashing stations immediately outside animal areas, with running water, soap, disposable towels and signs reminding visitors to wash before eating or drinking.

Thomas Jeffries is a senior lecturer in microbiology at Western Sydney University. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

World.title: Life can be hard. These Australians share their ingredients for happiness
World.content:
As part of the ABC's Your Say project, we've heard from thousands of people telling us that life is hard and it's getting harder.

Financially, many are doing it tough, as the cost of paying mortgages, rent, food, petrol and energy bills goes up.

And we've heard from you that life is getting more complicated, whether it's trying to get a loved one the aged care they need or navigating the NDIS system.

What do you want to tell us? Have Your Say Our best stories start with listening to yours. Tell us what Australia should know.

You've told us you are increasingly worried about global events and the environment.

Even just managing basic day-to-day life can be tricky, like trying to keep kids off screens or finding the time to exercise.

Most of us just want a happy life, but "comparison culture" and the high visibility of other people's lives on social media can compound a sense of anxiety about the future.

We asked a range of people what they think the key ingredients for that happy life are.

Some are universal, others are personal.

You might find some inspiration from what these Australians listed as their ingredients for a happy life.

Shaelyn Van Brecht, 32, dairy farmer and single mum to one

Knowing that people are there in times of need has been vital for Ringarooma dairy farmer Shaelyn Van Brecht. (ABC News: Laurissa Smith)

1. My people:

Time and time again, my people have been the reason that I have been able to get through all the things that we've had going on. I'm very grateful for them. Phone calls, or it might be a chat beside the cattle crush, or it's a post-netball chat. All of it helps, and I am eternally thankful for them.

2. Calm home:

There is so much of me now that is very thankful. I have a calm house, and I come home and I can just be here, and I am very thankful for the effort I've put in and for others that I've asked to help me build a calm home.

3. Supportive community:

All of the things that have been going on, people are always checking in with me. I am someone who doesn't always ask for help, but I've had to learn to and so I do really appreciate when people do stop at the supermarket or the coffee shop or check in with a text message to make sure that we're travelling alright. And if we're not, what they can do to help — so that is phenomenal as well.

4. Yummy food:

I love to cook for people. It's what I love doing. Now that I'm feeling a bit more like myself, it's really nice that I feel like I can cook for people and give them food when they're going through a rough time, and I love eating yummy food. It makes a really shit day better. Very thankful for good coffee as well.

I feel like in the last six months I have come a long, long way. I see a counsellor regularly, and so that process has helped me to figure out who I am and what I would like my home to look like for my son and I, or for anyone who visits our home. So I feel like in the last six months I've worked really hard to identify these things and know that that's what fuels my soul, and so to keep working hard to achieve them because that's what makes me, me.

Wayne Crawford, 81, retired journalist

Wayne Crawford finds joy in his enduring friendships. (Supplied: David Brill)

1. Good aged care:

I fought long and hard to stay in my apartment. Eighteen months ago it became clear I was not physically able to look after myself. I ended up coming into what is technically a nursing home. I've got my own bachelor pad with 24/7 room service. I am extremely content, very happy here. The staff are marvellous; they've become my family. The atmosphere here is just not like a nursing home. I come and go as I like.

2. Friendships and family:

Since Marg, my wife, died, I miss her terribly, but I am grateful for the friendships that have endured and the people who have continued to nurture me. I have regular coffee mornings with anything up to a dozen or so friends who come in, and we solve the problems of the world and drink caffeine and have a good relationship and good time together. I can't travel myself much anymore because I am confined to a wheelchair, but I have the good fortune to have made a friend … who has a maxi taxi and seems to devote his life to chauffeuring me around. He has changed my life. I still go to rock-and-roll concerts at night … with other old rocker friends. Life is pretty good.

3. Career:

I couldn't have asked for a better employer or better profession. I thoroughly enjoyed being a political journalist and political editor. As they say, if you enjoy your work, it's not really work, and that's the way I looked at my career. It wasn't work; it was a lifestyle, and I still look back very fondly on it and have maintained a lot of friendships, not just journalists, but many politicians, political leaders who have continued to be my friends. You can't put a price on that.

4. Financial security:

I am not rich, and I don't have a huge superannuation fund to dip into, but I've got enough to keep me going. And although it's fairly expensive to go into aged care as I am … for what I get, I don't think it's at all unreasonable. They look after all my meals, they do all my washing, I don't have to go to the supermarket.

I am very happy. I think a lot of it is to do with the fact that I've decided to be happy and decided to be content because life is good. I can still do what I want. I have friends who are happy to go out to lunch or to a concert in the evening.

Alex Betheras, 28, stay-at-home mum, with one child and another on the way

Alex Betheras, who lives in Ross in Tasmania, says it's important to have moments every day when you do something that brings you pure joy. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

1. Family:

Whether that's a larger extended family or a partner you have chosen, that's a really important ingredient.

2. Community:

I think there are a lot of different communities that you can find, whether that's through school or sport or maybe an interest like the Men's Shed or the Fire Brigade, or even a play group.

3. Time outside:

Whether you enjoy gardening or going for a walk, just being out in nature is very important. I spent a lot of time outside. We're on a larger property so we try and grow a lot of our own vegetables and fruit. We have pet sheep, and we are out amongst the animals.

4. The little things:

Whether that's your morning cup of coffee or spending five minutes just doodling at the end of the night, just finding a little thing that brings you a lot of joy and making time to prioritise doing those small things. For me, it would be baking. I really enjoy it. Having something I can share with other people — that ties back into the family and the community.

I feel very lucky that I get to spend most of my time doing the things that bring me a lot of joy. So I really enjoy being a parent. I always wanted to have children, and I wanted to be a very hands-on parent, and I love organising the activities and hosting this playgroup. Having a child gives you a lot of perspective on their own personality; they're figuring out what their own likes and dislikes are. So you get to sit and watch and see what they're doing. I remember when I was a kid, I used to love drawing, and you rediscover those parts of your life.

Joe Abernethy, 25, ICT security analyst

Joe Abernethy, originally from England, left his job to travel and see the world. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

1. Family:

Family is a big thing, because obviously you've got that close connection with your family. Having a supportive family helps me. The majority of my family are back in England, moving all the way out here (Australia) is quite hard. Obviously, the internet and technology are good these days, but (not being able to) see them in person is very hard.

2. Travelling:

I am currently travelling. I'm from Bolton, Manchester, England. It's just the excitement and adventure, not knowing what you're going to find. Obviously, Australia is a beautiful place. It's just nice to be able to get out and travel, meet people, see opportunities, see things.

3. Hobbies:

I do a lot of sport. Football, rugby, just any sport really. I used to be a semi-professional swimmer. I'm just passionate about sport.

4. Dream job:

I've left my job now to do some travelling, but I was in government doing security, and I just met so many lovely people with so many different cultures and backgrounds. It just opened my eyes to different opportunities.

Travelling is the big thing for me, just travelling and seeing the world. You've only got one life, one chance; you might as well just see it before you get old.

World.title: Breaking: Mistrial declared in Lindsay Clancy murder trial
World.content:
A mistrial has been declared in the trial of US mother Lindsay Clancy accused of murdering her three children in their Massachusetts home in 2023.

WARNING: This story contains content that may disturb some readers.

Ms Clancy was charged with three counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months old.

Ms Clancy did not deny killing her children, but her lawyer argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible.

Over seven days of deliberations, jurors repeatedly told the judge they could not come to a decision and were ordered to keep trying to come to a unanimous verdict.

The televised trial, spanning some six weeks, revived long-standing debates about how postpartum mental health in women is treated in the US, and how the country's legal system addresses cases when mothers kill their children.

Throughout the trial, Ms Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington sought to convince jurors she should be found not guilty by reason of insanity, arguing that she was a loving mother who had been in the midst of a psychotic episode when she killed her children.

Mr Reddington attempted to block or delay the mistrial, indicating a single juror was holding out on a unanimous decision, but the Massachusetts Supreme Court refused that appeal.

Ms Clancy, 36, strangled them to death in the basement of her Boston home using exercise bands in January 2023.

She then cut herself with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to take her own life that left her paralysed.

Testimony from family members including Ms Clancy's now ex-husband, Patrick, detailed how she had struggled with her mental health in the preceding months following the birth of her third child, repeatedly seeking treatment from healthcare providers ​who prescribed her a myriad of drugs.

Prosecutors did not dispute that Ms Clancy had been dealing with mental health issues.

But they argued that she was able to appreciate the wrongfulness of killing her children and intentionally chose to do so anyway.

They presented testimony from a psychologist who, after examining Ms Clancy, concluded that she had planned to take her own life and chose to kill her children because "she was convinced that they would suffer without her".

World.title: Russian drone attack hits Ukraine's SBU headquarters in Kyiv
World.content:
A Russian drone hit the headquarters of Ukraine's SBU security service in Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, vowing to retaliate as Moscow kept up its constant air attacks on the capital for the tenth day.

Heavy black smoke rose in Kyiv city centre following the attack, on Friday, local time, which signalled a new escalation in the conflict. At least seven people were injured, Kyiv's mayor said.

Twelve killed as Russia steps up aerial assault on Ukraine Russia carries out a sixth straight day of heavy attacks on Kyiv, with civilian infrastructure and residential buildings among the targets.

During more than four-and-a-half years of war with Russia, Ukrainian government buildings have rarely been damaged in drone and missile strikes.

The SBU is vital to Ukraine's war efforts as it executes high-impact, deep strikes to damage Russia's war machine and its energy infrastructure.

"The drone was aimed directly at the office of the Head of the Security Service in that building," Mr Zelenskyy said on the Telegram app.

It was not immediately clear if SBU members were among the injured.

Ukraine vows 'tangible' response

Mr Zelenskyy said that he ordered "an appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike, to the Russians once everything was ready".

Numerous ambulances and emergency services were heading to the scene in the historic part of the city close to the Saint Sophia Cathedral, a UNESCO World Heritage site.

The owner of a popular bakery, Zavertailo, said on the Telegram app that their building located opposite the SBU building was also destroyed in the attack.

Russian drones targeted downtown Kyiv and Ukraine's SBU headquarters, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. (AP: Francisco Seco)

One woman shouted into her phone that she had popped out to buy cigarettes and been startled by the explosion.

Ukraine's capital has been under continuous Russian drone attack for 10 days. On Wednesday, a university in the city centre was also hit.

"I think (people) can get used to this. In the centre of Kyiv, and in the centre of Moscow. It will get worse, I believe this," said Oleh, 33, who declined to give his last name.

'Rejection of diplomacy'

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha urged allies to step up pressure on Moscow after a Russian drone hit Ukraine's security service headquarters in central Kyiv.

"The Russian attack on Ukraine’s Security Service Headquarters is a major escalation that demands resolute responses," he said on X.

"Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace - laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy," he said.

The SBU is a vast and secretive agency responsible for ambitious operations against Russia, such as the 2022 bombing of a Russian bridge to occupied Crimea and a 2025 drone attack, codenamed Spiderweb, that struck Russian strategic bombers.

It is also widely seen as a leading player in a campaign of covert assassinations of senior Russian military and other figures blamed by Ukraine for carrying out war crimes. Russia has denounced those killings as terrorist attacks.

Reuters

World.title: Undercover sting targets Farage as protests disrupt his major address
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeUK politics Undercover sting targets Farage as protests disrupt his major address David Crowe September 5, 2026 — 4:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Birmingham: A media sting has thrown British right-wing leader Nigel Farage onto the defensive over political finance at a key moment for his Reform UK party, as thousands of supporters gather at its annual conference when it has lost its lead in the polls. Farage removed two key aides from their jobs after the sting revealed them discussing financial support from foreign donors who would be banned from funding British parties. Reform Party Leader Nigel Farage delivers a keynote speech at the party’s annual conference. Getty Images The exposure came the night before Farage addressed party members at his party’s annual gathering in Birmingham, where loyal supporters brushed off the scandal and Farage said the scrutiny showed his rivals were scared of him. In a revelation that rocked British politics, broadcaster Channel 4 showed one of the Reform aides discussing a plan to accept 500,000 from a wealthy American man by routing the money through his son.



The man promising the money was an actor hired by investigative group Verbatim and his “son” was a reporter from the group, and they were speaking at a lunch with Farage. In a separate moment caught on camera, another Reform aide seemed to welcome an approach from the “son” to fund opinion polls to assist the party. Reform UK has lost its lead in the polls. Getty Images Labour responded to the story by calling for a police investigation into the conversations, seeking to pile pressure on Farage when he is already the subject of two parliamentary inquiries into funding from wealthy investors heavily involved in cryptocurrencies. Farage drew rapturous applause from party members in Birmingham despite the news coverage, as they danced and sang while waiting for him to appear after security concerns delayed his appearance by about one hour.



Protesters in the audience yelled out during the early part of his address, but Farage laughed them off as “boring” and the crowd chanted at them to leave before security officials took them away. Protesters outside the Reform UK annual conference in Birmingham on Friday. Bloomberg Farage admitted there was “loose pub talk” by the two Reform aides but declared the party had not done anything wrong and had not broken the law. “The polls in question were not commissioned by Reform. The results are out there in the full public domain, and there is no issue,” he said. “What is problematic is loose pub talk, including a couple of quotes that were made that simply were not true.



Related Article Analysis

World politics Farage began a political farce. Binface missed his chance “But some of the comments made by two of our team were injudicious at best. Neither of these members have the right to act in this way. Accordingly, they stepped down, pending an investigation.” Reform members told this masthead the donations talk did not change their support because their priorities were issues such as migration, a key topic for the party when Farage is promising to stop asylum seeker boats crossing the English Channel. Farage blamed his opponents for the greater scrutiny on the party. “Ask yourself, why is all of this happening? Anyone got a clue why it’s happening?” he asked during his address. “Because they’re scared of us. That’s why it’s happening. And in my case, I’ve broken no laws, abused no public money.”



The furore undercut the party’s message when the high point of the conference was meant to be an agreement with a key French ally, National Rally president Jordan Bardella, to work together to stop asylum seeker boats if their parties formed government. Bardella could become prime minister if the right-wing party sweeps elections to be held in France next year. National Rally leader Marine Le Pen is running for president. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Britain’s budget blues will end Burnham’s honeymoon Britain has been unable to stop small boats carrying asylum seekers from France in recent years, although numbers are down so far this year. Farage and Bardella argued that those who tried to cross the channel would be returned to France, removing the incentive to get on boats. Reform and National Rally both propose tougher measures against migrants, including the removal of benefits that they believe encourages migrants to seek better lives in Britain and France.



Reform surged past Labour and the Conservative Party in the opinion polls over the past two years, and it had 23 per cent support in a YouGov survey released on September 1. It has lost its edge over Labour, however, after the rise of Andy Burnham as party leader and prime minister six weeks ago. Labour sank as low as 16 per cent in May but matched Reform on 23 per cent in the latest poll. Verbatim, the reporting group that supplied the video for the Channel 4 broadcast, was set up by Lawrence Carter and Louis Wilson, who previously worked at the Centre for Climate Reporting, which also used actors to trick politicians into speaking on hidden cameras. A report by the climate group made headlines in Australia last year when it showed US political adviser Chris LaCivita, a campaign aide to President Donald Trump, telling people he had been in Australia to advise the Liberal Party on issues it was having with the party’s leader at the time, Peter Dutton.
