World.title: Darren Klemm is usually the bearer of bad news. He’s OK with it
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWAEmergency services Darren Klemm is usually the bearer of bad news. He’s OK with it Hannah Murphy September 5, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Darren Klemm remembers a time when volunteers didn’t bother warning the public about every little spot fire. “We’d go to fires out at the back of Cullacabardee, and just not tell anyone anything. You know, roads would get closed, but it was just the way it was and people got on with it too,” he says. DFES Commissioner Darren Klemm. Hamish Hastie However, now in his ninth year as Western Australia’s Department of Fire and Emergency Services Commissioner, Klemm says in 2026, constant updates are non-negotiable. “The growth is unbelievable, and the expectation from community about what they’ll get told and when they get told it has grown exponentially,” he says.



“We’re always going to find it hard to keep up with that thirst – because the more that you give, the more that is expected.” Klemm is used to being the bearer of bad news. In his time as commissioner, he says the way he has gone about delivering warnings, wash-ups and incident details has changed immensely. Fitzroy Crossing Airport at the height of the floods. Police Media He has seen a transition from giving updates on the old AM radio, to massively scaling up of the state’s emergency’s website, which provides minute-by-minute information on bushfires, floods, cyclones and HAZMAT warnings. Now, he says, the public want information, they want it now – and it’s his job to deliver it.



“They want to be warned, and they want to inform themselves. That’s what we want as well,” Klemm says. Sitting down with this masthead in his Cockburn office at the beginning of the state’s bushfire season, Klemm is a long way from his hometown in Wagin and where he grew up in the Wheatbelt. “We’re getting overlapping [fire] seasons between the north and the south … and now, the flooding that we’ve had, it seems to be every year now.” DFES Commissioner Darren Klemm At an early age, Klemm remembers he always had to be doing something. Not content with university or sitting around inside, he was a prolific footballer – a midfield rover – and was eventually picked up by the South Australian National Football League. It is there, he says, where he picked up his love of firefighting.



“Some guys I was playing footy with, a lot of them were in the fire brigade,” Klemm says. Related Article Exclusive

Construction WA’s new building boss says we don’t build them like we used to – and that’s a good thing “I mean, there was just always something going on. That was motivating and stimulating.” He spent three years working as a firefighter in South Australia before picking up and moving back home with his wife, and taking up with the agency that would become his home for the next two decades. “FESA, as it was called then,” he laughs.



Klemm is coy about his meteoric rise through the agency, but attributes much of his success due to his time on the ground, actually doing the job. When he was tapped by outgoing commissioner Wayne Gregson in 2017, he had to sit on the news for a month before it was formally announced. He says it didn’t hit him until he walked into the office on his first day, and realised the weight on his shoulders. Every cyclone, bushfire, rescue – it was all in his control. Originally a career firefighter, Klemm spent years on the tools before moving to management. DFES “The state’s emergency framework is not just about bushfire and cyclones – it’s every emergency,” Klemm says. “Those are the things that people see the most because they happen every year.



“But then we have things like the pandemic, things like hazardous materials [incidents], and now AUKUS. They all have to be operated.” Related Article Planning and development WA’s Planning Commission boss talks housing, density – and pushback And in his time, Klemm has already had to navigate a series of some of the state’s worst catastrophes. There was flooding at Fitzroy Crossing that wiped out dozens of homes and a major arterial bridge, and Cyclone Seroja, which flattened Kalbarri – a coastal town that had up until that point been out of the reach of the state’s major cyclone events. And, in 2021, Wooroloo, where nearly 100 homes went up in flames as a bushfire tore through the hills suburb.



As commissioner, Klemm says he didn’t like leaving people in the lurch. “If you think about the experience for the community – we come and the fire’s put out, but then they’re left with a home that might be damaged, and then who’s there to help them do that? Who can they see in government that’s going to help them?” Klemm says. A burned fire ground near Wooroloo. AP So he and the agency began the arduous task of bringing recovery in-house. The change meant DFES was able to deploy its own crews to help people in Fitzroy Crossing who lost everything in 2022, and Klemm says his team’s work had made the transition “seamless”.



“It first really started in Wooroloo – we were really clear with the community that once the fire was put out, we weren’t just going to leave,” he says. It’s a method he and the agency had begun to deploy more regularly, and Klemm says this upcoming bushfire season will be no different. A firefighting plane dumps retardant on Wooroloo blaze. AP “We’re getting overlapping seasons between the north and the south … and now, the flooding that we’ve had, it seems to be every year now,” he says. “Things are changing, and you know any firefighter will tell you that we have difficulties at night now, where that never used to be the case.”



Klemm doesn’t mince words about the upcoming bushfire season in WA – it is set to be challenging, and difficult. While the agency has the resources to mitigate the impact, he warns, locals have to play their part too. “I’m not sure everybody in the eastern states quite understands how big WA is,” he says. “The risks are everywhere. “Just because you live in the western suburbs doesn’t mean you might not be adjacent to [bushland].



“I dare say there’s a lot of people that go down south on holiday, and it’s particularly difficult down there. “That’s why we have Emergency WA – people can go there and do their plans and actually educate themselves to make sure they’re making the best decisions for themselves, and not relying on someone putting a comment on social media, which may or may not be correct.”

World.title: Hit this Fremantle cafe for ace brunching, then return after dark for modern bistro thrills (if you can get a seat)
World.content:
Review Eating outFremantle Hit this Fremantle cafe for ace brunching, then return after dark for modern bistro thrills (if you can get a seat) Fuelled by traditional thinking and youthful energy, The Cool Room feels both reassuringly familiar and thrillingly novel. Max Veenhuyzen September 5, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

1 / 2 Seasonal fruit and soda bread. Supplied 2 / 2 Sesame sourdough bun plate. Supplied Previous Slide Next Slide 14.5 / 20 How we score The Cool Room Fremantle European$$$$ The Cool Room is one of Fremantle’s hottest, most interesting cafes. I write this with confidence, knowing full well that the standard of brunching across Freo is high; that hotness is at odds with the low-Celsius connotations of the cafe’s name; and that The Cool Room, having turned one in August, is way past its honeymoon period, so people aren’t seeking it out (just) because it’s new. Rather, many are drawn to this suburban cafe because it’s old. Or looks old, at least.



On Friday nights, The Cool Room hosts weekly set menu dinners showcasing the kitchen’s restaurant pedigree. Max Veenhuyzen They come to admire the retro beauty of this former butcher dressed with mismatched, garage sale-direct furniture and accessories. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up The result is a timeless, broadly Aussie reimagining of Grandma’s house that is free of potpourri but full of Freo types. Here’s a white-haired bloke with boardies and shapely calves. Over there, 20-somethings coo at a fat tyre bike. A young couple with small kids and a big dog turn the corner and see the crowd. Immediately, their brows furrow in a way that says, Goldilocks-style, “who’s been ordering alt-milk lattes in my local cafe?” If you’re a first-timer and the place is heaving, it can be hard to tell when The Cool Room ends and when Old Values – the vintage op-shop next door – starts.



Such confusion is testament to both the demand for weekend tables and the knack that Charlotte Beeton and Drew Dawson, owners of The Cool Room, have for vintage styling. This affinity with yesteryear is also evident in their food offering: familiar, brunch dishes that, at their best, both comfort and quietly surprise diners. Related Article 14 / 20 Review No, Google Maps isn’t playing up: this Perth gym really does house a great Malay cafe There is a plush omelette filled with whipped chevre packing more flavour than anything this lightweight has any right to. There is also an aspirational bacon and fudgy yolk fried egg bap: a morning-after lifesaver that is to servo bacon and egg rolls as former gas lobbyists are to by-election success. There is also a very convincing take on the a la mode Scandinavian breakfast plate starring a soft-boiled egg, waxy rectangles of semi-firm Tilsit cheese from Dellendale Creamery in Denmark, granola plus a sourdough bun studded with white sesame seeds. (The bun, meanwhile, is baked at the cafe, as are most of the breads, biscuits and cakes served.) On paper, none of these dishes sound especially ground-breaking, yet time after time, The Cool Room’s versions of these cafe classics tasted finer, livelier and more focused than what you’ll get around town.



One reason that explains the above: provenance. People like to talk about sourcing seasonal and local ingredients. This is one place where you can really taste it. (Still, there’s a blackboard by the entrance shouting out the cafe’s suppliers.) Another explanation: confident seasoning. Salt seems to be in everything here. It’s on the end of a sundae spoon served with the soft-boiled eggs on the brekky plate. It’s in the addictive granola bulked up with arcs of toasted coconut and pumpkin seeds candied in maple syrup. And it also helps emphasise the spicy richness of malleable chocolate and rye cookies. Olympia James-Ainslie, Charlotte Beeton, Rosie Fowkes, Drew Dawson and Megan Sullivan of The Cool Room. Max Veenhuyzen One aspect of The Cool Room that isn’t salty, however, is its service. Luka Burger and Georgia Gillett are a warm presence on the coffee machine while upbeat front-of-house personality Hannah Jawad feels like she’s constantly here, there and everywhere. While brunch is The Cool Room’s soda bread and cultured butter, the cafe also hosts Friday dinner services that show off the restaurant pedigree of Dawson (formerly of Lola’s and Nieuw Ruin in Fremantle, plus Melbourne’s Napier Quarter) and kitchen offsiders Olympia James-Ainslie, Rosie Fowkes and Megan Sullivan.



It’s also why writing this review has taken longer than I had hoped. The difficulty of snagging a booking suggests that many are already across the pleasures of this weekly offering. (Dinner is an $80 three-course set menu plus an additional fiver for corkage; only 28 seats are available each Friday.) But if this is news to you, this is one Friday dinner worth making happen. Related Article Exclusive After 15 years of active service, Rockpool Perth is getting a $3 million makeover While night mode sees tables set with (real!) candles and the playlist’s jazz-funk tunes reduced to a bassy hum by enthusiastic guests, the kitchen takes the same unshowy attitude to dinner as it does brunch. Sweet parker buns ride shotgun alongside a slab of poised chicken terrine shot through with a coin of confit leek. Thick, room-temperature slices of pink blade beef are cloaked by an aerated mess of horseradish-spiced sour cream. While the dish’s lightness struck me as a WeightWatchers-approved vitello tonnato – and I write that in a very good, very I-could-eat-this-all-summer kind of way – it’s more than likely a nod to the British heritage of Dawson. Not that our man has any aspirations to be the next Fergus Henderson or anything. Instead, like many of his peers, such introspection is simply one cook’s pursuit of nostalgic flavours from his past.



I had zero idea that flapjacks were a classic British oat bar, but my ignorance didn’t hinder my enjoyment of Beeton’s rendition (cleverly crunched up with buckwheat) one bit. I do, however, feel foolish that I didn’t get that the intriguing lilt of cumquat in a Friday night chocolate mousse dessert was an homage to England’s famous Terry’s Chocolate Orange. But like I was saying, it can be tricky to tell when old values end, and The Cool Room begins. The low-down Atmosphere: A suburban cafe (and youthful cafe crew) to watch. Go-to dishes: Sesame sourdough bun plate ($18), bacon bap with fried egg ($20). Drinks: All the cafe classics plus iced teas and fruit juices made from seasonal fruit. Cost: About $50 for two people, excluding drinks (dinner is $80 per person for a three-course set menu). Good Food reviews are booked anonymously and paid independently. A restaurant can’t pay for a review or inclusion in the Good Food Guide.

World.title: ‘Staying put’: WA homeowners spent $1.2 billion renovating their homes last year
World.content:
NationalWAProperty development ‘Staying put’: WA homeowners spent $1.2 billion renovating their homes last year Indigo Lemay-Conway September 5, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Over the last financial year Western Australian homeowners spent almost over a billion dollars on home renovations. Statewide renovation spending reached $1.2 billion in 2025-26, driven by everything from major kitchen and bathroom upgrades to general cosmetic work. Western Australians have spent over a billion dollars on home renovations in the last financial year. Of that, $934 million was invested across the Greater Perth region and $130.9 million was spent in June alone. The Australian Bureau of Statistics released new figures this month showing which SA3’s (geographic regions) saw the highest amount of money spent on fixing up homes.



And the list might surprise you. Cottesloe-Claremont was at the top of the table, which saw homeowners spend about $127 million doing up their homes over the past year, jumping up by $7 million from the previous year. Second in line was Perth City, with just over $108 million spent on renovations, followed by Stirling with $93 million invested. Architect and former deputy Lord Mayor of the City of Perth Sandy Anghie said it was a good sign to see home renovations up. “Overall there has been an increase of $120 million in renovations across the board … and Cottesloe-Claremont is still on top in 2025-26,” she told this masthead.



“But interestingly in Stirling, which is holding the number three spot this year, the investment in renos has gone up by $30 million. It’s shown the highest increase. And then spots four and five on the list both went up by about $20 million.” Anghie said she believes homeowners will continue to invest in renovations for a littany of reasons. “We’ll probably continue to see renovations increase in WA because of the record low housing supply, soaring property prices, new build delays taking so long, and land supply challenges and transaction costs,” she said. “It is obviously an increasing trend in WA, which is actually a good thing for sustainability reasons. But it looks like [more] people are staying put and upgrading, which is also more practical and cost-effective.



“A number of my clients have been younger couples, and they’re keen to retain character homes and renovate. I think an appreciation of our character neighbourhoods is a really good thing as well.” She said it was positive to see people opting to renovate apartments within Perth’s CBD, and common works often included updating kitchens and bathrooms. Perth architect Sandy Anghie. Sandy Anghie “With apartments, you can make cosmetic changes. Typically in renovations, people are updating kitchens, bathrooms and modernising them, which not only improves amenity for the current residents, but obviously increases future sales value as well,” she said. The regions which saw the least amount of money put into home renovations were Kwinana with just $9 million over the financial year, Serpentine-Jarrahdale with $13 million and Gosnells at $17 million.



Master Builders WA chief executive Matt Moran said he believes renovations have become more attractive because of the current housing market. “If someone already owns a property in a suburb they like, many are opting to improve what they have rather than jumping back into a very competitive property market,” he told this masthead. “In many cases people are sitting on a valuable piece of land in exactly the location they want to live in and decide the expenditure into their existing property ... can make more sense than trying to reproduce what they already have somewhere else.” Moran said this is likely the case in Stirling, Joondalup and Melville, particularly because they all have large areas of well-established housing, a big inventory of older housing stock and relatively high underlying land values. “A big factor is [also] the lifestyle. People are attached to schools, neighbours, beaches, parks, transport and family networks,” he said.



Master Builders WA chief executive Matt Moran. Hamish Hastie “A renovation gives [people] the opportunity to get the additional bedroom, larger kitchen, better entertaining area, home office or whatever else they now need.” However, Moran said renovations weren’t necessarily cheaper than building a home from scratch. “Renovations can actually carry a higher construction cost per square metre than a new home because you are working around an existing structure,” he said. “There is demolition, temporary works, restricted access, matching old construction to new, working around existing services and inevitably things you cannot see until you open the building up.



“What this means is somebody might spend less overall because they are only altering part of their home, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the building work itself is cheaper.” Meanwhile, Nu Wealth managing director Daniel McQuillan said homeowners should be cautious not to overspend on renovations. “[We have] found that there are particular renovations that appeal to property buyers and will maximise the resale value of the property when it comes to selling it,” he said. “In particular, anyone proceeding with a home renovation should focus on improving highly visible areas around their home that would impress future home buyers and would enhance the value of the property,” he said.

World.title: ‘People might be sick of us, and they can be’: The Cats might just be getting started
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘People might be sick of us, and they can be’: The Cats might just be getting started Michael Gleeson September 5, 2026 — 1:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

As predictable as history demands it, Geelong won a final a night after Hawthorn. Of course. Is it not always such? The Cats halted the ride of Josh Fraser’s Blues and ended what had been, according to Andrew Dillon in his pre-game speech at the AFL function, the greatest resurrection story since the Bible. Had they won, Carlton fans might argue their story is better. Yet again, Patrick Dangerfield stood strong when it counts. AFL Photos And so, with the loss, the story of the season (the football story, not the news story for the Swans presently seem to have that covered) comes to an end. The ride stopped. The wave broken. Coming from 10th, they had to find their level at some point, and leading Geelong by 21 points midway through the second term to then be overwhelmed and outplayed in the second half to lose by 33 points is their level.



Fraser cautioned at the idea that next year just picks up where this one left off, that the ride will inevitably continue and roll on into pre-season like it is “Carlton 2026: The sequel”. With the coaches’ eye for next week, Fraser preferred not to focus on how far the Blues had come in a short time this season, but how much further they still have to go. If they have brought back Carlton swagger to fill the MCG to 96,680 and the second-biggest elimination final crowd ever, there was also a crackling Carlton restlessness about where they can get to. View post on X “Tonight was disappointing, and we certainly don’t want to be a club that lives in mediocrity ... we don’t want to be a club that’s satisfied with finishing eighth,” Fraser said. “We’ve made some big improvements, there’s no doubt about that, but there are still parts of our game that we need to get to work on, and there’s some individuals that need to continue to grow. In fact, all of our players need to continue to grow.



“You know, I think there’s an expectation on the way the break looks and the way they return … I just don’t think we can turn up [in the] pre-season and think that this keeps rolling on. Related Article AFL 2026 Vintage Dangerfield breaks Blue hearts in front of more than 96,000 at the MCG “I feel like I’ve got a really good handle on where we’re at, and understand that a lot of work is in front of us.” Geelong played the role of spoiler when the sizeable Carlton portion of the crowd hoped they would carry on from the first quarter and a half in their role of straight man, as an enabler for the Blues rollicking ride. But what is momentum, Chris Scott asked rhetorically afterwards. He wished to remind us that Carlton did not have the mortgage on momentum for his side had just won six games in a row before this game. Was that not momentum? Are you not entertained?



In football, you reap what you sow and Fremantle have sown doubt, which is something of a foreign concept to the Cats. Fraser has not sown self-confidence at Carlton, for it is a club that has never lacked that trait, but he has teased it back to the surface. For all of Carlton’s brilliance over the past 15 weeks, there is something brilliant about Geelong’s past 25 years that made the gradual grind over Carlton after giving up a near four-goal lead inevitable. They overpowered the Blues with the assuredness of a side that does not understand that some clubs don’t play football in September. The Cats play finals like the best Carlton teams used to. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 Cats v Blues player ratings: From Geelong’s ‘Superman’, to those who had ‘horror’ nights for Carlton Danny Russell and Sam McClure Geelong now face the chastened Fremantle in Perth next week in a semi-final with Max Holmes nursing the soreness of a bloke who has rushed to be fit from an ankle injury in round 19 and had to get himself through the game. Tanner Bruhn looked proppy for much of the night, and Jeremy Cameron was still short of touch after missing five games late in the season. Scott started Cameron, who won his second Coleman Medal just last year, at half-back. We can’t say we weren’t told – Chris Scott had flagged at the end of the season that he might do it. Cameron then migrated to the wing and eventually returned forward.



Scott liked what he saw of him as a defender, but liked more what he saw of him growing into the game the longer it went on. Patrick Dangerfield kicked five goals, three of which came in the last quarter as the Cats jollied away. Last September he had a great preliminary final and then struggled to back it up the next week. This year, even with a flight to Perth for a semi-final and every week being a knockout final, Scott said Dangerfield felt “like he is coming good at the right time”. Shaun Mannagh celebrates a goal. AFL Photos The difference in Friday night’s game shifted not off the boot of the usual Geelong suspects, but the underrated Shaun Mannagh, who was excellent all night but especially so in the third quarter when his run and craft opened the game up as the Cats kicked six goals to two. The forward spent a lot more time playing midfield and continues to look like a better player the more that is asked of him. With each new step in his career, he appears get better.



“I am still a forward at heart – still a forward,” he said. “[Assistant coach] James Kelly says some funny things. He goes, ‘Everyone wants to be in a CB [centre bounce] until they’re in there, and then all hell breaks loose and everything’s on you’. So sometimes it feels like that, but a lot of us boys love that pressure and we step into it as best we can. But, nah, I’m a forward at heart.” Loading Mannagh embraced the crowd and the moment, and understood the Carlton surge. He also understood the difference in attitude to the excitement of the Blues, and his side winning a final again. “It’s another elimination game. We have an elimination [game] all the way through. We respect Fremantle like we respect Carlton, and it’s going to take our best footy again [next week], so hopefully we can do it again. Another four points (um, no).

World.title: Housing affordability craters to record low despite fall in prices
World.content:
PoliticsFederalProperty prices Housing affordability craters to record low despite fall in prices Shane Wright September 5, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Housing affordability has slumped to its lowest level on record, two separate measures have revealed, with falling house prices not enough to offset the financial hit delivered by the Reserve Bank’s three interest rate rises. Both realestate.com.au and the Housing Industry Association’s affordability indicators slipped in the June quarter, with some of the biggest hits to people hoping to buy in smaller capitals, while Sydney remains the nation’s least affordable city and Melbourne’s market goes sideways. Despite a drop in house prices, affordability has dropped to record lows as higher interest rates bite. Dion Georgopoulos The indicators cover the period in which the RBA lifted the cash rate from 3.6 per cent to 4.35 per cent. Financial markets put the chance of another quarter-percentage-point increase at the bank’s late September meeting at four in five. According to realestate.com.au, a median-income household earning $125,000 a year could afford just 12 per cent of all homes sold in the 2025-26 financial year. There had been a slight improvement the previous year as official interest rates fell.



Victoria is the most affordable state, where 16 per cent of homes were within financial reach, although this was down from the 19 per cent level in 2024-25. South Australia, which has gone through a surge in property prices over the past two years, is now the least affordable state, overtaking NSW, which has held that position since 2011. A median-income household in SA could afford just 7 per cent of homes sold across the state. It now takes just over six years for an average household to save a 20 per cent deposit on a median-priced home. At the turn of the century, it took three years. Senior economist with realestate.com.au, Angus Moore, said the February, March and May rate increases delivered by the Reserve Bank had added to the pressure facing people wanting to buy a home.



“Looking ahead, affordability may improve marginally if home prices continue to soften, but this is unlikely to be a turning point for many buyers,” he said. Related Article Property prices It will take a generation to fix the housing crisis, says top economist “Without a meaningful increase in housing supply, affordability will remain a significant challenge, particularly for lower-income households.” Figures released this week by property analytics firm Cotality showed house values have fallen for five consecutive months. The Commonwealth Bank is expecting price falls of up to 13 per cent in Sydney by April. The HIA’s dwelling-price-to-earnings measure has fallen in Sydney, Canberra and Melbourne since March, each city having experienced drops in prices since the RBA started lifting rates.



But affordability deteriorated in all other capital cities, with Brisbane and Perth almost as difficult to buy into as Sydney. Both cities have experienced price rises of more than 20 per cent over the past two years, though they are now starting to fall. HIA senior economist Tom Devitt said the recent lift in interest rates meant mortgage costs were climbing faster than incomes, reducing the affordability of the entire housing market. He said buyers, particularly investors, had pulled back from the market, which had led to the recent drop in prices that would probably continue through the rest of 2026. “This will not be the makings of a sustainable improvement in affordability because it does not address the fundamental demand-supply mismatch that persists in Australian housing,” he said.



“When established home prices fall but the cost of land, labour, materials, infrastructure, finance and regulation does not, fewer new housing projects are financially viable.” The drop in housing affordability may be feeding into the jobs market. Figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Friday showed a record 1.05 million people now have a second job, an 11 per cent jump over the past 12 months. More than one in 14 people holds down at least two jobs, the highest rate since the bureau started tracking the data in 1994.



The federal government has been accused by the Coalition of actively trying to push down house prices and “destroy” the wealth of Australian families. Related Article Property prices $40,000 wiped off the value of the average house over winter But Housing Minister Clare O’Neil said the government’s budget changes to property taxation, such as negative gearing, on top of its efforts to build more public and social housing, were recognition that homes were out of the reach of ordinary people. O’Neil, who on Friday opened a 285-home development in Melbourne’s south-east made up of social, affordable and market rent properties partly financed by the federal government, noted the drop in affordability was not due to the government’s budget measures. “The challenge we face is that Australian house prices have increased by around 400 per cent since 2000. If that happens again over the next generation, Australia will become a fundamentally less equal country where home ownership is beyond the reach of too many young people,” she said.



“The Coalition are the only ones remaining defending a broken status quo.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Undercover sting targets Farage as protests disrupt his major address
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeUK politics Undercover sting targets Farage as protests disrupt his major address David Crowe September 5, 2026 — 4:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Birmingham: A media sting has thrown British right-wing leader Nigel Farage onto the defensive over political finance at a key moment for his Reform UK party, as thousands of supporters gather at its annual conference when it has lost its lead in the polls. Farage removed two key aides from their jobs after the sting revealed them discussing financial support from foreign donors who would be banned from funding British parties. Reform Party Leader Nigel Farage delivers a keynote speech at the party’s annual conference. Getty Images The exposure came the night before Farage addressed party members at his party’s annual gathering in Birmingham, where loyal supporters brushed off the scandal and Farage said the scrutiny showed his rivals were scared of him. In a revelation that rocked British politics, broadcaster Channel 4 showed one of the Reform aides discussing a plan to accept 500,000 from a wealthy American man by routing the money through his son.



The man promising the money was an actor hired by investigative group Verbatim and his “son” was a reporter from the group, and they were speaking at a lunch with Farage. In a separate moment caught on camera, another Reform aide seemed to welcome an approach from the “son” to fund opinion polls to assist the party. Reform UK has lost its lead in the polls. Getty Images Labour responded to the story by calling for a police investigation into the conversations, seeking to pile pressure on Farage when he is already the subject of two parliamentary inquiries into funding from wealthy investors heavily involved in cryptocurrencies. Farage drew rapturous applause from party members in Birmingham despite the news coverage, as they danced and sang while waiting for him to appear after security concerns delayed his appearance by about one hour.



Protesters in the audience yelled out during the early part of his address, but Farage laughed them off as “boring” and the crowd chanted at them to leave before security officials took them away. Protesters outside the Reform UK annual conference in Birmingham on Friday. Bloomberg Farage admitted there was “loose pub talk” by the two Reform aides but declared the party had not done anything wrong and had not broken the law. “The polls in question were not commissioned by Reform. The results are out there in the full public domain, and there is no issue,” he said. “What is problematic is loose pub talk, including a couple of quotes that were made that simply were not true.



Related Article Analysis

World politics Farage began a political farce. Binface missed his chance “But some of the comments made by two of our team were injudicious at best. Neither of these members have the right to act in this way. Accordingly, they stepped down, pending an investigation.” Reform members told this masthead the donations talk did not change their support because their priorities were issues such as migration, a key topic for the party when Farage is promising to stop asylum seeker boats crossing the English Channel. Farage blamed his opponents for the greater scrutiny on the party. “Ask yourself, why is all of this happening? Anyone got a clue why it’s happening?” he asked during his address. “Because they’re scared of us. That’s why it’s happening. And in my case, I’ve broken no laws, abused no public money.”



The furore undercut the party’s message when the high point of the conference was meant to be an agreement with a key French ally, National Rally president Jordan Bardella, to work together to stop asylum seeker boats if their parties formed government. Bardella could become prime minister if the right-wing party sweeps elections to be held in France next year. National Rally leader Marine Le Pen is running for president. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Britain’s budget blues will end Burnham’s honeymoon Britain has been unable to stop small boats carrying asylum seekers from France in recent years, although numbers are down so far this year. Farage and Bardella argued that those who tried to cross the channel would be returned to France, removing the incentive to get on boats. Reform and National Rally both propose tougher measures against migrants, including the removal of benefits that they believe encourages migrants to seek better lives in Britain and France.



Reform surged past Labour and the Conservative Party in the opinion polls over the past two years, and it had 23 per cent support in a YouGov survey released on September 1. It has lost its edge over Labour, however, after the rise of Andy Burnham as party leader and prime minister six weeks ago. Labour sank as low as 16 per cent in May but matched Reform on 23 per cent in the latest poll. Verbatim, the reporting group that supplied the video for the Channel 4 broadcast, was set up by Lawrence Carter and Louis Wilson, who previously worked at the Centre for Climate Reporting, which also used actors to trick politicians into speaking on hidden cameras. A report by the climate group made headlines in Australia last year when it showed US political adviser Chris LaCivita, a campaign aide to President Donald Trump, telling people he had been in Australia to advise the Liberal Party on issues it was having with the party’s leader at the time, Peter Dutton. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Darren Klemm is usually the bearer of bad news. He’s OK with it
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWAEmergency services Darren Klemm is usually the bearer of bad news. He’s OK with it Hannah Murphy September 5, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Darren Klemm remembers a time when volunteers didn’t bother warning the public about every little spot fire. “We’d go to fires out at the back of Cullacabardee, and just not tell anyone anything. You know, roads would get closed, but it was just the way it was and people got on with it too,” he says. DFES Commissioner Darren Klemm. Hamish Hastie However, now in his ninth year as Western Australia’s Department of Fire and Emergency Services Commissioner, Klemm says in 2026, constant updates are non-negotiable. “The growth is unbelievable, and the expectation from community about what they’ll get told and when they get told it has grown exponentially,” he says.



“We’re always going to find it hard to keep up with that thirst – because the more that you give, the more that is expected.” Klemm is used to being the bearer of bad news. In his time as commissioner, he says the way he has gone about delivering warnings, wash-ups and incident details has changed immensely. Fitzroy Crossing Airport at the height of the floods. Police Media He has seen a transition from giving updates on the old AM radio, to massively scaling up of the state’s emergency’s website, which provides minute-by-minute information on bushfires, floods, cyclones and HAZMAT warnings. Now, he says, the public want information, they want it now – and it’s his job to deliver it.



“They want to be warned, and they want to inform themselves. That’s what we want as well,” Klemm says. Sitting down with this masthead in his Cockburn office at the beginning of the state’s bushfire season, Klemm is a long way from his hometown in Wagin and where he grew up in the Wheatbelt. “We’re getting overlapping [fire] seasons between the north and the south … and now, the flooding that we’ve had, it seems to be every year now.” DFES Commissioner Darren Klemm At an early age, Klemm remembers he always had to be doing something. Not content with university or sitting around inside, he was a prolific footballer – a midfield rover – and was eventually picked up by the South Australian National Football League. It is there, he says, where he picked up his love of firefighting.



“Some guys I was playing footy with, a lot of them were in the fire brigade,” Klemm says. Related Article Exclusive

Construction WA’s new building boss says we don’t build them like we used to – and that’s a good thing “I mean, there was just always something going on. That was motivating and stimulating.” He spent three years working as a firefighter in South Australia before picking up and moving back home with his wife, and taking up with the agency that would become his home for the next two decades. “FESA, as it was called then,” he laughs.



Klemm is coy about his meteoric rise through the agency, but attributes much of his success due to his time on the ground, actually doing the job. When he was tapped by outgoing commissioner Wayne Gregson in 2017, he had to sit on the news for a month before it was formally announced. He says it didn’t hit him until he walked into the office on his first day, and realised the weight on his shoulders. Every cyclone, bushfire, rescue – it was all in his control. Originally a career firefighter, Klemm spent years on the tools before moving to management. DFES “The state’s emergency framework is not just about bushfire and cyclones – it’s every emergency,” Klemm says. “Those are the things that people see the most because they happen every year.



“But then we have things like the pandemic, things like hazardous materials [incidents], and now AUKUS. They all have to be operated.” Related Article Planning and development WA’s Planning Commission boss talks housing, density – and pushback And in his time, Klemm has already had to navigate a series of some of the state’s worst catastrophes. There was flooding at Fitzroy Crossing that wiped out dozens of homes and a major arterial bridge, and Cyclone Seroja, which flattened Kalbarri – a coastal town that had up until that point been out of the reach of the state’s major cyclone events. And, in 2021, Wooroloo, where nearly 100 homes went up in flames as a bushfire tore through the hills suburb.



As commissioner, Klemm says he didn’t like leaving people in the lurch. “If you think about the experience for the community – we come and the fire’s put out, but then they’re left with a home that might be damaged, and then who’s there to help them do that? Who can they see in government that’s going to help them?” Klemm says. A burned fire ground near Wooroloo. AP So he and the agency began the arduous task of bringing recovery in-house. The change meant DFES was able to deploy its own crews to help people in Fitzroy Crossing who lost everything in 2022, and Klemm says his team’s work had made the transition “seamless”.



“It first really started in Wooroloo – we were really clear with the community that once the fire was put out, we weren’t just going to leave,” he says. It’s a method he and the agency had begun to deploy more regularly, and Klemm says this upcoming bushfire season will be no different. A firefighting plane dumps retardant on Wooroloo blaze. AP “We’re getting overlapping seasons between the north and the south … and now, the flooding that we’ve had, it seems to be every year now,” he says. “Things are changing, and you know any firefighter will tell you that we have difficulties at night now, where that never used to be the case.”



Klemm doesn’t mince words about the upcoming bushfire season in WA – it is set to be challenging, and difficult. While the agency has the resources to mitigate the impact, he warns, locals have to play their part too. “I’m not sure everybody in the eastern states quite understands how big WA is,” he says. “The risks are everywhere. “Just because you live in the western suburbs doesn’t mean you might not be adjacent to [bushland].



“I dare say there’s a lot of people that go down south on holiday, and it’s particularly difficult down there. “That’s why we have Emergency WA – people can go there and do their plans and actually educate themselves to make sure they’re making the best decisions for themselves, and not relying on someone putting a comment on social media, which may or may not be correct.”

World.title: Hit this Fremantle cafe for ace brunching, then return after dark for modern bistro thrills (if you can get a seat)
World.content:
Review Eating outFremantle Hit this Fremantle cafe for ace brunching, then return after dark for modern bistro thrills (if you can get a seat) Fuelled by traditional thinking and youthful energy, The Cool Room feels both reassuringly familiar and thrillingly novel. Max Veenhuyzen September 5, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

1 / 2 Seasonal fruit and soda bread. Supplied 2 / 2 Sesame sourdough bun plate. Supplied Previous Slide Next Slide 14.5 / 20 How we score The Cool Room Fremantle European$$$$ The Cool Room is one of Fremantle’s hottest, most interesting cafes. I write this with confidence, knowing full well that the standard of brunching across Freo is high; that hotness is at odds with the low-Celsius connotations of the cafe’s name; and that The Cool Room, having turned one in August, is way past its honeymoon period, so people aren’t seeking it out (just) because it’s new. Rather, many are drawn to this suburban cafe because it’s old. Or looks old, at least.



On Friday nights, The Cool Room hosts weekly set menu dinners showcasing the kitchen’s restaurant pedigree. Max Veenhuyzen They come to admire the retro beauty of this former butcher dressed with mismatched, garage sale-direct furniture and accessories. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up The result is a timeless, broadly Aussie reimagining of Grandma’s house that is free of potpourri but full of Freo types. Here’s a white-haired bloke with boardies and shapely calves. Over there, 20-somethings coo at a fat tyre bike. A young couple with small kids and a big dog turn the corner and see the crowd. Immediately, their brows furrow in a way that says, Goldilocks-style, “who’s been ordering alt-milk lattes in my local cafe?” If you’re a first-timer and the place is heaving, it can be hard to tell when The Cool Room ends and when Old Values – the vintage op-shop next door – starts.



Such confusion is testament to both the demand for weekend tables and the knack that Charlotte Beeton and Drew Dawson, owners of The Cool Room, have for vintage styling. This affinity with yesteryear is also evident in their food offering: familiar, brunch dishes that, at their best, both comfort and quietly surprise diners. Related Article 14 / 20 Review No, Google Maps isn’t playing up: this Perth gym really does house a great Malay cafe There is a plush omelette filled with whipped chevre packing more flavour than anything this lightweight has any right to. There is also an aspirational bacon and fudgy yolk fried egg bap: a morning-after lifesaver that is to servo bacon and egg rolls as former gas lobbyists are to by-election success. There is also a very convincing take on the a la mode Scandinavian breakfast plate starring a soft-boiled egg, waxy rectangles of semi-firm Tilsit cheese from Dellendale Creamery in Denmark, granola plus a sourdough bun studded with white sesame seeds. (The bun, meanwhile, is baked at the cafe, as are most of the breads, biscuits and cakes served.) On paper, none of these dishes sound especially ground-breaking, yet time after time, The Cool Room’s versions of these cafe classics tasted finer, livelier and more focused than what you’ll get around town.



One reason that explains the above: provenance. People like to talk about sourcing seasonal and local ingredients. This is one place where you can really taste it. (Still, there’s a blackboard by the entrance shouting out the cafe’s suppliers.) Another explanation: confident seasoning. Salt seems to be in everything here. It’s on the end of a sundae spoon served with the soft-boiled eggs on the brekky plate. It’s in the addictive granola bulked up with arcs of toasted coconut and pumpkin seeds candied in maple syrup. And it also helps emphasise the spicy richness of malleable chocolate and rye cookies. Olympia James-Ainslie, Charlotte Beeton, Rosie Fowkes, Drew Dawson and Megan Sullivan of The Cool Room. Max Veenhuyzen One aspect of The Cool Room that isn’t salty, however, is its service. Luka Burger and Georgia Gillett are a warm presence on the coffee machine while upbeat front-of-house personality Hannah Jawad feels like she’s constantly here, there and everywhere. While brunch is The Cool Room’s soda bread and cultured butter, the cafe also hosts Friday dinner services that show off the restaurant pedigree of Dawson (formerly of Lola’s and Nieuw Ruin in Fremantle, plus Melbourne’s Napier Quarter) and kitchen offsiders Olympia James-Ainslie, Rosie Fowkes and Megan Sullivan.



It’s also why writing this review has taken longer than I had hoped. The difficulty of snagging a booking suggests that many are already across the pleasures of this weekly offering. (Dinner is an $80 three-course set menu plus an additional fiver for corkage; only 28 seats are available each Friday.) But if this is news to you, this is one Friday dinner worth making happen. Related Article Exclusive After 15 years of active service, Rockpool Perth is getting a $3 million makeover While night mode sees tables set with (real!) candles and the playlist’s jazz-funk tunes reduced to a bassy hum by enthusiastic guests, the kitchen takes the same unshowy attitude to dinner as it does brunch. Sweet parker buns ride shotgun alongside a slab of poised chicken terrine shot through with a coin of confit leek. Thick, room-temperature slices of pink blade beef are cloaked by an aerated mess of horseradish-spiced sour cream. While the dish’s lightness struck me as a WeightWatchers-approved vitello tonnato – and I write that in a very good, very I-could-eat-this-all-summer kind of way – it’s more than likely a nod to the British heritage of Dawson. Not that our man has any aspirations to be the next Fergus Henderson or anything. Instead, like many of his peers, such introspection is simply one cook’s pursuit of nostalgic flavours from his past.



I had zero idea that flapjacks were a classic British oat bar, but my ignorance didn’t hinder my enjoyment of Beeton’s rendition (cleverly crunched up with buckwheat) one bit. I do, however, feel foolish that I didn’t get that the intriguing lilt of cumquat in a Friday night chocolate mousse dessert was an homage to England’s famous Terry’s Chocolate Orange. But like I was saying, it can be tricky to tell when old values end, and The Cool Room begins. The low-down Atmosphere: A suburban cafe (and youthful cafe crew) to watch. Go-to dishes: Sesame sourdough bun plate ($18), bacon bap with fried egg ($20). Drinks: All the cafe classics plus iced teas and fruit juices made from seasonal fruit. Cost: About $50 for two people, excluding drinks (dinner is $80 per person for a three-course set menu). Good Food reviews are booked anonymously and paid independently. A restaurant can’t pay for a review or inclusion in the Good Food Guide.

World.title: ‘Staying put’: WA homeowners spent $1.2 billion renovating their homes last year
World.content:
NationalWAProperty development ‘Staying put’: WA homeowners spent $1.2 billion renovating their homes last year Indigo Lemay-Conway September 5, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Over the last financial year Western Australian homeowners spent almost over a billion dollars on home renovations. Statewide renovation spending reached $1.2 billion in 2025-26, driven by everything from major kitchen and bathroom upgrades to general cosmetic work. Western Australians have spent over a billion dollars on home renovations in the last financial year. Of that, $934 million was invested across the Greater Perth region and $130.9 million was spent in June alone. The Australian Bureau of Statistics released new figures this month showing which SA3’s (geographic regions) saw the highest amount of money spent on fixing up homes.



And the list might surprise you. Cottesloe-Claremont was at the top of the table, which saw homeowners spend about $127 million doing up their homes over the past year, jumping up by $7 million from the previous year. Second in line was Perth City, with just over $108 million spent on renovations, followed by Stirling with $93 million invested. Architect and former deputy Lord Mayor of the City of Perth Sandy Anghie said it was a good sign to see home renovations up. “Overall there has been an increase of $120 million in renovations across the board … and Cottesloe-Claremont is still on top in 2025-26,” she told this masthead.



“But interestingly in Stirling, which is holding the number three spot this year, the investment in renos has gone up by $30 million. It’s shown the highest increase. And then spots four and five on the list both went up by about $20 million.” Anghie said she believes homeowners will continue to invest in renovations for a littany of reasons. “We’ll probably continue to see renovations increase in WA because of the record low housing supply, soaring property prices, new build delays taking so long, and land supply challenges and transaction costs,” she said. “It is obviously an increasing trend in WA, which is actually a good thing for sustainability reasons. But it looks like [more] people are staying put and upgrading, which is also more practical and cost-effective.



“A number of my clients have been younger couples, and they’re keen to retain character homes and renovate. I think an appreciation of our character neighbourhoods is a really good thing as well.” She said it was positive to see people opting to renovate apartments within Perth’s CBD, and common works often included updating kitchens and bathrooms. Perth architect Sandy Anghie. Sandy Anghie “With apartments, you can make cosmetic changes. Typically in renovations, people are updating kitchens, bathrooms and modernising them, which not only improves amenity for the current residents, but obviously increases future sales value as well,” she said. The regions which saw the least amount of money put into home renovations were Kwinana with just $9 million over the financial year, Serpentine-Jarrahdale with $13 million and Gosnells at $17 million.



Master Builders WA chief executive Matt Moran said he believes renovations have become more attractive because of the current housing market. “If someone already owns a property in a suburb they like, many are opting to improve what they have rather than jumping back into a very competitive property market,” he told this masthead. “In many cases people are sitting on a valuable piece of land in exactly the location they want to live in and decide the expenditure into their existing property ... can make more sense than trying to reproduce what they already have somewhere else.” Moran said this is likely the case in Stirling, Joondalup and Melville, particularly because they all have large areas of well-established housing, a big inventory of older housing stock and relatively high underlying land values. “A big factor is [also] the lifestyle. People are attached to schools, neighbours, beaches, parks, transport and family networks,” he said.



Master Builders WA chief executive Matt Moran. Hamish Hastie “A renovation gives [people] the opportunity to get the additional bedroom, larger kitchen, better entertaining area, home office or whatever else they now need.” However, Moran said renovations weren’t necessarily cheaper than building a home from scratch. “Renovations can actually carry a higher construction cost per square metre than a new home because you are working around an existing structure,” he said. “There is demolition, temporary works, restricted access, matching old construction to new, working around existing services and inevitably things you cannot see until you open the building up.



“What this means is somebody might spend less overall because they are only altering part of their home, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the building work itself is cheaper.” Meanwhile, Nu Wealth managing director Daniel McQuillan said homeowners should be cautious not to overspend on renovations. “[We have] found that there are particular renovations that appeal to property buyers and will maximise the resale value of the property when it comes to selling it,” he said. “In particular, anyone proceeding with a home renovation should focus on improving highly visible areas around their home that would impress future home buyers and would enhance the value of the property,” he said.

World.title: ‘People might be sick of us, and they can be’: The Cats might just be getting started
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘People might be sick of us, and they can be’: The Cats might just be getting started Michael Gleeson September 5, 2026 — 1:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

As predictable as history demands it, Geelong won a final a night after Hawthorn. Of course. Is it not always such? The Cats halted the ride of Josh Fraser’s Blues and ended what had been, according to Andrew Dillon in his pre-game speech at the AFL function, the greatest resurrection story since the Bible. Had they won, Carlton fans might argue their story is better. Yet again, Patrick Dangerfield stood strong when it counts. AFL Photos And so, with the loss, the story of the season (the football story, not the news story for the Swans presently seem to have that covered) comes to an end. The ride stopped. The wave broken. Coming from 10th, they had to find their level at some point, and leading Geelong by 21 points midway through the second term to then be overwhelmed and outplayed in the second half to lose by 33 points is their level.



Fraser cautioned at the idea that next year just picks up where this one left off, that the ride will inevitably continue and roll on into pre-season like it is “Carlton 2026: The sequel”. With the coaches’ eye for next week, Fraser preferred not to focus on how far the Blues had come in a short time this season, but how much further they still have to go. If they have brought back Carlton swagger to fill the MCG to 96,680 and the second-biggest elimination final crowd ever, there was also a crackling Carlton restlessness about where they can get to. View post on X “Tonight was disappointing, and we certainly don’t want to be a club that lives in mediocrity ... we don’t want to be a club that’s satisfied with finishing eighth,” Fraser said. “We’ve made some big improvements, there’s no doubt about that, but there are still parts of our game that we need to get to work on, and there’s some individuals that need to continue to grow. In fact, all of our players need to continue to grow.



“You know, I think there’s an expectation on the way the break looks and the way they return … I just don’t think we can turn up [in the] pre-season and think that this keeps rolling on. Related Article AFL 2026 Vintage Dangerfield breaks Blue hearts in front of more than 96,000 at the MCG “I feel like I’ve got a really good handle on where we’re at, and understand that a lot of work is in front of us.” Geelong played the role of spoiler when the sizeable Carlton portion of the crowd hoped they would carry on from the first quarter and a half in their role of straight man, as an enabler for the Blues rollicking ride. But what is momentum, Chris Scott asked rhetorically afterwards. He wished to remind us that Carlton did not have the mortgage on momentum for his side had just won six games in a row before this game. Was that not momentum? Are you not entertained?



In football, you reap what you sow and Fremantle have sown doubt, which is something of a foreign concept to the Cats. Fraser has not sown self-confidence at Carlton, for it is a club that has never lacked that trait, but he has teased it back to the surface. For all of Carlton’s brilliance over the past 15 weeks, there is something brilliant about Geelong’s past 25 years that made the gradual grind over Carlton after giving up a near four-goal lead inevitable. They overpowered the Blues with the assuredness of a side that does not understand that some clubs don’t play football in September. The Cats play finals like the best Carlton teams used to. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 Cats v Blues player ratings: From Geelong’s ‘Superman’, to those who had ‘horror’ nights for Carlton Danny Russell and Sam McClure Geelong now face the chastened Fremantle in Perth next week in a semi-final with Max Holmes nursing the soreness of a bloke who has rushed to be fit from an ankle injury in round 19 and had to get himself through the game. Tanner Bruhn looked proppy for much of the night, and Jeremy Cameron was still short of touch after missing five games late in the season. Scott started Cameron, who won his second Coleman Medal just last year, at half-back. We can’t say we weren’t told – Chris Scott had flagged at the end of the season that he might do it. Cameron then migrated to the wing and eventually returned forward.



Scott liked what he saw of him as a defender, but liked more what he saw of him growing into the game the longer it went on. Patrick Dangerfield kicked five goals, three of which came in the last quarter as the Cats jollied away. Last September he had a great preliminary final and then struggled to back it up the next week. This year, even with a flight to Perth for a semi-final and every week being a knockout final, Scott said Dangerfield felt “like he is coming good at the right time”. Shaun Mannagh celebrates a goal. AFL Photos The difference in Friday night’s game shifted not off the boot of the usual Geelong suspects, but the underrated Shaun Mannagh, who was excellent all night but especially so in the third quarter when his run and craft opened the game up as the Cats kicked six goals to two. The forward spent a lot more time playing midfield and continues to look like a better player the more that is asked of him. With each new step in his career, he appears get better.



“I am still a forward at heart – still a forward,” he said. “[Assistant coach] James Kelly says some funny things. He goes, ‘Everyone wants to be in a CB [centre bounce] until they’re in there, and then all hell breaks loose and everything’s on you’. So sometimes it feels like that, but a lot of us boys love that pressure and we step into it as best we can. But, nah, I’m a forward at heart.” Loading Mannagh embraced the crowd and the moment, and understood the Carlton surge. He also understood the difference in attitude to the excitement of the Blues, and his side winning a final again. “It’s another elimination game. We have an elimination [game] all the way through. We respect Fremantle like we respect Carlton, and it’s going to take our best footy again [next week], so hopefully we can do it again. Another four points (um, no).

World.title: Housing affordability craters to record low despite fall in prices
World.content:
PoliticsFederalProperty prices Housing affordability craters to record low despite fall in prices Shane Wright September 5, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Housing affordability has slumped to its lowest level on record, two separate measures have revealed, with falling house prices not enough to offset the financial hit delivered by the Reserve Bank’s three interest rate rises. Both realestate.com.au and the Housing Industry Association’s affordability indicators slipped in the June quarter, with some of the biggest hits to people hoping to buy in smaller capitals, while Sydney remains the nation’s least affordable city and Melbourne’s market goes sideways. Despite a drop in house prices, affordability has dropped to record lows as higher interest rates bite. Dion Georgopoulos The indicators cover the period in which the RBA lifted the cash rate from 3.6 per cent to 4.35 per cent. Financial markets put the chance of another quarter-percentage-point increase at the bank’s late September meeting at four in five. According to realestate.com.au, a median-income household earning $125,000 a year could afford just 12 per cent of all homes sold in the 2025-26 financial year. There had been a slight improvement the previous year as official interest rates fell.



Victoria is the most affordable state, where 16 per cent of homes were within financial reach, although this was down from the 19 per cent level in 2024-25. South Australia, which has gone through a surge in property prices over the past two years, is now the least affordable state, overtaking NSW, which has held that position since 2011. A median-income household in SA could afford just 7 per cent of homes sold across the state. It now takes just over six years for an average household to save a 20 per cent deposit on a median-priced home. At the turn of the century, it took three years. Senior economist with realestate.com.au, Angus Moore, said the February, March and May rate increases delivered by the Reserve Bank had added to the pressure facing people wanting to buy a home.



“Looking ahead, affordability may improve marginally if home prices continue to soften, but this is unlikely to be a turning point for many buyers,” he said. Related Article Property prices It will take a generation to fix the housing crisis, says top economist “Without a meaningful increase in housing supply, affordability will remain a significant challenge, particularly for lower-income households.” Figures released this week by property analytics firm Cotality showed house values have fallen for five consecutive months. The Commonwealth Bank is expecting price falls of up to 13 per cent in Sydney by April. The HIA’s dwelling-price-to-earnings measure has fallen in Sydney, Canberra and Melbourne since March, each city having experienced drops in prices since the RBA started lifting rates.



But affordability deteriorated in all other capital cities, with Brisbane and Perth almost as difficult to buy into as Sydney. Both cities have experienced price rises of more than 20 per cent over the past two years, though they are now starting to fall. HIA senior economist Tom Devitt said the recent lift in interest rates meant mortgage costs were climbing faster than incomes, reducing the affordability of the entire housing market. He said buyers, particularly investors, had pulled back from the market, which had led to the recent drop in prices that would probably continue through the rest of 2026. “This will not be the makings of a sustainable improvement in affordability because it does not address the fundamental demand-supply mismatch that persists in Australian housing,” he said.



“When established home prices fall but the cost of land, labour, materials, infrastructure, finance and regulation does not, fewer new housing projects are financially viable.” The drop in housing affordability may be feeding into the jobs market. Figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Friday showed a record 1.05 million people now have a second job, an 11 per cent jump over the past 12 months. More than one in 14 people holds down at least two jobs, the highest rate since the bureau started tracking the data in 1994.



The federal government has been accused by the Coalition of actively trying to push down house prices and “destroy” the wealth of Australian families. Related Article Property prices $40,000 wiped off the value of the average house over winter But Housing Minister Clare O’Neil said the government’s budget changes to property taxation, such as negative gearing, on top of its efforts to build more public and social housing, were recognition that homes were out of the reach of ordinary people. O’Neil, who on Friday opened a 285-home development in Melbourne’s south-east made up of social, affordable and market rent properties partly financed by the federal government, noted the drop in affordability was not due to the government’s budget measures. “The challenge we face is that Australian house prices have increased by around 400 per cent since 2000. If that happens again over the next generation, Australia will become a fundamentally less equal country where home ownership is beyond the reach of too many young people,” she said.



“The Coalition are the only ones remaining defending a broken status quo.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.
