Tech.title: How a Secret Orangutan Breeding Program Is Creating a Baby Boom
Tech.content:
“It’s a girl!” Melissa Peterson exclaims.

Just outside the operating room, the hallway erupts in cheers. Joseph Dewane, an ob-gyn, has just delivered a healthy baby via C-section; Autumn Joi Goodwin-Samson, a neonatalist, tends to the newborn still slick with a waxy film.

It’s a successful delivery just like any other except for one, minor, difference: The patient is an orangutan.

Ruhana—or just “Ru” for short—is one of eight orangutan babies born in a collection of US zoos since the beginning of 2025. For these critically endangered primates, that’s a staggering figure. It’s also not random: The baby boom is the result of a meticulous breeding plan and decades of research to weave a conservation safety net, one birth at a time.

“It might seem like it was all a coincidence that everyone was born at the same time, but it was very carefully planned,” says Angie Selzer, a senior animal care specialist with the Fort Wayne Zoo in Indiana and the Orangutan Species Survival Plan (SSP) program coordinator.

The SSP has been coordinating breeding recommendations since 1985; every two years, the program creates a breeding and transfer plan for animals at zoos accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA). Geneticists from the SSP consult a “studbook,” which contains the pedigree of all the animals in their system.

“We want to maintain a healthy and sustainable population that mimics the natural history of wild orangutans while ensuring successful mother-rearing of offspring,” Seltzer tells WIRED. Their recommendation accounts for a number of breeding factors, including underrepresented genetic lines, each animal’s unique personality, and group dynamics—always aiming for the lowest relation between breeding pairs.

Tech.title: The 6 Best Monitors That Actually Work Well With Macs
Tech.content:
Just about any monitor can work with a Mac. It doesn’t need to be made by Apple or have any official certification. There’s a case to be made for using a cheap 1080p monitor, but most Mac users will want something a bit more premium. As you can see from options like the Dell 27 Plus 4K, that doesn’t have to mean overly expensive. Either way, here are the four elements to consider when shopping for a good monitor to go with your Mac.

Size and resolution: 27- and 32-inch monitors are the most common sizes these days, but there are larger options. I would also consider a 34-inch ultrawide monitor if you like the wider 21:9 aspect ratio with the curved shape. With Apple, resolution is king. There's a reason it invests so much in high pixel density for every screen it sells, even in midrange options like the MacBook Air. Pixel density is what gives a screen its sharpness, and you need a lot more pixels when they're stretched across a large external monitor. If you want to keep fidelity up, I wouldn’t buy anything less than 4K, and bumping up to 5K or 6K on a 32-inch monitor can be helpful. Read more to learn the details on the funky way macOS handles resolutions and scaling. You should also consider the refresh rate: a 120-Hz refresh rate is what the MacBook Pro supports, offering smoother animation, especially in games.

Adjustability: Apple monitors and iMacs aren’t exactly known for adjustability. They often have none at all, and cost more when they do. That isn’t the best for your posture and ergonomics. Famously, the discontinued Pro Display XDR charged an extra $1,000 for a Pro Stand with proper adjustability (now a $400 add-on for the newer Studio Display XDR). For ergonomics, the top of the screen you're working on should be as close to eye level as possible, and that ranges depending on someone’s height. If a monitor doesn’t have height adjustability, you’ll need a separate monitor stand or arm. Beyond height adjustment, many monitors also have stands that can swivel, tilt, and rotate, all of which matter when using multiple monitors. This is also needed if you want to use a second monitor vertically, which has become increasingly popular.

Ports: Even the cheapest monitors will always have HDMI, which is all you need to connect directly to a Mac Mini, Mac Studio, Mac Pro, or MacBook Pro. Some monitors have USB-C that supports video, which will let you connect to one of a Mac’s Thunderbolt ports. The Mac Mini comes with three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, and an Ethernet jack. The Mac Mini Pro model has the same ports, except three of them support faster Thunderbolt 5 instead of 4. You’ll need to use at least one of these Thunderbolt ports to connect more than one external monitor. These monitors also tend to have other ports, such as USB-A. These can be useful, as the Mac Mini doesn't have any on its own.

Image quality: Apple prides itself on the image quality of its Macs, so in the case of the Mac Mini, you’ll likely want to get something worthy of your Mac. This is especially important for content creators, photographers, and designers. So, consider a monitor’s brightness, color accuracy, color coverage, and contrast. While some IPS displays offer decent color and contrast, mini-LED or OLED displays will guarantee better image quality. These also have significantly higher peak brightness in HDR content, which really brings games and movies to life.

Tech.title: Measles Outbreaks Are Forcing Parents of Immunocompromised Kids to Make Hard Choices
Tech.content:
As students head back to school, parents have all the usual worries about their kids, like remembering to pack lunch and making it to the bus stop on time. But parents of immunocompromised kids have a new one: How to deal with the resurgence of measles.

Cases of the highly transmissible disease have reached a 35-year high in the US, with nearly 3,000 confirmed infections in 2026 so far. The first two measles-related deaths of the year were recorded in Pennsylvania, right as the school year is getting going. With vaccination rates dropping across the country, parents of kids who aren’t able to get vaccinated or don’t mount a strong enough immune response due to weakened immune systems are weighing whether it’s safe enough to go to school.

Victoria Schiano, national community engagement coordinator for Little Lobbyists, a nonprofit that advocates for children with complex medical needs and disabilities, says the return of measles is “absolutely terrifying.”

While it’s not known exactly how many US children have compromised immune systems, a study by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimated that 2.6 percent of children are immunocompromised. Immune deficiencies can have genetic causes or secondary reasons, such as chemotherapy for cancer treatment.

Schiano’s kid is among them. Her 10-year-old has mitochondrial disease. The family lives in Chester County, Pennsylvania, which has the second-highest number of measles cases in the state right now. Schiano has been closely monitoring the vaccination rates in her son’s school district, which have dipped below the 95 percent threshold needed for community protection against measles. Measles is breaking through in places where vaccination has dropped below that threshold. In neighboring Lancaster County, for example, just 87.6 percent of kindergartners are fully vaccinated against measles and 83.3 percent of seventh graders are.

Her son can’t be vaccinated, and he receives weekly infusions of immunoglobulin—concentrated antibodies from donated human blood plasma—to help his body fight infections.

“Measles is dangerous for anyone, but for him, this absolutely could be life or death,” she says.

The virus can cause severe, life-threatening complications such as pneumonia and brain swelling. Measles can also wipe out the body’s memory of past infections—a phenomenon known as immune amnesia—leaving people susceptible to other diseases.

Her son already wears a mask and uses a plexiglass screen at school, and the family is diligent about handwashing. Now, Schiano says they’ve had to make the difficult decision to limit her son’s time with friends and after-school activities like karate. She says it’s hard as a parent to balance his quality of life with his safety.

“He just wants to play and to do all the things that he sees other kids doing,” she says.

Her son did online school for a time during Covid-19, and she says she’s prepared to take him out of school if there’s even one confirmed measles case. That comes with a different set of risks, though. During the pandemic, remote learning was associated with an increase in social isolation and behavioral and mental health issues among students.

Amalia, a parent in South Carolina who asked to go by a pseudonym for privacy reasons, has already chosen to keep her 16-year-old son home this year and do online schooling due to concerns about measles. Her son has immunoglobulin A deficiency, in which the body doesn’t produce enough of an antibody found in mucous membranes, body fluids, and digestive tracts that help fend off germs.

“Even if there’s just a flu going around, he gets sicker than the average kid will,” she says.

Her son was able to get the measles vaccine, but doctors monitor his antibody levels regularly to check for waning immunity.

Tech.title: I Watched a Floor Washing Robot Mothership Deploy a Roomba Using a Mechnical Arm
Tech.content:
There’s not much the robot vacuum industry can do to surprise me these days. I’ve seen robots that have mechanical arms to pick up objects, robot vacuums with legs and tread systems to climb stairs, and even wilder humanoid concepts. But iRobot genuinely surprised me with its Roomba Duo, a floor-washing robot module that carries a little baby Roomba on top. I saw this contraption in action at iRobot’s booth at IFA Berlin, and I honestly don’t know what to make of it.

I briefly spoke to Adam Pope, iRobot’s chief engineer at the booth, who explained that the Roomba Duo is currently just a concept, but it’s an example of the kinds of things iRobot is considering to address consumer pain points. In the case of the Duo, the main egg-like mothership module includes a powerful floor washer and steamer that’s more capable than the type of hardware you can put. iRobot tells me that the main unit’s power is equivalent to that of a traditional wet-and-dry vacuum, offering powerful cleaning but lacking the autonomy of a robot vacuum.

The Duo solves this problem by also incorporating a slim Roomba that can be deployed. I watched it do so after the main unit sucked up some spilled spaghetti from the carpet for the demo and sanitized the spill area. It then used a top-mounted mechanical arm and what I can best describe as a landing craft to lower the Roomba onto the floor, where it started cleaning in the narrow spots of iRobot’s obstacle course. The movement reminded me of a bulldozer or a forklift because the mechanical arm itself looks quite industrial and sturdy, which iRobot says is necessary to ensure stability under the additional weight.

After the main unit finished its heavier cleaning job, it moved closer to its docking area while the smaller Roomba puttered around, cleaning corners and navigating iRobot’s barriers.

Both units operate autonomously, but they share a home map and an autonomous mobile dock, so they won’t duplicate efforts. They communicate in real time and are connected via the Rooma Home app, which uses AI to coordinate cleaning tasks. iRobot says the main unit vacuums and mops the large, open floor areas, while the slim baby Roomba goes under furniture and into narrow spaces the bulky main module can’t reach.



While this is just a concept product with no indication it’ll come to market, iRobot did share some specs with us. The main mothership has a wet-and-dry floor-washing module, a high-performance motor, and a high-capacity battery. It also uses the company’s PowerSpin Max Roller map, applying 46 newtons of downward pressure, which is a huge jump from the 12 to 14 newtons you typically get from a robot vacuum. iRobot says it scrubs the floor as thoroughly as if you were cleaning by hand.

It also has an internal heater that generates steam to loosen tougher, dried-on grime and stains. The roller is self-cleaning, as we’ve come to expect and iRobot says it can handle everything from dirt to pasta sauce and cooking grease. There’s also a hot-air dryer behind the roller that dries the floor after the roller is done mopping, so the wood flooring doesn’t get damaged by moisture.

The companion robot used for the demo is the Roomba Plus 575 Combo, which we covered after it launched earlier this year. It’s just 8.35 centimeters tall and 29.8 centimeters wide, making it one of the slimmest models we’ve seen, which is why it was selected as the companion unit. Right now, it’s not clear whether the mothership can accommodate other robot vacuum models, but I would guess it’s only compatible with this one for now.

The main Duo unit is equipped with the company’s ClearView Pro dual-line lidar and AI to detect and navigate household objects. It also has a top-mounted AI camera, giving it a better, higher view of rooms and floor layouts, and creating more detailed maps than a standard robot vacuum. It should also be able to better identify stains.

To move this fairly bulky unit, it uses 17-centimeter wheels powered by hub motors. There’s a shared AutoWash dock (the self-emptying and cleaning docking station that most newer Roomba models use). It has a centralized clean water supply, a waste water tank, and like a standard stationary dock, it automatically washes and dries the mop and collects dust in a dustbag, letting you go months before it needs to be emptied.

Tech.title: Apple Is Full of Surprises. Here’s What CNET Readers Anticipate Ahead of Wednesday’s Event
Tech.content:
The third and final round of CNET’s Big Guessing Game is now closed, which completes our contest. We’ll be back after Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event on Wednesday, Sept. 9 to share the final answers and determine the winners

The CNET Group’s Big Guessing Game contest was held across CNET, Lifehacker, Mashable, PCMag and ZDNET. There were three rounds of guessing to predict what Apple will unveil this year. Each correct answer earns one chance in a drawing to win the latest Apple Watch announced in this month. Before we get into your answers in the final round, here’s a recap of the first round and second round.

Over 70% think Apple’s new and former CEOs will appear together

Most (71%) contest participants say we can expect Apple’s new CEO John Ternus and former CEO Tim Cook to appear together at the event.

As of Sept. 1, Ternus is Apple’s new CEO after 15 years of Cook’s leadership, and Cook has become the company’s executive chairman. Ternus sent a memo to the Apple team thanking Cook and the Apple team for their work and expressing excitement for a “huge launch.” Have we ever seen two of Apple’s CEOs share the stage before?

Cook’s predecessor, Steve Jobs, didn’t appear on stage with him at Apple’s September event in 2011. Ternus and Cook didn’t appear together at Apple’s WWDC event in June, the last before Cook stepped down, but that doesn’t mean we won’t see Ternus and Cook next week.

Three new iPhone models are what readers expect

Half of CNET’s respondents (50%) expect three new iPhone models next week. In round two, 80% of respondents guessed Apple’s first foldable phone would appear at the fall event. We could also see the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max models make an appearance next Wednesday. Some analysts don’t expect to see a iPhone 18 base model this year. Apple could be doing a split launch where some additional models from the iPhone 18 series lineup are announced next week and others in 2027.

Guesses indicate the new foldable iPhone could cost close to $2,000

CNET readers’ guesses about the price of Apple’s foldable iPhone averaged $1,847, but analysts predict the phone will cost between $2,000 and $2,500. A TrendForce report says the foldable could cost even more, starting between $2,099 and $2,299 due to the RAM shortage and increase in hardware costs.

How much people are willing to spend on a foldable iPhone is quite different. A recent CNET survey found that US adults interested in the phone are only willing to spend an average of $781, significantly less than the expected price.

Most think a new Apple Watch Ultra 4 will be part of the fall lineup

Close to 3 in 4 (74%) contestants expect Apple to release the Apple Watch Ultra 4 on Wednesday, while 26% don’t think it will happen. Bloomberg reports we can expect new health and fitness features in Apple’s new watch, plus a faster chip. However, the design will likely remain the same. There’s also a chance Apple could unveil the Apple Watch Series 12 with a familiar design and biometric authentication.

The Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Apple Watch Series 11 were both released last September, but the Ultra 2 was released 2023, with no new model in 2024.

Readers think a foldable iPhone will be Apple’s ‘One More Thing’ moment at Surprise and Shine

Apple is full of surprises and could unveil new devices that we didn’t see coming. But CNET readers seem fairly certain that the foldable iPhone will be next week’s “One More Thing” moment.

The foldable iPhone (18%) is at the top of the list of potential surprise reveals. It’s closely followed by a new Home hub (14%), which could double as an AI-powered smart display hub that was expected earlier this year but was delayed due to Siri issues.

Some CNET readers also suspect Apple could reveal new AirPods (10%), and others expect smart glasses (8%) will likely be unveiled until later in 2027 due to rumors of “bumps” in development next year. Some readers also predict a new Apple TV (7%), which could have an upgraded processor and Apple Intelligence.

Read and watch all of CNET’s Apple event coverage next week to learn if your guesses were correct.

Tech.title: The iPhone 18 Pro Max Could Start at $1,300, an Analyst Predicts. You Can Thank RAMageddon for That
Tech.content:
We’re days away from Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event, where we expect the tech giant to unveil its first foldable iPhone (which could be called the iPhone Ultra), along with the premium models of the iPhone 18. You can expect better battery life and a variable aperture camera. But that’s not what everyone really wants.

When we asked CNET readers one thing they’d change about the iPhone in our Big Guessing Game, 16% said they want it to cost less. But that’s wishful thinking.

TrendForce, a global market research firm, released a report on Thursday suggesting you can expect higher prices instead of steep discounts. The firm expects the iPhone 18 series to cost 10 to 20% more due to the ongoing RAM shortage and higher hardware costs.

“For the 256GB Pro model, memory costs in [the third quarter of 2026] are expected to be nearly 400% higher than a year earlier,” TrendForce said. “Despite Apple’s efforts to negotiate lower prices for other components, these savings are unlikely to offset the resulting pressure on overall [materials] costs.”

Apple raised prices on select products in June due to the RAM shortage, but excluded iPhones from the price hikes. Now there’s a chance that Apple could release some iPhone 18 models with higher prices at the September event. TrendForce said it expects Apple to absorb some of the costs to keep prices for the new models as part of a “relatively moderate” pricing strategy.

So exactly how much more are we talking about? Some analysts believe the foldable iPhone Ultra could cost between $2,000 and $2,500. TrendForce predicts the starting price will be slightly higher — between $2,099 and $2,299. The phone could go up to $3,000.

As for the premium models of the iPhone 18, TrendForce expects the iPhone 18 Pro to start between $1,199 and $1,299, and $1,299 to $1,399 for the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

A TrendForce representative said in an email to CNET that even though upgrades to the processor and optical system are part of the reason for higher costs, the “sharp surge in memory component prices is indeed the single biggest factor driving this price adjustment.”

But higher costs aren’t equivalent to big improvements.

TrendForce says we shouldn’t expect major performance upgrades from Apple’s upcoming iPhone lineup. Instead, we should expect a more powerful processor for AI features and power efficiency, better chip cooling technology and power-efficient displays. And the iPhone 18 Pro models’ main camera could have a “mechanical variable aperture” to improve depth-of-field control and dynamic range for different lighting settings.

The really big upgrade is the potential release of the folding iPhone Ultra and bigger batteries for premium iPhone 18 models, TrendForce predicts. The iPhone 18 Pro Max could see the biggest upgrade due to a larger chassis. CNET’s Patrick Holland tested smartphone batteries last year and found that the iPhone 17 Pro Max was the best for battery life, so iPhone 18’s premium models could be an even bigger upgrade from the current model.

Tech.title: 9 Air Fryer Wins That Permanently Changed How I Cook Every Week
Tech.content:
My air fryer gets used every day. These nine foods are the specific reason it earned that place in my kitchen. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Years of using an air fryer almost every day taught me two things: how impressive the appliance can be at its best, and which specific foods most consistently hit that mark. The oven is still in my kitchen. It still gets used. But the category of things I’d choose the oven for over the air fryer has narrowed considerably since I started paying attention to the comparison. Nine foods drove that narrowing, dishes where the air fryer’s results were different enough from the oven’s to make the switch feel permanent rather than experimental.

When I first hauled in an air fryer many years ago, I was mostly making the classics: wings and fries. However, my air fryer repertoire has expanded to include items I never thought I’d be cooking in a small countertop contraption. I’m talking about fresh salmon, cheeseburgers and even whole roasted chicken.

The air fryer is fast, forgiving, easy to use and even easier to clean. It’s no wonder the appliance has enjoyed unparalleled popularity over the last decade — a true once-in-a-lifetime kitchen craze.

Best Air Fryers for 2026 See at CNET

So what are the most surprising foods I make in the air fryer? I’ve listed nine below, but the list grows longer every year. And if you’re searching for an air fryer or to upgrade your existing oven, we have a new favorite model with a glass cooking chamber that’s easy to clean and doubles as a food storage container.

9 foods I’ll only make in the air fryer from now on

1. Hard-‘boiled’ eggs

All you need is 10 minutes and an air fryer and you’ll never boil an egg again. Pamela Vachon/CNET

From runny yolks to jammy to hard-cooked, the air fryer can do it, and there’s no waiting for water to boil or forgetting to set a timer (air fryers have a built-in timer). There’s a lot of internet voodoo about dos and don’ts for boiling eggs in the air fryer, but in my experience, you can disregard most of it and still end up with beautifully cooked eggs with perfectly set yolks every time.

Here’s how to make “hard-boiled eggs” in the air fryer

2. Salmon (and most other fish)

Just 8 minutes in the air fryer and you have perfectly medium rare salmon. David Watsky/CNET

Broiled salmon is a simple, healthy weeknight dinner staple. It’s not difficult to make in the oven, but if you’re only cooking for one or two people, the preheating time is a pain, and you’ll waste a lot of energy for a small amount of food. Pan-seared salmon is excellent and quick, but there’s almost no way to cook salmon on the stove without creating an oily and odorous mess.

I tried cooking roasted salmon in the air fryer, and it came out perfectly in about 10 minutes, including preheating time. The closed cooking chamber captures all the grease and even helps hide some of the fishy smell from taking over the space.

OK, so you might catch me throwing the occasional filet of salmon on the grill during warmer months, but gone are the days of me wiping fish grease from the backsplash behind my kitchen stove.

Here’s how to make perfect air fryer salmon.

3. Roasted chicken

Air-fryer roasted chicken is a revelation. David Watsky/CNET

This one surprised me the most because I make roast chicken most Sundays and had grown content with my oven method. I learned quickly that the air fryer does an even better job because it crisps the skin quickly without overcooking the meat. Air-fryer roasted chicken takes about 45 minutes — about 15% quicker than the oven — and it’s nearly impossible to screw up.

Here’s how to make a quick roasted chicken in the air fryer.

4. Bacon cheeseburgers

You can cook a burger to perfect medium or medium rare with an air fryer. Pamela Vachon/CNET

Air fryer cheeseburgers have become a staple around my home. The exception is during summer when the grill is in full swing but during cooler months, I turn to the air fryer for this American classic. It’s cleaner than pan frying, but the burger doesn’t cook in its own grease, so you get a lighter, healthier meal (if you’re into that sort of thing). You can also add the bun and a couple of slices of bacon to the burger, making it a complete meal with minimal cleanup.

Here’s how to make a cheeseburger from top to bottom in the air fryer.

5. Chicken cutlets

Air fryers turn out picture-perfect chicken cutlets. David Watsky/CNET

Before the air fryer, I used to pan-fry breaded chicken cutlets for chicken Parmesan and other recipes but the air fryer does the same job with less mess and produces less oily fried chicken, too.

I recommend using boneless chicken thighs, which have enough fat to withstand convection heat without drying out. Simply coat the chicken in a beaten egg wash, followed by breadcrumbs mixed with salt, pepper, and other spices. Cook at 375°F for about 15 minutes.

You can spray the cutlets lightly with oil before cooking to achieve an extra-crispy crust, but it’s not necessary. I’ve tried the same method with chicken breasts; it works well, but there is a greater risk of drying out the meat.

Best Places to Buy Chicken Online See at CNET

6. Cauliflower steak

Cauliflower steak made in the air fryer has become a staple side dish in my kitchen. David Watsky/CNET

One of my favorite things to cook in the air fryer is cauliflower. A cauliflower slab makes an excellent, hearty side dish or main course if you’re going plant-based. Simply toss a thick slice or two of cauliflower with olive oil, salt, pepper, or your preferred seasoning, then air-fry at high heat for 10-12 minutes. The air fryer gives it a beautiful caramelized crust and it cooks the dense veggie fast enough so that the inside of the cauliflower doesn’t become mushy.

7. Leftover pizza

This leftover pizza got a whole new life thanks to a short trip to the air fryer. David Watsky/CNET

While not every type of food is best reheated in the air fryer, many are. Air fryers are the perfect way to revive leftover pizza, fried chicken, grilled meats and vegetables. A microwave heats food unevenly and tends to impart a rubbery texture. Air fryers give food a second life with convection heat, delivering a crispy crust and even heating.

Here’s the best way to reheat every type of leftover.

8. Hot dogs and sausage

You can cook an entire package of hot dogs in just a few minutes. David Watsky/CNET

It’s hard to screw up a hot dog but if you want a perfectly charred wiener in less than five minutes with essentially no cleanup, look to the air fryer. Air fryer hot dogs are as simple as they get, and the super convection oven gives them perfect browning in two or three minutes.

Here’s how to make hot dogs in the air fryer all summer.

9. Baked potatoes

Air fryer baked potatoes have crispy skin and are light and fluffy inside. Brian Bennett/CNET

OK, so technically, this one starts in the microwave and finishes in the air fryer. The microwave softens the inside in less than 8 minutes, while the air fryer blasts the edges and skin to crispy perfection. It’s a restaurant-quality baked potato in less than 12 minutes. Here’s how to make the best air-fryer baked potato ever.

And if you’re still not sure what an air fryer is and how it works, check out our complete guide to air fryers.

9. Grilled cheese

This air fryer grilled cheese is as good as it looks. Pamela Vachon/CNET

For a grilled cheese, the air fryer cooks both the bread surfaces and the cheese at once, resulting in a quicker melt. This adheres the cheese to the bread slices together, making for a much easier flip. (Flipping is still recommended but with far less drama.)

Here’s the secret to perfect air fryer grilled cheese.The air fryer’s ability to crisp, roast and even boil makes it the most versatile appliance on my counter.

Tech.title: The Right Way to Use AI for Better Grades (That Doesn’t Get You Expelled)
Tech.content:
The temptation to use an AI chatbot to do your actual work is real and understandable, and academic institutions are spending considerable energy trying to prevent it. But the energy focused on AI as a cheating tool has somewhat obscured the case for AI as a legitimate study tool, one that, used correctly, can help students understand material more deeply, prepare more effectively for exams and manage the organizational demands of coursework more efficiently than most traditional methods. Here’s how to use it in ways that improve your grades without putting your academic record at risk.

Simulate and customize tests and tutorials

Even when a guide is provided, studying for a test can prove fruitless for people who learn best in unconventional ways. Hands-on and visual learners are at a natural disadvantage to those who pick up concepts via words on a page, but AI tools like ChatGPT can take learning materials and easily translate them into tests or study guides that fit your unique learning needs.

A long collection of links or pages — the mind-numbing text wall of death — can be turned into a video, illustrated slides or flash cards using AI tools.

If you’re more comfortable studying with a partner, you could also use AI to simulate a verbal test of the materials.

Organize group work

Group assignments and presentations are academic torture for some students. The project management element of this type of school work is what a majority of my students complain about. Someone isn’t pulling their weight, or someone else is overdoing it and leaving the group out.

Students are tasked with balancing their busy schedules and are also expected to keep their peers on task, which can get super awkward and result in conflicts petty enough to rival any reality show drama.

AI tools like Taskade, an AI-infused project management app that has free and paid versions ranging between $10 and $50 per month, can reduce the stress associated with managing a group project by putting elements like deadline enforcement and division of duties into the cold, calculated, unbiased hands of a robot. No one can get pissed off at the project manager if the project manager has no feelings.

Spice up discussion posts

Discussion posts in online classes tend to deeply irk the students I’ve spoken with about what grinds their academic gears. The repetitive nature of responses is the No. 1 complaint, with students citing serious fatigue from reading the same soulless posts from other students trying to get the assignment over with as quickly as possible.

Students can use AI tools like Google’s Gemini and ChatGPT to quickly scan the current discussion posts for commonalities and find a post with a fresh take you can respond to, rather than wading through a sea of sameness.

You could also ask the AI chatbot to scan the discussions and tell you what points haven’t been brought up yet, so you can easily chime in with a unique contribution.

Adapt to your teacher’s preferences

We’ve all had teachers who like to do things their way, and any deviation from their preferred methods can result in points lost that quickly add up. I once had a professor dock points from an otherwise perfect essay because I hadn’t read his mind and discovered he preferred the course’s keywords to be highlighted and in bold.

AI can help you avoid hard-to-spot pitfalls buried deep in addenda, instructional documents and RateMyProfessors.com reviews by quickly scanning web pages and documents for any out-of-the-ordinary requirements you should keep on your radar.

Tech.title: This New Auto-Pet Feeder Is Basically an Instant Pot for Cats
Tech.content:
Automatic pet feeders aren’t new, but most are limited to dispensing dry food. Strolling a press preview ahead of IFA 2026 in Berlin, I spotted a wild new take on the handy pet parent helper, and it’s basically an Instant Pot for cats.

OK, maybe it doesn’t pressure cook, sauté and steam like most multicookers, but it does churn out fresh meals on demand for your feline friend. Like an Instant Pot, all you have to do is add two ingredients, set it and forget it.

The Best Tech, All Tested by CNET Editors See at CNET

Riko, the latest release from Neakasa, is a self-contained smart wet-food maker that prepares meals on demand (or whenever you schedule them via the app) and serves them to your cat at mealtime.

The unit, which is about the size of an average drip coffee maker, houses a compartment for freeze-dried food and a water reservoir. When activated, it rehydrates and mixes the cat food for a gourmet autonomous feeding experience.

As strange as it may sound, this one makes great sense for busy or forgetful owners of cats that prefer wet food. While it’s not advertised for dogs, we can’t see why this system wouldn’t work for small canines.

The Rika holds enough food for 7 days of meals. David Watsky/CNET

The Shenzhen-based brand is known for its self-cleaning litter boxes and automatic feeders. Until now, it didn’t have an answer for owners who feed their cats wet grub. Wet food feeders from other brands rely on refrigeration to keep preloaded meals cold until chow time, and most are limited to two or three meals. This is the first one we’ve seen that whips up your cat’s lunch in real time.

Rico retails for $200 and is available on Neakasa’s website.

Editors’ note: David Watsky’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by IFA. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.
